name: VTDigger
title: Upper Valley’s member-owned co-op battles rising food prices
text:
Gayle Giovanna, of Strafford, goes through her shopping list as she finds items in the aisles of the co-op in Hanover, N.H., on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Giovanna has been a customer of the co-op for over 40 years. Photo by Sophia Sahni/Valley News

This story by Sophia Sahni was first published by the Valley News on Oct. 30, 2026.
During the Great Depression, 17 neighbors across Hanover, New Hampshire, and Norwich combined their resources to create a collective buying group. What started in a basement as an informal way to source cases of affordable citrus and maple syrup has, 90 years later, grown into the Hanover Consumer Cooperative Society, also known as the co-op.
Now the co-op is facing a different kind of economic squeeze. Since March 2020, grocery store prices have risen by approximately 31%, according to data collected by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
“It honestly feels like it has been tough since the pandemic,” said Amanda Charland, the co-op’s CEO. “Right now the price of food has been really tough to keep up with. It’s also really tough for us to continue to try to meet our mission and our values, because we are trying to give food at the lowest prices possible while competing with megalithic companies that have these massive supply chains.”
Based in the Upper Valley, the co-op is the second-oldest and second-largest consumer grocery cooperative in the United States, according to the organization. It has three food stores, including one in Vermont, two auto service centers and one commissary kitchen.
The organization is driven by four key pillars: employees, community, local and environment. According to Charland, these pillars are the foundation of everything they do.
While many grocery stores in the Upper Valley are part of a regional or national chain, the co-op is owned by more than 35,000 members who vote on the organization’s governance and values. To become a member, one has to purchase 10 shares of stock, each costing $5. Members get access to the Co-op Rewards program and have the opportunity to get their money back if they ever choose to leave.
“We work to meet the members’ and therefore the community’s needs,” Charland said. “As we are owned by the community, there are not a bunch of shareholders who are making a profit off of the store. Everything that we get goes back into the business and the community.” 
The organization is focused on investing in the Upper Valley. About 75% of its staff work full time and are eligible for benefits. The co-op also partners with over 400 local vendors to source produce from regional farms and businesses.
Keeping up with changing prices
When it comes to competition, Charland said that “a lot of our competitors in the area can get products on the shelf cheaper than we can even buy it from our vendors.”
She is referring to slotting fees, payments that vendors can make to retailers to obtain prime shelf space for their products in a highly competitive environment.
“Because of our structure, we don’t do practices like that,” Charland said. The practice of slotting fees can affect what customers see on shelves and the products they have access to in the market. “We are not here for our vendors. We’re here for our customers,” she added.
Another hurdle for the co-op is the spike in fuel surcharges, a fee charged by freight carriers to account for changing fuel costs. As of Oct. 26, the national average for on-highway diesel reached $6.35 per gallon, a $2.63 increase from a year ago, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Lisa Thibodeau, cashier, helps customer Lindley Shutz, of Lebanon, N.H., check out at the co-op in Hanover, N.H., on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Photo by Sophia Sahni/Valley News

Charland said that growing fuel surcharges can affect the co-op’s operations tremendously, especially for products where it has already set a price. “When you receive that product the next time, it may have a higher price and it may have got a ton of fuel surcharges to it,” Charland said. “If you don’t get that price changed quickly, you’re selling at a loss.”
“But you don’t want to pass a lot of that to the consumer. It’s just hard for everybody, and shoppers are looking for lower and lower prices,” she added.
In these moments of instability, Charland said, the network of the cooperative can move into action. “Our staff knows the pressure points that our members feel and what they are asking for. We have relationships with local vendors and farmers where we can work together and come up with ways to help our community.”
In partnership with a local dairy farm, the co-op has launched an everyday low-price milk at $2.99 a gallon. Currently, the co-op is working to create a similar initiative with a local bread company.
However, the rise of fuel prices is only the tip of the iceberg. Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that in September, the annual inflation rate was 3.7%. As grocery stores operate on thin profit margins, Charland said there is very little room to cover unforeseen expenses.
According to Charland, if a dollar represents the revenue of the co-op, 70 cents goes toward the cost of the products, 25 cents goes to paying employees, and the last 5 cents goes toward everything else.
With recent increases in the cost of electricity, heating and health insurance, the co-op is struggling to pay employees fair compensation while simultaneously meeting consumers’ demands for lower prices.
“For those in the service industry, the wages are just not going up as quickly as they need to,” Charland said. “I wish we could do more, but that’s why we try to invest in a lot of benefits for our people.”
The co-op offers employees health insurance as well as a 401(k) retirement plan with a 3% employer match. In addition, through the co-op’s auto service centers in Vermont and New Hampshire, employees have access to a program providing zero-interest loans for their auto repairs.
“We have an amazing team that’s working to try to solve these problems, but I think the hardest part of the current economic situation is the rate at which these issues are happening. There are just a lot of different pressures,” Charland said.
A commitment to sustainability
Despite recent challenges, the co-op remains committed to its values and particularly its impact on the environment. For Charland, sustainability holds a special place in her heart. Before the co-op she worked for various environmental nonprofits, and when she first joined the organization 15 years ago, she began as the sustainability coordinator.
For the co-op, food waste management is a priority. Currently, the organization diverts approximately 70% of its waste from landfills through a “pyramid of food management.”
“The first step is, if it can feed people, get it to people,” Charland said. The co-op redistributes food through partnership organizations including Willing Hands, a regional food recovery organization founded by a former co-op employee.

Mary Gail Neroni, of Hanover, N.H., looks through items in the deli section at the co-op in Hanover on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Photo by Sophia Sahni/Valley News

If the food is not edible for humans, it is transferred to local pig farms. Food beyond this stage reaches the final level: composting. The co-op is striving to become a zero-waste company with a diversion rate of 90%.
Additionally, the co-op is working to increase the sustainability of its refrigeration systems. Most traditional grocery stores use refrigerants like hydrofluorocarbons, a greenhouse gas with a high global warming potential.
To make matters worse, these systems also have high refrigerant leakage rates. According to Charland, a pound of a refrigerant like this can have a warming impact equivalent to about 3,000 pounds of carbon dioxide going into the atmosphere.
In an effort to be more sustainable, the co-op is upgrading its infrastructure and reducing its refrigerant leaks. Renovations to the commissary kitchen this year included implementing a carbon dioxide refrigeration system that is more climate friendly than hydrofluorocarbon-based systems.
“CO2 refrigerants are one of the best refrigerants you can get. We hope that we can start to roll this technology out in other stores as we need to replace old systems,” Charland said.
A community built around co-op values
Grocery stores are busy places, with people and food constantly moving in and out their doors. Yet at the co-op, people come back time and time again because of the organization’s values.
Gayle Giovanna, of Strafford, has shopped at the co-op for the past 40 years. “I come back because I’d rather have the money stay here in the local economy than go off to who knows where,” Giovanna said.
Bruce Follett started as a produce department manager 27 years ago and is now the director of operations. He said he takes great pride in working at the co-op. “The staff care about one another. They care about their community, and they care about their customers,” Follett said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Upper Valley’s member-owned co-op battles rising food prices.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: With mining, remember: The people who may need the water in 50 years won’t be at the hearing
text:
Water polluted by acid rock drainage is stored on July 17, 2023, in the Anchor Hill Pit, to eventually be treated and discharged at the Gilt Edge Mine, an Environmental Protection Agency Superfund cleanup site near Lead, South Dakota. (Photo Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Rapid City residents have packed public meetings debating data centers’ enormous electricity demands and potentially significant water consumption.
Meanwhile, the proposed Dewey–Burdock uranium mine in the southwestern Black Hills is seeking permission to use groundwater to deliberately change its chemistry, potentially threatening a major underground aquifer extending beyond South Dakota’s borders.
The first controversy has attracted considerable public attention, and the second deserves at least as much.
Dewey-Burdock isn’t the only uranium proposal in the vicinity of Edgemont. Another company is pursuing exploratory drilling near Craven Canyon.
South Dakota’s Water Management Board is preparing to consider two water permits for Dewey-Burdock. The state’s chief water rights engineer recommends approving both, partly because of his determination that the project meets the legal definition of a “beneficial use” of water.
Whether the project truly lives up to the beneficial use standard is an open question.
Public comment period opens as company seeks state permits for uranium mine

Dewey-Burdock would use in-situ recovery. Instead of excavating a large open pit, the company would circulate groundwater containing oxygen and carbon dioxide through uranium-bearing sandstone underground.
The altered chemistry dissolves uranium, allowing it to be pumped for processing. Most water would be recirculated, but the process could mobilize naturally occurring contaminants, including radium, arsenic and selenium.
The company proposes to contain the altered water through pumping and pressure controls. Federal permits require monitoring and safeguards.
But what happens when the pumps stop?
The Black Hills Clean Water Alliance and tribal opponents have raised questions about geological faults, fractures and thousands of prior exploration boreholes that could connect aquifers. Groundwater in the uranium-bearing aquifer generally moves southwest toward Wyoming. If contaminated water escapes containment, it could travel beyond the mining area.
Federal regulators maintain that testing and controls can protect groundwater. Opponents question whether the underground geology is sufficiently understood.
The difficulty of restoring groundwater isn’t just speculation by environmental opponents.
The U.S. Geological Survey examined historical restoration records at in-situ uranium mines in Texas. In a subsequent technical review, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that all 22 production areas studied still had at least some water-quality measurements exceeding their original baseline levels after restoration.
That doesn’t mean all 22 aquifers were rendered unusable. But it raises a serious question about what restoration actually accomplishes.
If a mining company is unable to restore water as its permit proposed, it can ask the state to lower the standard. In other words, an aquifer could be declared restored without returning to its original condition.
That’s a definition of “restored” worth thinking about.
South Dakota law defines “beneficial use” as water use that is reasonable and useful to the applicant while also being consistent with the public’s interest in the best utilization of water supplies.
It’s the second half that matters.
Uranium has considerable value. Nuclear power provides reliable electricity without burning fossil fuels, and domestic uranium production can strengthen energy security.
There’s money involved, too.
The company’s own economic assessment projects $70.6 million in state severance, sales and conservation taxes and local property taxes over the mine’s life. That’s enough to get attention from legislators and county commissioners.
Government has a curious relationship with economic development. It welcomes the jobs, celebrates the investment and anticipates the tax collections. Governors attend ribbon cuttings. Nobody shows up to celebrate an aquifer that remains uncontaminated.
Mining’s economic benefits can be calculated and tax money spent. The value of an aquifer that remains clean for future generations is harder to calculate. And the people who may depend on that water 50 years from now won’t have a seat at the hearing.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
We’ve seen things go badly before. At the Gilt Edge gold mine near Lead, Brohm Mining went bankrupt in 1999, leaving 150 million gallons of acidic, heavy-metal-contaminated water. The resulting cleanup has cost well over $100 million.
Near Ellsworth Air Force Base, PFAS contamination has affected private drinking-water wells, requiring millions in federal spending to provide replacement water supplies. The full cost of that contamination is unknown.
Neither situation involved in-situ uranium mining. But both demonstrate that environmental consequences can leave the public with costs that weren’t anticipated when those activities began.
The Water Management Board doesn’t regulate every environmental consequence of uranium mining. EPA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and state mining regulators have those responsibilities.
The Board must determine whether water is available, existing rights are protected, the use is beneficial and the appropriation serves the public interest within its authority. If the evidence is insufficient, state law allows the board to deny applications or defer a decision for further study.
That’s not hostility toward mining. It recognizes that a natural resource can be valuable for reasons that never appear in a tax projection.
We spend considerable time discussing what valuable minerals might be beneath South Dakota. Perhaps we should devote just as much attention to what we’re willing to leave there.
Uranium can be mined once. Groundwater may be needed forever.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Art isn’t a luxury. It’s what helped me through my hardest times.
text:
The House Lounge on the third floor of the Missouri Capitol, home of Thomas Hart Benton's mural "The Social History of Missouri" (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).The bronze bust of John Brown by Kansas sculptor Jim Brothers has the passion and movement of any Hellenistic masterpiece. Louis Copt’s painting of the Fox Creek Schoolhouse on the Kansas Tallgrass Prairie rivals the great Dutch master Johannes Vermeer’s “View of Delft.” The work of these fellow Midwesterners fires my imagination, inspires me, compels me to work harder, and pushes me to be a better teacher and writer.
Art is a catalyst in my life. It urges me from bed in the wee hours to plan a better way to convey some difficult concept to my students. It drives me to write, even when the words don’t come easily. Visual, literary, and musical art have pushed me to work and achieve my entire life. This has been especially true during the most trying times.
In the late ‘80s, fresh out of college, I started my first “real” job at an accounting firm, Laventhol & Horwath, in Philadelphia. Little did I know the firm was in dire straits. After eleven months I was laid off, and two months later the firm declared bankruptcy.
I was abruptly out of a job and unsure how I’d make rent. But I didn’t want friends or family to worry, so I kept my unemployment a secret.
In the morning, I dressed in a business suit like nothing was wrong and commuted to the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where I found solace. I absorbed the tranquility of the Japanese teahouse, and the sheer age of the medieval cloister put my short-term problems in perspective.
I sat with the work of great American painters. Among Thomas Eakins, Henry Ossawa Tanner, William Harnett, Charles Wilson Peale and others, I chose my next path. Their work renewed me, giving me the strength to carry on, the courage to decline opportunities in the corporate world, and the confidence to choose a more difficult road.
Soon I found a job at the University of Pennsylvania. My objective was to go back to school, and I knew the job provided tuition benefits. At Penn, once again, I found art to be my chief motivator. The fine arts library was designed in the nineteenth century by the great American architect Frank Furness. His masterpiece inspired me to keep going.
Every time the pressures of full-time work and graduate school made me want to drop out, I went to Furness’ library. I’d study in the main reading room for hours, and when fatigue set in, I needed only to look up at the vaulted ceiling, the strange American mix of Gothic and Romanesque influences, the terra-cotta, the leaded-glass windows ringed with maxims of encouragement and aphorisms like “Talkers are no great doers.”
Then I’d return to my books, sometimes studying through the night.
That inspiration helped carry me through my studies and eventually to graduate school at the University of Kansas.
Art drives us through adversity. It is the stimulus package we need in hard times. My own experience taught me that art can provide comfort, perspective and inspiration when we need them most. And that is why access to art matters.
Too many American political leaders think they’re projecting pragmatism when they treat art as an amenity, a luxury that we can indulge in only when times are good.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe cut state arts funding, while President Donald Trump’s administration has pursued cuts to federal arts and humanities programs. These decisions treat art as expendable, ignoring the role it plays in education, community life and individual well-being.
I know what art gave me when I was struggling. And I know I am hardly alone. Cutting support for the arts means fewer opportunities for others to find that same inspiration, particularly in communities where access is already limited.
Art is more than a luxury. It is a necessity, especially in difficult times. A society that values education, creativity and freedom should recognize that supporting the arts is not an indulgence. It is an investment in all three.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: From floods to wildfires, Nebraska knows what extremes cost
text:
An aerial view of wildfire damage in western Nebraska in mid-March 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Nebraska Governor's Office)When the Platte and Missouri rivers surged in March 2019, they didn’t just spill over their banks — they washed out bridges, drowned livestock and submerged one-third of Offutt Air Force Base. Floodwaters covered part of the runway and wrecked high-tech flight simulators, triggering an estimated $650 million military rebuild at the time and leaving an estimated $1.3 billion in preliminary statewide losses in its wake.
Then came the fires. After the state’s second-warmest and fourth-driest winter on record, wind-driven grass fires erupted across the Sandhills and central Nebraska in March 2026. The Morrill Fire burned more than 643,000 acres, the largest wildfire in state history, and the outbreak scorched over 800,000 acres in about a week. One person died, more than 35,000 cattle were displaced, and ranchers lost grazing land, hay and miles of fence that can cost up to $15,000 a mile to replace. The toll reaches household budgets, too. Nebraska homeowners already pay some of the nation’s highest insurance premiums, up about 20% since 2023 as hail, wind and rebuilding costs climb, and wildfire adds another risk to price.
Nebraskans have always weathered tough conditions, but research from the Nebraska State Climate Office indicates these risks are rising. Its projections show our region faces more damaging downpours alongside hotter dry spells that can sap soil moisture when crops need it most. These extremes aren’t distant worries for decades down the road — they carry immediate consequences for family farms, household budgets and local taxpayers.
Managing these swings requires a complete playbook: strong defense to protect what we have, and smart offense to keep things from getting worse. Resilience means proactively fortifying our infrastructure, water supplies and working lands so communities can withstand the next shock. But even the best defense eventually gets overwhelmed. Lasting security also demands going on offense — taking practical steps to cut the emissions driving these extremes before they outpace our ability to adapt.
The good news is that Nebraska doesn’t have to choose between protecting against weather extremes and strengthening its economy. Homegrown solutions are already proving that stewardship pays dividends.
On working farms, replacing diesel irrigation engines with electric motors can cut fuel and maintenance bills while clearing the air. Smarter soil stewardship can act like a natural sponge — holding vital moisture during flash droughts and absorbing downpours before they wash topsoil away. To help scale up these opportunities, Nebraska secured a $307 million federal grant — the largest in the state environment department’s history — to develop its ONE RED climate program (Opportunity for Nebraska: Reducing Emissions and Decarbonization), which includes planned rebates for electric irrigation engines, biochar and biogas as final federal approvals are completed.
In our energy sector, Nebraska holds a unique advantage as the nation’s only 100% public-power state. Because Nebraskans own their utilities, public power districts like OPPD can plan directly for our communities’ long-term interests — expanding wind, solar and battery storage to meet surging demand while working to keep the grid dependable through freezing winters and scorching summers.
None of this progress happens by accident. It requires leadership with the foresight to invest before the next crisis hits. In Nebraska, with federal, state and local candidates up for election — voters hold the steering wheel.
Before casting ballots this fall, we should ask every candidate:

How will you strengthen our infrastructure, farms, and military installations against flooding, drought, and wildfires? 
What concrete steps will you take to support agricultural solutions — like planned electric irrigation rebates and soil-health practices — that can cut costs for producers while reducing emissions?
How will you guide public power to expand clean energy while preserving reliability and keeping electric rates affordable?

Nebraskans built the Good Life by meeting hard realities with grit, ingenuity and common sense. When our rivers rise or our fields run dry, we don’t look away. We can prepare for the weather risks at our doorstep — and elect leaders ready to protect Nebraska’s future.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska’s projected deficit for 2028-29 budget worsens to $1.2 billion
text:
Former State Treasurer Tom Briese, a former state senator who is also one of the newest members of the the Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board, during a board meeting at the Nebraska State Capitol on Oct. 30, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska lawmakers will likely enter the 2027 session looking to fill a projected budget deficit around $200 million, but a larger problem emerged for the next two-year budget after new economic forecasts dropped Friday.
Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board met Friday to update state revenue projections for the ongoing budget cycle and make new predictions for the next biennium. Their predictions kept the current projected deficit flat, but lowered expected revenues in the next cycle by about $355 million, according to legislative fiscal analyst Keisha Patent.
Before Friday, Nebraska’s projected budget deficit stood at $208 million by the end of the current budget period ending June 30, 2027, and $846 million at the end of the next biennium.
The board projected revenues would increase by about $23 million by the end of fiscal year 2027. However, Patent said, those additional dollars will automatically go into the state’s cash reserve under existing law.
The Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board meets at the Nebraska State Capitol on Oct. 30, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Projections for the next biennium spanning fiscal years 2028 and 2029 told a different story, lowering expected revenues by about $355 million, according to Patent’s estimates. This would bring the projected deficit for Nebraska’s next budget to about $1.2 billion.
These are not the final numbers lawmakers will be working with come January. Patent said the projections will change again after the next Tax Rate Review Committee meeting in November, and the forecasting board will have another chance to update their projections in February.
This puts 2027 on track to be the third consecutive legislative session to deal with a projected deficit.
State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, the term-limited chair of the Appropriations Committee, said the board’s projections for the next biennium were more extreme than he expected. However, he anticipates that Gov. Jim Pillen’s ongoing initiative to cut state spending will aid the budget-balancing effort.
“It’s still going to be a belt-tightening year,” Clements said.
In a press release, Pillen estimated the latest forecast means that lawmakers have to find about $393 million each year for the next three years to balance the budget. He said accomplishing this will require “tough decisions” and continued advocating for his plan to shrink government.
“The foundations of Nebraska’s economy are stable and resilient,” Pillen said. “We must have the courage to reduce the size of government instead of growing it. Just like ordinary Nebraskans, state government must live within its means.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In September, Pillen drew criticism over two new appointments he made to the board — former state Sens. Tom Briese of Albion and Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn. Both were key allies who helped pass several of Pillen’s tax proposals. Pillen elevated Briese to state treasurer in 2023, a position he held for two years, and appointed both Briese and Linehan to the new School Financing Review Commission last year.
Clements said he doubted that the board’s new members had any impact on the latest projections. State Sen. Brad von Gillern of the Elkhorn area, chair of the Revenue Committee, agreed and said Friday’s meeting was conducted the same as previous meetings he has attended.
Though she acknowledged she was a Pillen ally, Linehan attributed the suspicions to the proximity of the midterm elections, and claimed people were “making things up that aren’t true.”
“Who else would you appoint?” Linehan said. “It’s just a silly season.”
Most of the forecasting board referred to the growing development of data centers as one of the biggest factors impacting Nebraska’s economy, but members had different takes on it.
Board member Steve Seline said data centers are good for contributing to property tax revenues, but they also drag capital away from other industries.
Richard McGinnis, who chairs the forecasting board, said the amount of money being invested into data centers could provide an incredible economic development opportunity for Nebraska communities.
The board also had differing opinions on Nebraska’s agricultural economy. Board member Tim Wilson said he was less optimistic than other members, saying he expected Nebraska cattle feeders to lose money this year.
Briese said although there are challenges facing Nebraska farmers and ranchers, he believes there are also plenty of positive factors on the way. He pointed to oil-generated inflation — largely driven by the Iran war — being a good sign for ag, and he predicted the ongoing beef shortage would continue to raise prices on beef.
“Ag has plenty of headwinds, but there are some tailwinds out there as well,” Briese said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Gubernatorial candidates make final pitch to voters ahead of Tuesday’s election
text:
Hannah Pingree campaigns in Portland with Planned Parenthood on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)On the final day of early voting, Hannah Pingree campaigned in Portland with President and CEO of Planned Parenthood Alexis McGill Johnson to remind voters that their reproductive rights are on the ballot. In Kittery, Rick Bennett wrapped up his walking tour that he started in Fort Kent several months ago. And Bobby Charles held a forum in Auburn, inviting people who disagreed with him — including “Gen Z liberals” and “Somali immigrants” — to debate at the Auburn mall.
Their different approaches to the final few days of the election reflect each of the candidates’ campaigning styles: Bennett has focused on meeting voters where they’re at, Pingree has highlighted her prominent endorsements, and Charles has gone on the offensive.
“Bobby is holding a forum where he’s actually asking people to come argue with him,” Pingree, the Democratic nominee, said at her event Thursday. “I think now, five days before the election, this election is about how we actually come together to envision something better for Maine’s future.”
Pingree has raised more money than both of her opponents combined. According to most recent reports filed with the Maine Ethics Commission, the Democrat raised more than $4.9 million. Charles has raised just over $2 million, and Bennett has raised slightly below a million dollars.
Pingree is also considered the frontrunner in the race, having led consistently in the polls. In a mock election held across the state with more than 12,000 students across 115 participating schools, she won with 41.8% of votes. Charles came in second with 30.4% and Bennett got 24.4% of the student vote, overperforming in comparison with the polls, which have put him between 8 and 11%.
Dueling events
On a stage in the middle of the Auburn mall, Charles debated willing participants. A mother concerned about reproductive rights. A low-income high school student worried about affording higher education. A Black woman asking how she can trust him to stand up to racism. 
About 50 people filtering in and out Thursday evening to observe the conversations, a campaign event aimed at connecting with voters who disagree with the Republican gubernatorial nominee, though many in the audience were his supporters. 
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles speakers with high schooler Ricky Whitmore in the Auburn Mall on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Ricky Whitmore, a high school senior from Turner, who has been canvassing for the Democratic Party, asked Charles if he would commit to keeping the state’s free community college program intact. 
Charles said he’d want to adjust it, mentioning his disagreement with how people who recently moved to Maine can participate. Charles told Whitmore he wanted to “fortify” him in knowing that his commitment to education “is about as high as it gets.” When Whitmore asked again for a clear answer, Charles said his “instinct is that everything that’s working about the program stays in place,” before adding, “There’s an awful lot of the state that presents itself as working, but it’s not working.”
Afterward, Whitmore told Maine Morning Star that he felt Charles danced around the topic. Charles had mentioned that he came from a low-income family like Whitmore. But Whitmore said he sees the free community college program “as an integral piece of how low-income families get their kids to college.”
Emily Angela, a 29-year-old content creator from Lewiston, told Charles she’s faced a lot of racism as a Black woman living in Maine, a predominantly white state. 
“I think the biggest thing for me is having trust in who I vote for,” she said. “How can I be confident that you will stand up for racism?”
Charles has faced criticism from his opponents, elected officials and civil rights groups for statements and social media posts they’ve condemned as racist, specifically targeting the Somali-American community. In his response Thursday night, Charles said, “we ought to be measuring ourselves by how we treat each other… You deserve a governor who isn’t just full of words, but lives this idea. And I have lived this idea all my life.” 
Emily Angela told Maine Morning Star after that she likely still would not vote for Charles but respected his answer. 
“I do respect that he said in front of a crowd of people that he would have my back and the back of people of color, but I want to see action,” she said. “If he’s elected governor, is that going to happen?”
Planned Parenthood Executive Director and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson in Portland campaigning for Hannah Pingree (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
A focus on reproductive rights
She, Whitmore and others shared personal stories to frame their questions to Charles. That was also the case for Margaret Rinaldi, 35 of Wales, who said she had two miscarriages and asked what he would do to protect reproductive rights if elected. In ads, Charles has called abortion “abhorrent” but on Thursday he reiterated his stance from recent debates: he opposes late-term abortion but thinks it should be allowed if the mother’s life is in jeopardy or in cases of rape or incest. 
His record on the issue has come up throughout his campaign, notably when his sister cited his opposition to abortion as part of the reason she backed Pingree.  
At Pingree’s press conference, she said she would want to ask Charles to justify his statement that the issue of abortion “does not matter,” referring to a comment he made during debates.
McGill Johnson and Planned Parenthood of Northern New England CEO Nicole Clegg — who also heads the organization’s political action committee in Maine — also criticized the Republican nominee Thursday for his previous comments about reproductive rights. These also included alleging during an interview with Maine Newsroom in September that he could talk pregnant women out of having  an abortions.
“Maybe instead of inviting women into his office to tell them what they should do when they are pregnant and inserting himself into (their) deeply personal and private decisions, Bobby Charles should spend a little less time talking and a lot more time listening,” Clegg said.
“Because if we listen to them, reproductive freedom isn’t an abstract political issue. It’s about decisions about our bodies, our families, and our future.”
Pingree contrasted that with her own record of supporting reproductive freedom, and promised to enshrine abortion rights in the Maine Constitution if elected, “so we never have to again depend on who’s in the White House or the governor’s office.”
McGill Johnson said Maine’s next governor will be essential in continuing to build on the protections for reproductive freedom Gov. Janet Mills’ administration put into place after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v Wade in June 2022, including ensuring abortion remains legal in the state, making sure that insurance covers it, and protecting abortion patients and providers from out-of-state prosecutors.
“Even when we win majorities for reproductive freedom in Congress … Donald Trump will be in the White House for two more years,” McGill Johnson said. “That’s why this election is so important. Governors are the best defense against his cruelty.”
Indepedent gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett at his walking tour in Kittery on Thursday. (Courtesy of Bennett campaign)
The press conference was also intended to encourage people to vote, particularly first time voters. Pingree said many elections in Maine, particularly for local office, are decided by a handful of votes, making it essential for everyone to show up at the polls this year. Already, more than 273,984 Mainers have voted early, according to the University of Florida Election Lab national tracker. 
University of Southern Maine student Reese Achorn voted for the first time in this year’s Democratic primaries, after she got an internship that required her to watch all the gubernatorial primary debates and said that Pingree stood out to her among the field.
On Thursday, she told the attendees, “I know a lot of us feel like our vote doesn’t really count, but believe me when I tell you, it truly does.”
“However, the people who want to take away our rights are hoping we stay home, making it our job to prove them wrong,” Achorn added.
Meanwhile, Bennett wrapped up his walking tour of more than 40 stops across the state, which his campaign said has allowed the independent candidate to meet voters in their communities. Over the past few months, several campaign videos have shown him meeting Mainers in local businesses and in their neighborhoods, asking them what they love about their home state.
“I’m running for governor because Maine needs a different kind of leadership,” he told supporters at a town hall in Brunswick earlier this month. “A leadership that’s centered on integrity, not ideology, and a leadership that actually unites us for a change around our many shared values and a leadership with a relentless focus on actually getting things done.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Early voting, mail-in ballots in Maryland likely to top 1 million before Election Day
text:
Dozens of Prince George's County voters stand in line and cast their ballots on the last day of early voting Thursday inside Upper Marlboro Community Center. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Record numbers of voters in a gubernatorial election year turned out for early voting over the last week, with early voting and mail-in ballots likely to top 1 million before Election Day, according to the latest  data from the Maryland State Board of Elections.
A total of 604,396 voters cast ballots in person during the eight days of early voting that started Oct. 22 and ended Thursday, with a record-breaking 124,189 on the final day. Additionally, local election officials had received 357,650 mail-in ballots as of Thursday, with nearly 300,000 more that had been mailed out but had yet to be returned.
By comparison, a total of 1.5 million people voted in Maryland’s last gubernatorial election, in 2022, and most of them turned out on Election Day.
State Elections Administrator Jared DeMarnis said in a social media post Friday that more than 124,000 voters cast ballots Thursday, which represented “a record breaking last day of early voting” in a gubernatorial election year. DeMarinis added more than 7,300 voters did same-day registration during the early voting period.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Maryland turnout reflected a national surge in early voting, with more than 46 million having already cast ballots through Friday by some estimates. It came despite the fact that Maryland does not feature a marquee race as some other states do, as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of Congress.
“I think we’re looking at the top of the numbers, but I think we’re looking at some real turnout better than we’ve seen in quite a few elections,” Nikki Tyree, executive director of Maryland’s League of Women Voters, said Friday.
“It also looks like voter turnout is skyrocketed across the country as well, so that tells us that voters are really paying attention and super engaged in what’s happening,” she said.
According to unofficial early voting figures, Talbot County had the highest percentage of voter turnout at about 24% of the county’s nearly 29,000 eligible voters casting ballots in an early voting center over the past week. The Eastern Shore jurisdiction was the only one to exceed 20% of voters to cast ballots early.
Two other counties came close in early voting, with 19.3% of Queen Anne County’s 41,730 registered voters turning out and just under 19.2% of the eligible 70,346 voters in Calvert County voting.
Tyree attributes some of the voter turnout to a response to what’s happening on the federal level with the Trump administration, including aggressive immigration enforcement and constant filing and threats of lawsuits.
“Some of the voters we’ve talked to honestly, they’re just sick of the scare tactics [and] the fear mongering,” she said. “People are tired of trying to be scared into being quiet, I think that is what’s really driving some of this.”
Voters have questions on Question 3, the congressional redistricting amendment

In addition to electing a governor and all eight members of the state’s U.S. House delegation, the biggest issue on most voters’ ballots this fall is Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment that would remove many of the restrictions on how the state draws congressional boundaries.
Tyree called Question 3 “confusion to voters.” After she and others with the league explain what the question means to voters who ask, she said many pause. Some don’t realize the question affects congressional redistricting and would likely end up targeting the 1st District, the Eastern Shore district held by Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st), the only GOP member of the state’s congressional delegation.
“A lot of them [voters] are grappling with this idea of they don’t like what’s happening across the country, but at the same time, we only have the one seat,” Tyree said. “So, I think a lot of people, just in their hearts or heads or souls, are just looking at it as like, ‘But would we be disenfranchising these people and does that make us better than anyone else?’”
She continued: “I can’t tell you how to vote. I can just tell you what this vote would do. I don’t know if there’s many other ballot measures that have been presented to Marylanders where we’re asking them preemptively respond to something that is happening across the country.”
Early voting ended Thursday, but polling places will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. statewide on Tuesday, Election Day.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Thank goodness President Trump will return to Kansas. Now he can check out all our hot GOP men!
text:
From left, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt attend a Topeka rally featuring Vice President JD Vance on Oct. 26, 2026, in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)We know that President Donald Trump appreciates the finer points of a masculine physique.
He’s told rally audiences repeatedly in recent weeks about the primo posteriors of Republicans running for office. He’s praised their good looks, straight from “central casting.”
“I looked at his ass and then I looked at his legs,” Trump said of U.S. Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio. “I said his ass — it’s like a pile of muscle.”
“Rick Jackson’s a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy,” he opined about the Florida gubernatorial candidate. 
I was concerned when news came Thursday that Trump had canceled a Saturday rally in Salina. Think of all the missed opportunities to ogle the glorious glutes of Kansas candidates! Surely they had good looks to spare.
But my worries were assuaged when Trump reconsidered and decided to visit Kansas on Sunday instead. Hopefully, we can hear his tributes to the macho men of the Sunflower State’s GOP. Allow me to offer a few pointers. As a gay man, I obviously have opinions about the attractiveness of various menfolk, but I have made a practice of keeping such opinions to myself.
The president has shown me a new way. (And thanks to photographer Thad Allton for capturing these stunning shots of top Republicans at Vice President JD Vance’s recent Topeka appearance.)
 
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall points into the crowd at an Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
Look at this silver fox! U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall has a beautifully blended mane, mixing light and dark shades. Move lower on his face and you’ll glimpse blindingly white choppers. Some might say they’re a bit too much, but just as Marshall took a bite out of all the low-income Kansans he sued for not paying their medical bills, he’ll take a bite out of liberal priorities in Washington, D.C.
You might want to watch for his skin tone, though. In a recent Fox News appearance, Marshall appeared to be emulating the president’s pumpkin-hued face. We all know how attractive that is, of course, but we don’t want Marshall to just be a copycat.
 
U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt raises his arms in enthusiasm at the Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
What a meaty mountain of a man!
U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt‘s campaign website declares that he’s “standing tall for Kansans,” and the towering 2nd District congressman has the height to spare. Schmidt served three terms as Kansas attorney general, but he fell short in challenging Gov. Laura Kelly’s reelection bid four years ago. No worries — the prettiest face doesn’t always win in the popularity contest.
Schmidt faces a surprisingly competitive race this year from Democrat Don Coover, but perhaps he has the standing to persuade voters.
 
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach gestures to the crowd at the Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
Just look at that jawline! Kris Kobach might have lost his bid for U.S. Senate against Marshall back in 2020. He might have lost his bid for the Kansas governor’s race against Kelly back in 2018. But he hasn’t lost his bid for the squarest face of any Kansas politician.
If any single Kansas Republican could be described as being built out of LEGO bricks, that politician is Kris Kobach. Those sharp edges complement his sharp approach to immigration and crime. They don’t necessarily reflect the sharpest legal mind, though.
He also really likes guns, so look for his pin-up calendar any day now.
 
Kansas gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson speaks at the Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
We’ve saved the dreamiest for last.
Republican Senate President Ty Masterson is a vision of well-oiled brilliance. First off, look at that pompadour. It’s a pompadour that says: “It doesn’t matter how much I do at my Wichita State University ‘GoCreate’ director job, my style sense gets me through.”
Second, look at that snazzy suit. Always well-tailored, Masterson has been a vision on two legs at the Kansas Statehouse for years. If the polling is to be believed, he might soon bring that incendiary hotness to Cedar Crest.
I kid, of course.
Trump, 80, may enjoy verbally caressing the highs and lows of younger candidates’ bodies (as well as the derriere of Trinidad-born rapper Nicki Minaj). Kansas has been blessed with a bountiful harvest of buff hopefuls. But does any of that really serve our cities and towns and farms? Do external qualities represent who’s best to guide us all into the future?
I think we all know the answer.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Maryland Matters
title: Frederick GOP wants investigation of Baltimore campaign consultant
text:
Frederick County Republicans are asking state election officials to investigate a high-profile Maryland political fundraiser who they say violated state laws barring coordination between a super PAC and a candidate. (File photo by Danielle Gaines/Maryland Matters)Frederick Republicans say a high-profile Maryland political fundraiser violated state laws barring coordination between candidates and a super PAC.
The complaint, filed this week with the state Board of Elections by the Frederick County Republican Party, alleges that Baltimore-based consultant Sophia Silbergeld was paid last fall to work on a fundraising effort for Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater, a Democrat.
Silbergeld now serves as treasurer of United Frederick, a political action committee that had spent nearly $500,000 as of Friday on mailings and online advertising attacking Jeff Holtzinger, Fitzwater’s Republican opponent for county executive. That constitutes an illegal coordination of campaigns, the Republicans charge.
“A consultant cannot work for a candidate and also run the Super PAC supporting that candidate,” said a statement from Justin Wages, chairman of the Frederick County Republican Central Committee.
“The law presumes coordination in exactly this situation,” the statement said. “Voters deserve to know whether it happened, and whether the people spending … to influence this election are legally separate from the campaign.”
The two events occurred within the state’s 18-month exclusion window meant to prevent coordination between candidates and independent groups.
Lierman seeks another term, Dunn just wants an ear in subdued comptroller’s race

“None of these facts alone proves coordination,” the county Republicans said in their statement. “Together, they raise questions the Board should answer. The Committee has filed a complaint with the Board asking it to investigate.”
Silbergeld is president of Baltimore-based Adeo Advocacy’s political division, which counts a number of high-profile clients, including Comptroller Brooke Lierman and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). She said Fitzwater “is not a client,” but declined to speak about the complaint.
She said she has not yet received a copy or formal inquiry from state elections officials. “When I receive a complaint, I plan to respond to it,” Silbergeld said.
In a statement, the Fitzwater campaign said Adeo Advocacy was hired “to manage a standalone event” roughly nine months before the formation of United Frederick. The campaign said Adeo had no access to “proprietary information.” Adeo has not worked for Fitzwater since, according to campaign and state records.
“The campaign does not coordinate or communicate with PACs such as United Frederick,” the campaign said.
The Republican complaint is the latest twist in a Frederick County executive race that appears tighter than expected.
Silbergeld’s website links to a Baltimore Banner story listing Fitzwater as a client, but in comments to the Frederick News-Post she said the reference in the Banner was an error. She said she organized a single campaign event for Fitzwater at the behest of David Trone, the former congressman and a Fitzwater supporter.
Trone is one of three donors who has helped pump $550,000 into the United Frederick PAC, along with the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees and the Maryland State Education Association.
Reports filed in January by the Fitzwater campaign show a $5,000 payment in November 2025 to Paul Fulcher as a reimbursement for fundraising expenses. Fulcher is the treasurer for the Fitzwater campaign.
The payment notes Silbergeld’s firm as the ultimate recipient of the payment. Maryland Matters asked the campaign how it reported the payment and was told Fulcher was reimbursed after he “used his personal credit card to pay” Silbergeld.
Maryland has one of the toughest independent expenditure laws in the country, requiring an 18-month separation period to ensure consultants and staffers are not enabling coordination between a candidate and super PAC activities.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
So-called independent expenditure groups can raise and spend almost unlimited amounts. Maryland law sets 48-hour reporting deadlines to provide transparency. Other provisions are meant to ensure candidates and those outside entities are not coordinating.
“The whole point of this law is to protect the political process,” said Jared DeMarinis, state election director.“We want to make sure that when we say that they’re independent, they truly are independent from the candidate.”
DeMarinis said the law is an attempt to balance concerns about the flood of money in campaigns with constitutionally protected political speech.
“What you can protect is the integrity,” he said. “Maryland has taken a very hard line in saying, when we say independent spending, you are independent and you will be spending this money without coordination or without any sort of consultation with a benefiting candidate.”
DeMarinis confirmed receipt of the Republican complaint. He declined to discuss any specifics.
Complaints related to campaign coordination are rare. The one involving Silbergeld is just the second. Elections officials were also asked to issue a “declaratory ruling” for a Republican consultant looking to ensure they were not violating the law.
Violations of election law related to coordination are considered misdemeanors. The accused carries the burden of proving they are false.
One way to do that is to show there was a firewall between the “insider information” and the consultant.
DeMarinis said it is possible for candidates and independent expenditure groups to have shared vendors — even consultants — “as long as there is a firewall established restricting the sharing of strategic campaign information between those individuals.”
The Republicans, in their letter to state elections official, acknowledge the possibility of a firewall or a declaratory ruling from elections officials sanctioning the shared vendor.
“We have seen no indication that ether exists,” they said in their letter.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Bill Clinton tells Tupelo crowd Scott Colom will put Mississippi, not MAGA, first
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
TUPELO — Former President Bill Clinton campaigned for Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom on Friday, casting Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as out of touch with Mississippians struggling with surging consumer prices and lack of healthcare.
Clinton, joined by longtime adviser James Carville, argued that Colom, a district attorney in northern Mississippi, would work across party lines and put “Mississippi first,” while accusing Hyde-Smith of putting President Donald Trump first and rubber-stamping his agenda.
“I’m supporting Scott because he will honestly give you his opinion, and if you disagree, he’ll have a conversation with you. And if you can change his mind, he’ll change his mind,” Clinton said. “You can’t put MAGA first. You have to put Mississippi first.”

The crowd of roughly 400 people broke out with chants of “We want Scott” and “If we vote, we win,” mirroring other Colom rallies in Columbus and Biloxi. 
Colom’s campaign has drawn national attention to Mississippi, prompting pundits to ask whether a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 could flip to blue. 
Former President Bill Clinton speaks to a crowd of Scott Colom supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayFormer President Bill Clinton speaks to a crowd of Scott Colom supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayFormer President Bill Clinton greets the crowd in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayDesoto county residents Kelly Jacobs, left, and Betty Sheffield-Fargo, right, hold signs welcoming former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026.Democratic candidate for US Senate Scott Colom speaks to a crowd of supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodaySupporters stand in line before a Scott Colom rally featuring former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodaySupporters stand in line before a Scott Colom rally featuring former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayFormer President Bill Clinton speaks to a crowd of Scott Colom supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
If elected, Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction and the first elected by popular vote, in a state with a history of some of the nation’s most brutal racial violence.
The former president panned a Hyde-Smith interview on WLOX, where she said “you know, you have so many proteins to choose from” when asked about high beef prices. 
Clinton said that was “a shopping tip, not a policy.” 
“I don’t believe we need a senator to explain the existence of chicken,” Clinton said. 
Larry Lambert, a Booneville resident, stands in line for a Scott Colom rally featuring former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Colom has repeatedly hammered Hyde-Smith for supporting Trump’s tariffs because he believes they’ve hurt farmers in Mississippi, a state where agriculture is the top industry. Clinton also criticized tariffs and gave a nod to how much they’ve impacted the furniture manufacturing industry in Tupelo. 
“Because you make so much furniture, you not only pay more for the food, you pay more to sit down at the table and eat it,” Clinton said. 
Clinton said Mississippians are smart enough to decide what the government should spend money on, contrasting affordable health care with Trump’s Rose Garden renovation at the White House, which he said looks like ‘the entrance to Liberace’s bedroom.” 
Hyde-Smith’s campaign has tried to use the steady string of national politicians such as Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg stumping for Colom as a liability, and label him as part of the far-left faction of the Democratic Party. 
If Colom were to pull off an upset in ruby-red Mississippi, it would be a stunning defeat for President Donald Trump in the Deep South and make the incumbent Republican a casualty of the president’s sinking popularity. 
Colom’s campaign has homed in on issues of affordability, access to health care and a rejection of Trump’s tariffs in the home stretch of his campaign. He has pledged to tackle the cuts to Medicaid that the Republican-majority Congress passed as part of the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill. 
At a Thursday night Jackson rally alongside U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, Colom said his pitch to Republicans who may be on the fence about his campaign is to deliver what Trump originally promised to deliver for them in 2024. 
“They were promised lower grocery prices. That’s what I’m going to fight for,” Colom said. “That’s my message to them. I’m going to give you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised no more endless wars. I’m going to give you no more endless wars.”
Colom told reporters he wants to end partisan gerrymandering by largely taking redistricting out of state lawmakers’ hands. He also said he would advocate for the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, which would restore federal oversight of voting changes in states with a history of discrimination.
“We cannot allow people like Gov. Reeves to draw lines in ways where they get to pick the voters that matter. We have to make sure that independent commissions draw lines that empower the voters to pick the leaders.” 
Clyburn told a crowd of roughly 100 people they should elect Colom because he is interested in being a public servant and “not interested in being a partisan.”
Clyburn said he has encountered people who have grown dissatisfied with politics and don’t plan to vote because they believe one vote won’t make enough of a difference. He pushed back on that idea.
“The most critical things that happened to fairness in this country were each decided by one vote,” Clyburn said.
He pointed to the 1876 presidential election, when no candidate won a majority of Electoral College votes amid disputed results in several states. Congress formed a 15-member commission to settle it, and the commission voted 8-7 to award the presidency to Rutherford B. Hayes. Hayes later withdrew federal troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction. 
Like Clyburn, Colom has urged the crowd to “write a new chapter” in Mississippi’s history that lifts the state as a whole and depart from the chapters stained with divisive history. 
“There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed with what’s right about Mississippi,” Colom said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: In a tight battle for a WA legislative seat, a PAC tries influencers to reach voters
text:
Democratic state Rep. Amy Walen is running for reelection and faces a tough challenge from Jessica Forsythe, a fellow Democrat. (Walen Campaign photo)Tiffany knows fashion. Lita opines on the outdoors. Their online content creations draw thousands of views from those seeking their advice and recommendations.
Recently Tiffany and Lita veered into politics, posting Instagram videos urging their followers to back the re-election of Democratic state Rep. Amy Walen of Kirkland over Jessica Forsythe, a Democratic challenger.
Neither influencer lives in the 48th Legislative District in King County that Walen represents.
Both creators — and a handful of others — got paid for their pitch from the resources of Washington Needs to Compete, a political committee with a huge treasury and savvy leaders betting this approach, used increasingly in campaigns across the country, will pay dividends in the smaller battleground of a legislative district.
“Working with creators is simply another way to reach voters and share information about the issues that matter to them,” said Nick Streuli, an officer with the political committee who worked as a top policy adviser to Washington’s Democratic former Gov. Jay Inslee.
“Campaigns have long used a variety of channels to communicate with voters, and social media is increasingly part of that mix. This effort is no different,” said Streuli, managing partner of Sundial Advocacy.
Jessica Forsythe, a Democrat, is challenging Democratic state Rep. Amy Walen in Tuesday’s election. (Forsythe Campaign photo)
The tactic drew fire from the leader of a political committee funded by statewide unions and Democratic legislative caucuses that is spending a small warchest to unseat Walen.
“Amy Walen’s campaign is so uninspiring that her corporate special interest backers needed to pay a firm in Wyoming $105,000 to buy phony influencer support from people who don’t even live in the 48th District,” said Kurt Fritts, director of New Direction PAC.
High Stakes
Walen, a moderate Democrat, is a business owner and former Kirkland City Council member. She won her House seat in 2018 and is seeking a fifth term. Last year, in a special election, she lost to Sen. Vandana Slatter, a Democrat to her political left. 
This year, she’s locked in a fierce battle with Forsythe, a two-term Redmond City Council member who is a progressive Democrat. She enjoys backing of Slatter and former governor Jay Inslee.
Forsythe won the primary by 17 votes, setting the stage for a potential nail-biter in Tuesday’s election.
A major policy on which they diverge is the state’s new income tax, a 9.9% levy on households with earnings of more than $1 million a year.
Walen voted against the income tax bill that her Democratic colleagues passed and Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson signed. In this election, she said she is voting for Initiative 645 to repeal the tax. Even so, Ferguson has endorsed her reelection. So too have former governors Gary Locke and Christine Gregoire, both Democrats.
Forsythe said she supports the tax  and will vote to keep it in place. She’s said she’ll work “really hard to ensure that it stays at the million-dollar threshold.”
Big money
Entering the weekend, Walen had reported spending roughly $382,000 to Forsythe’s  $128,000. The combined total of the candidates pales in comparison to the nearly $2 million spent by political committees boosting and attacking each of them.
Leading the way is Washington Needs to Compete, the brainchild and political vehicle of Microsoft president Brad Smith. Of the $13.8 million it has raised, nearly $5.1 million is from Microsoft, followed by T-Mobile at $1 million, according to filings with the state Public Disclosure Commission. 
The PAC had shelled out close to $3.2 million as of Wednesday, with $700,068 worth of independent expenditures aimed at boosting support for Walen.
New Direction PAC is keeping pace with money from its largest donors, including the Washington Education Association, Washington Federation of State Employees, SEIU and the Kennedy Fund, which is the political arm of the state Senate Democratic Caucus. That fund has contributed $950,000 since June.
In this race, New Direction has spent close to $690,000, based on state campaign finance records. Roughly $400,000 has gone to support Forsythe and the remainder trying to bring down the incumbent.
The Influencers entered the fray earlier this month when Washington Needs to Compete paid $105,000 to Ryegrass LLC in Wyoming for what is described in campaign finance records as social media management and posting. Ryegrass describes itself as the “leading influencer agency” with access to more than 17,000 creators and influencers in Washington.
“In a time of trust & efficacy erosion in digital media, Ryegrass engineers virality that earns votes, creates conversations, and impacts policy and elections,” reads its website.
At least six influencers posted Instagram videos endorsing Walen. Each video notes that they are paid for their post by Washington Needs to Compete.
How much those videos influence voters is uncertain. More clear is that with two Democrats on the ballot, the district’s independent and Republican-aligned voters could swing the outcome.
At a recent forum, each was asked to make their best pitch to win over a Republican voter.
“I guess what I would say is I have demonstrated my independence in the Legislature,” Walen said. “I listen to everyone. I’ve demonstrated my willingness to get into the nuance, consider the unintended consequences, and to partner with my friends, offer amendments, and stand up to my caucus.”
Forsythe said she has had “a long history of working with a variety of folks. I’m not afraid to get into difficult conversations and find common ground. I believe that if we move past talking points, we can all find common threads and common realities that we want to work on and we want to fix.”
The winner of Tuesday’s election will serve a two-year term in the district that takes in Hunts Point and Medina and portions of Redmond, Bellevue and Kirkland.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Voters have questions on Question 3, the congressional redistricting amendment
text:
Signs for and against Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting, on display outside a voting center in Calvert County on Thursday, the last day of early voting. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)If approved by voters, Question 3 would amend the Maryland Constitution to change the rules applying to the ways congressional districts are drawn, making it easier for the party in control to draw a map that favors it, and limiting court challenges.
Got that? Not all voters do.
The ballot question was the product of a two-day rushed special legislative session in August and it was subsequently rewritten a month later by the Supreme Court of Maryland after a two-hour hearing in which the justices found the question “misleading.” The rewrite came on the same day ballots had to go to the printer.
The rewritten version still leaves some voters, such as Linda Frazier, a Democrat from Prince George’s County, had having to read the question “two or three times” to comprehend it.


 










View this post on Instagram






















 
A post shared by Maryland Matters (@marylandmatters)



For Frazier, the deciding factor was the support of Gov. Wes Moore (D), a vocal supporter of Question 3.
The measure was a response to President Donald Trump’s push get Republican-led states to redistrict this year, ahead of schedule, in an effort to gain a partisan advantage in this fall’s elections. It’s being championed by Moore and many other Maryland’s Democratic leaders with a simple message: It’s needed to combat Trump’s push in GOP-controlled state legislatures redraw maps and decrease voter representation.
For Frazier, hearing from Moore was enough. And Frazier, who voted Tuesday, said the Trump administration’s “not for the greater good.”
If passed, the bill would have no effect this year, but could affect elections in 2028, as Trump is scheduled to leave office. And the best Maryland Democrats could do is pick up one seat: Currently, seven of Maryland’s eight congressional districts are held by Democrats, with eight-term Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) holding the only GOP seat.
Maryland’s Republican leaders are saying “partisan gerrymandering” and eliminating of their voices would be the result of Question 3 passing.
“It’s intentionally written to be confusing to the average person,” said Jason Scaggs, a Republican who’s seeking an at-large seat on the Board of County Commissioners in Calvert County.
“It gives ultimate control for all of the laws and tax and everything to one central power, and that’s not how our government was designed to work,” Suggs said on the last day of early voting Thursday. “Two [political] parties that fight and bicker back and forth … it kind of keeps everybody honest.”
Voters interviewed during the eight-day early voting period acknowledged they were confused and had to read and research the question several times. A Calvert County voter, who declined to be identified, called it a “reluctant vote” in favor of Question 3.
Even an expert in Maryland politics needed to conduct some research to understand Question 3.
“I’ve said it several times. I have a freaking Ph.D. in political science and American politics, and if I didn’t know what that amendment was about, I would have no idea what that amendment was about,” Todd Eberly, political science professor at St. Mary’s College, said in an interview this month.
“For the folks that will see it for the very first time in the voting booth, where they can’t even pull out their phone and try to Google, ‘What the heck does this mean?’” he said.



Questioning Question 3
Rather than reject the “misleading” ballot question on congressional redistricting this fall, the Supreme Court of Maryland decided to rewrite the question. This is what voters see on their ballots:
FOR the purpose of clarifying that certain requirements apply only to districts for the election of members of the Senate of Maryland and the House of Delegates; authorizing the General Assembly to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the State; and providing that nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan.
