name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Sandy Hook families urge Supreme Court to uphold bans on AR-15-style rifles
text:
Relatives whose loved ones were killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting are making an impassioned plea to the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on certain semiautomatic rifles, citing the high body counts and devastating injuries the weapons can inflict.
The parents of five of the 20 first-graders killed in the 2012 Connecticut shooting and relatives of one of six educators who died filed a “friend of the court” brief on Wednesday, weighing in on two cases challenging bans in Connecticut and the Chicago area. Justices are scheduled to hear oral arguments in both cases on Dec. 2.
“The assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School, carried out by an untrained, 112-pound youth armed with an AR-15-style rifle, is graphic proof of the unusual and extreme lethality of that firearm and the harm it is capable of inflicting on American communities,” the relatives’ filing says. They added that they “seek to protect other American families from becoming casualties in another AR-15 killing spree.”
Gun rights advocates and groups whose lawsuits led to the two Supreme Court cases are arguing that it’s unconstitutional under the Second Amendment to ban semiautomatic rifles, which are legally owned by millions of Americans. Supporters of the bans say such rifles were designed for military use, are too dangerous for civilians and should be regulated like machine guns.
More than 40 other people and groups — most in favor of the rifle bans — also filed “amicus curiae” briefs on Wednesday. Such filings are submitted by parties who are not directly involved in the litigation.
Sandy Hook shooter killed 26 people with AR-15-style rifle
The 20-year-old Sandy Hook gunman, Adam Lanza, shot his way into the locked school in Newtown, Connecticut, and unleashed a fury of more than 150 bullets in about four minutes with a Bushmaster AR-15-style rifle fueled by high-capacity ammunition magazines. The massacre led Connecticut to ban such rifles in 2013 — the same law now before the Supreme Court.
Jennifer Hensel, whose 6-year-old daughter Avielle Richman was killed in the shooting, was quoted in the relatives’ brief saying Avielle was shot multiple times in the face and authorities told her that she would not recognize her daughter if she saw her body.
“A moral imperative is truly at hand,” Hensel said in supporting weapons bans. “Please, do not allow more blood to soak our Connecticut soil from assault-style weapons. A fundamental duty to protect all in Connecticut is at stake.”
A similar brief filed Wednesday by Sandy Hook Promise, the gun violence prevention group started by Newtown families, said another victim, 6-year-old Dylan Hockley, was shot five times — “his body destroyed so completely, his mother was told not to touch him to say goodbye as he lay in his coffin.”
[RELATED: Sandy Hook Promise’s ‘Start With Hello’ enlists teens to end gun violence]
“The effects of these weapons on children’s bodies are catastrophic and obscene,” the filing said.
Dylan’s mother, Nicole Hockley, a co-founder of Sandy Hook Promise, urged the Supreme Court to consider children’s safety.
“I know firsthand the devastation a semiautomatic rifle can inflict in minutes on the bodies, hearts, and minds of children — and the families who love them,” she said in a statement. “No family should have to live with that pain. As the Court considers this case, the consequences being experienced by children and communities cannot be an afterthought.”
Gun rights advocates filed suit to block rifle bans
Gun rights supporters say that while they sympathize with gun violence victims’ families and condemn mass shootings, the solution isn’t to curtail Second Amendment rights. They say school shootings happen despite bans on so-called “assault weapons.”
“Solving or at least mitigating school shootings is not about banning a type of gun,” said Konstadinos Moros, director of legal research and education for the Second Amendment Foundation, a plaintiff in the challenges to both the Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, bans.
“While some guns are obviously more capable than others, school shooters inflict harm not because of the capability of their firearms, but because of the helplessness of their targets,” he said in an email to The Associated Press. “The real solution lies in proper school security, which can both more quickly respond to shootings, and deter attacks from happening in the first place, given that the depraved individuals who commit these sorts of crimes tend to pick ‘soft targets.’”
Justices to weigh whether bans violate Second Amendment
The current Supreme Court, which has expanded gun rights, announced in June that it would hear appeals challenging bans on the AR-15 and similar semiautomatic firearms in Connecticut and the Chicago area. The ban in Cook County was first passed in 1993. Lower courts have upheld both laws.
Similar laws are in place in about a dozen states, covering major cities like New York, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. Congress allowed a national assault weapons ban to expire in 2004, but Democrats have supported renewing it in response to mass shootings. States have also continued to pass their own laws, including recent measures in Virginia and Rhode Island.
It is the latest high-profile dispute over guns to reach the court since its conservative majority handed down a landmark ruling in 2022 that expanded Second Amendment rights and spawned challenges to firearm laws around the country. The court said that any gun laws must have a strong grounding in the nation’s historical traditions.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi has 23 public colleges and universities. Can the state sustain them?
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
When Rep. Trey Lamar, a Republican from Senatobia, introduced House Bill 1284 in January to merge six community college districts, college leaders and students quickly launched a petition to shut it down. 
The bill died in committee, but the question behind it did not: Does Mississippi still need 23 public colleges and universities? 
“I wanted to start a conversation,” said Lamar, who is also a member of the House Select Committee on Consolidation. “What worked for our colleges decades ago doesn’t always work today.” 
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Trey Lamar, R-Senatobia, speaks in the House chamber during legislative session on Wednesday, Feb. 25, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
House Bill 1284 would have merged Coahoma Community College with Mississippi Delta Community College; Meridian with East Mississippi; and Southwest Mississippi with Copiah-Lincoln. The mergers would not have closed any campuses but were meant to reduce administrative costs by consolidating college districts from 15 to 12. Any money saved from merging would have been put back into the community college system, Lamar said. 
Lamar’s bill intensified discussions about college mergers, said Rep. Donnie Scoggin, a Republican from Ellisville who co-chairs the House consolidation committee. Scoggin also chairs the House Colleges and Universities Committee, which he said allowed the bill to die because there wasn’t enough time to study the issue. 
“We didn’t want to do anything that was rushed and just start closing colleges,” Scoggin said. “But now we’re taking time to examine all factors to make informed and better decisions.” 
Rep. Donnie Scoggin, left, and Rep. Trey Lamar have a conversation during legislative session at the Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, March 23, 2023. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Mississippi’s public universities and community colleges are funded through a mix of state appropriations, federal funds, student tuition and local tax revenue. Overlapping districts can leave some property owners paying more in taxes to support multiple colleges — a situation Lamar said is unfair. 
Meridian Community College serves Lauderdale County, which is also part of East Mississippi Community College’s six-county district. Merging the two districts could reduce duplicative administrative costs, he said. 
Dips in population across the districts are also driving the move to consolidate. Over the past decade, thousands fewer residents have lived within the Coahoma and Mississippi Delta community college districts. In 2010, there were 26,000 residents in Coahoma County; a decade later, there were 21,000 residents, according to Census data. In Sunflower County, home to Mississippi Delta Community College, the population dropped by 4,000 people over the same period. 
For Cole Cooksey, a sophomore studying pre-political science at Southwest Community College, attending the school was the next logical step after high school graduation. He received scholarships that covered his first year of tuition, and the campus’ proximity to his parents’ home in McComb made college more affordable and accessible, he said. 
When Lamar’s bill threatened to merge Southwest with Copiah-Lincoln Community College, rumors of closure began circulating online. Cooksey said he wanted to raise awareness about the importance of the state’s oldest public college system and its benefits to students in rural and underserved communities. 
A student walks the campus at Copiah-Lincoln Community College on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
So, Cooksey launched an online petition to “Stop The Progression of House Bill 1284,” on Jan. 23 which received more than 330 supporters in its first day. When the bill died in the House committee, the petition had attracted the support of 750 people.  
“Community colleges help fill in the gaps of support and education that high schools are not able to do and they fill in the gaps that universities refuse too,” Cooksey said. “The more conversations we have about their benefits and services, the more we are able to open other people’s eyes to the good community colleges do within our state.” 
The state should not have to maintain separate community college boards  in areas serving fewer people, Lamar said. 
Southwest Mississippi Community College is pictured in Summit on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Mississippi Community College Board operates as the statewide coordinating board for each of the 15 colleges. Each college also maintains its own local board of trustees, which works with the college board. The local boards are responsible for the day-to-day operations, local administration, facilities, personnel decisions and local tax support for their respective campuses, according to state law. 
Legislators’ consolidation discussions have also questioned if colleges in overlapping communities have duplicate academic programs or services and whether students are earning college credentials that lead to jobs, he said. 
Legislators are asking similar questions about the state’s eight public universities.
Southwest Mississippi Community College is pictured in Summit on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford, is pushing trustees overseeing the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning to tie state funding to graduation rates, job placement and earnings.
The state college board’s new performance-based funding formula  would aim for universities to meet the state’s workforce and education attainment priorities. 
In June, IHL trustees took a step toward adopting a proposed public university funding formula that would tie a portion of state money to graduation rates, student retention and workforce outcomes. As of October, the college board is still working to define specific metrics and goals for the universities. It is also unclear when it will be fully implemented. 
Sen. Nicole Boyd, R-Oxford, asks a question about a bill in the Senate chamber at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In 2024, Boyd introduced Senate Bill 2725, which would have created a 10-member task force to examine funding formulas as Mississippi approached a looming enrollment cliff because of a predicted sharp decline in high school graduates. That same year, former Sen. John Polk, a Republican from Hattiesburg, also authored Senate Bill 2726, which would have required college board trustees to close three universities based on  similar factors such as graduation rates, enrollment and student retention outcomes.  
An enrollment dropoff could put pressure on the state’s regional universities, particularly Mississippi University for Women, Delta State, Alcorn and Mississippi Valley State by forcing them to compete with the state’s flagship universities, University of Mississippi and Mississippi State University, for a shrinking pool of students.  
The conversations around university funding are about more than finances, Boyd said. It’s about centering students. 
Copiah-Lincoln Community College is pictured in Wesson on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“These conversations are a cultural shift for Mississippi,” Boyd said. “We just want to make sure students aren’t leaving school saddled with debt and now worse off because of it.” 
Consolidating the state’s smaller colleges and universities could hurt rural students’ access to higher education, said Pernell Goodwin, vice president of Copiah-Lincoln Community College’s Natchez campus. Having to travel further for college would make it more difficult for students to visit campuses and increase their overall college costs, he said.
Accessibility was the goal behind the creation of Mississippi’s community college system, Goodwin said.
“It was to ensure that no matter where a student attends college, he is at least within a certain distance from his home to get to campus and access education.” 
Bruce Hanson, who was a state representative in the 1980s, has pushed back against closing or consolidating universities. 
A student sits on the steps of a campus building at Southwest Mississippi Community College is pictured in Summit on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
As chair of the Citizens Coalition for MUW and Mississippi School for Mathematics and Science, Hanson has sought to protect the two campuses from consolidation proposals seeking to close schools that enroll fewer students. He said smaller public universities play a crucial role in providing affordable tuition and easy access to higher education for Mississippi students.
They nevertheless generate millions of dollars and produce graduates who are essential to the state’s economy and workforce, Hanson said.
“If these institutions disappear, where will the children in our community go?”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Final pitch over Missouri abortion ban turns to fight over voter power
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway speaks at a Yes on 3 rally hosted by Her Health, Her Future, on Tues. Oct. 27 at Encounter Church in Arnold (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).As Missouri voters prepare to decide whether to reinstate the state’s abortion ban, the final arguments over Amendment 3 are reaching beyond abortion itself.
The campaigns are linking the measure to other questions on Tuesday’s ballot and framing the election as a fight over who holds power in Missouri — voters, politicians or wealthy outside interests.
To supporters of Amendment 3, which aims to repeal the state’s 2024 reproductive rights amendment, the threat comes from wealthy out-of-state liberals trying to turn Missouri into a haven for abortion.
“No on 6. Tell billionaires keep their paws off our laws,” read signs at a Yes on 3 rally Tuesday in Arnold.
To opponents of Amendment 3 who are aiming to keep abortion legal, the threat comes from Republican politicians trying to overturn the will of Missouri voters.
“Vote No on 3. Vote No on A. Voters decide. Not politicians,” read signs at a Stop the Ban rally Saturday in St. Louis.
Proposition A is a referendum on a gerrymandered congressional map drawn last year by Republicans. Amendment 6 would require support from at least 80% of both legislative chambers for lawmakers to put a change to a voter-approved initiative back on the ballot. 
Both measures appear on the Nov. 3 ballot alongside Amendment 3.  
If Amendment 3 fails and Amendment 6 passes, it would be nearly impossible for the Republican-led statehouse to put another measure with abortion restrictions before voters.
Amber Jones, program manager with the nonprofit LeadMO, said tying Proposition A to Amendment 3 is about protecting the people’s power. It’s a message she said resonated with voters as she helped collect signatures from Missourians across the state to put the gerrymandered map on the ballot.
“A handful of powerful people shouldn’t be able to rig the rules to protect themselves,” Jones said. “That is what this fight is about. They want to divide communities, manipulate who gets represented together and make it harder for voters to hold politicians accountable.” 
More than 600 volunteers with abortion-rights groups, labor unions and voter advocacy groups knocked on 14,000 doors across the state Saturday, urging voters to oppose Proposition A and Amendment 3, according to a press release from Abortion Action Missouri.
Leaders with Missouri abortion rights and labor groups gather for a canvassing event on oct. 24 in St. Louis (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
On Tuesday, Tim Jones, a Republican radio host and former speaker of the Missouri House, said the initiative petition process has become “an abhorrent abomination to our constitution.” He accused out-of-state donors of deceiving Missourians by pouring millions of dollars into progressive campaigns. 
The 2024 campaign to legalize abortion, and the 2026 campaign to keep it legal, have been backed by small donations from thousands of Missourians. But most of the more than $27 million raised by Stop the Ban this year has come from large out-of-state donors and progressive nonprofits that aren’t required to disclose their donors. 
Her Health, Her Future, the campaign supporting the abortion ban, has drawn far fewer donors, with significant financial backing from Missouri-based contributors, including a newly formed nonprofit that does not have to disclose its donors. As of Thursday, the campaign had raised more than $7 million.
Amendment 3 would reinstate an abortion ban with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and rape or incest within the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
It would also allow the state to reinstate dozens of regulations on abortion providers struck down this summer by Jackson County Circuit Judge Jerri Zhang, who ruled they were unconstitutional under the reproductive rights amendment voters approved in 2024. Those included a 72-hour waiting period, special licensing requirements for abortion providers and hospital admitting privileges.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway criticized the ruling at Tuesday’s rally in Arnold, asking supporters if they would protect women and “stand up to that judge who overruled every single safety protection for women.”
But Zhang did not strike down every regulation. She upheld requirements that medication abortion be administered in person and that only doctors can perform abortions or prescribe abortion medication. She also wrote that several safeguards remained in place even without the regulations she overturned.
Amendment 3 would also place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors. State law prohibits gender-transition surgery for minors and bars minors from beginning cross-sex hormones or puberty blockers. The restrictions on hormones and puberty blockers are set to expire in August 2027, though lawmakers have discussed making the ban permanent. 
Former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who recently stepped down as co-deputy director of the FBI, speaks at a Yes on 3 rally hosted by Her Health, Her Future, on  Tuesday at Encounter Church in Arnold (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
Former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who recently stepped down from the FBI, also made an appearance in Arnold as part of what he called an effort to barnstorm Missouri for Amendment 3. 
He recently teamed up with U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley to launch a political action committee called Vote Yes on Amendment 3. An Oct. 26 report filed with the Missouri Ethics Commission showed the campaign had received one donation — for $1 million — from America Next Inc., a conservative Louisiana-based nonprofit launched by former Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal.
America Next does not disclose its donors. 
Bailey told the Arnold crowd that “voters were deceived by the lie behind reproductive freedom a few years back.” 
The 2024 reproductive rights amendment passed with 51.6% of the vote. Polling shows the potential for another very close race.
Those rallying in opposition to Amendment 3 reject the suggestion that voters were deceived when they approved abortion rights two years ago. 
“Powerful politicians think they know better. They say we didn’t know what we were doing when we voted to legalize abortion,” Nancy O’Brian, a volunteer with Abortion Action Missouri, said at a rally Saturday in St. Louis. “They say that we didn’t mean it when we kicked politicians and lawyers out of private medical decisions between families and doctors. But they don’t know Missouri like we do. We know how Missourians feel about abortion because we already asked them.” 
O’Brian, who had an abortion when she was a young woman after she said she was targeted by an older man who became abusive, said access to that care allowed her to have her current career and family, which includes two children.
Knocking on doors, she said, has shown her that Missourians have nuanced feelings about abortion. 
“But I also know that no matter how we personally feel about abortion, Missourians agree that politicians should never get to decide for us and our families,” she told a cheering crowd. “They certainly shouldn’t get to just overturn any vote of the people just because they don’t like it. Politicians don’t get the final say. We get the final say.”

name: California
title: Jane Kim and Ben Allen squabble over state-run wildfire insurance
text:
Insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim speaks to the press at the Curran Theater in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters




How do you distinguish between the two Democrats running for insurance commissioner? Well, one of them wants state-backed public insurance. We have more on that, as well as details on a move campaigns are using to dodge spending limits this fall.
But we have more than election news in your inbox today. California employers scored a big win in federal court against a new state law that would limit anti-union messaging in workplaces. More on that below.
Insurance commissioner candidates Jane Kim and state Sen. Ben Allen have attacked each other over their main plans to improve California’s property insurance market: A public option and broad wildfire mitigation, respectively. 
Their latest back-and-forth is around what Kim’s plan to create a public wildfire insurer — a proposal that critics say would shift big risks to the state — might cost homeowners.
Kim recently released a policy brief that lays out how such a plan could work. Funding the program would involve having a two-part wildfire premium, collected by private insurers and diverted to the state, which would be based on each home’s wildfire risk, plus a “small, capped share that every home in the state contributes to cover the bad wildfire seasons.”
Her brief cited a proposal included in a California Earthquake Authority report that could serve as a model. It estimated that such a program would need about $25 billion for a very bad wildfire year. The program would buy reinsurance for that risk, which would cost $2 billion to $3 billion a year, or about $150 to $230 a policy. Without reinsurance, a “once-in-a-century fire” would mean a charge of $1,900 to $2,000 per policy over several years, the report said. 
On social media and elsewhere, Allen’s campaign is using Kim’s brief to say her plan would cost policyholders “$230 a year added to every homeowner’s policy” and “$2,000 or more in assessments on every policyholder.”
That’s not the case, Kim told reporters this week.

Kim: “Either he is being intellectually disingenuous, or he doesn’t know how to read a policy brief … we were referring to a study that if we do not buy reinsurance that it would cost homeowners, on average, $2,000 more.”

CalMatters contacted Allen’s campaign about Kim’s pushback. Allen spokesperson Joe Arellano repeated his campaign’s claim. 
The two Democratic candidates have also tussled over campaign finance, including their promises not to take money from the insurance industry.
For the record: The Oct. 8 WhatMatters newsletter contained an error about what the Public Interest Legal Foundation agreed to in a confidential 2019 settlement of a lawsuit by plaintiffs who claimed they were falsely accused of voting improprieties. 
The foundation’s president, J. Christian Adams, says the foundation did not admit to falsely accusing thousands of Virginia voters of being noncitizens, as an earlier version of this newsletter stated. The foundation apologized to the three plaintiffs for relying on what he said were inaccurate government records, when the foundation falsely labeled them as noncitizens in its reports. 
The newsletter and article have been updated to provide corrected and additional details about the settlement.



We’re bringing our voter guide to life through VotingMatters events across California, in collaboration with on-the-ground partners: Local news organizations, colleges and nonprofits. Our next event is today at 12 p.m. in Fresno at Fresno State University.

Other Stories You Should Know


How candidates dodge spending rules


Assemblymember Jeff Gonzalez speaks during a floor session at the state Capitol in Sacramento on June 30, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




More would-be California lawmakers are employing a controversial tactic that sidesteps campaign finance laws to spread their influence on potential voters, write CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe and Nadia Lathan. 
Donors in state elections are only allowed to give candidates as much as $5,900 per election. But independent expenditure committees, which can run ads supporting or opposing candidates, do not have a spending limit. 
These groups cannot directly coordinate with campaigns. But over the past decade, candidates have been using a method known as “red boxing” to leave instructions on their campaign sites, typically outlined in a red box, for independent spenders to follow when creating ads. 
Critics say the tactic can create the appearance of corruption. But the California Fair Political Practices Commission is unlikely to rein in the behavior soon. 

Steven Maviglio, Democratic strategist: “Like it or not, the state watchdog doesn’t have the capacity to do their job.”

Read more.



CA employers win in challenge to workplace meeting law


A waitress sets tables at a restaurant in Alturas on Sept. 3, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




A federal court handed California business groups a win Thursday in their fight to stop a pro-labor law limiting so-called captive audience meetings.
In 2024 the state passed a law banning employers from punishing workers who refuse to attend workplace meetings about political, anti-union or religious matters. Three major industry groups — California Chamber of Commerce, the California Restaurant Association and the Western Growers Association — sued the state, arguing that the measure violated their First Amendment rights.
A district court issued a preliminary injunction last year preventing the law from taking effect. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the ruling on free speech grounds, agreeing with the industry groups’ argument. 

Judge Richard C. Tallman, in his opinion: “The potential for any employee to expose an employer to liability for damages (including punitive damages) based on the employee’s perception of the workplace’s history and culture surrounding meetings ‘creates its own chilling effect’ on the employer’s ability to speak on political matters in the workplace.”

In a joint statement, the industry groups praised the ruling, saying that “the state cannot limit the speech of any business owner simply because the contents of that speech might differ from the political viewpoint of elected officials or outside interest groups.”
The office of the California attorney general said it was reviewing the ruling but did not comment on whether it plans to appeal.



And lastly: What does Prop. 45 mean for data centers?


An Amazon Web Services data center under construction in Gilroy on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Opponents of Proposition 45, which would lift some restrictions on the state’s environmental review law, say the measure would make it easier for developers to build data centers. Data center backers say the proposal doesn’t do that, but that hasn’t stopped the beneficiaries of such centers from pouring millions of dollars into supporting the measure. Read more from CalMatters’ Katherine Ortiz.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: Though there were plenty of chaotic events for political junkies to savor this California election season, candidates did not meaningfully address the many challenges facing California, including its budget deficits, homelessness or rising living costs.
Prop. 13 was sold in 1978 as a way to save families from unpredictable property tax bills, but it also became a permanent discount for wealthy, corporate property owners that has resulted in billions of dollars in lost tax revenue, writes John Kim, president and CEO of Catalyst California.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Majority or bust: Michigan parties make final push for legislative control
text:
The statue of former Gov. Austin Blair at the Michigan Capitol | Susan J. DemasMuch of the 2026 election attention has been on Michigan’s must-watch U.S. Senate and congressional races, but the battle for control of the state Legislature has emerged as another major contest.
In a highly favorable year for Michigan Democrats, the party is hoping that President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, pegged at 57% in a recent Marist poll, and stagnant economy on his watch will help the party retake the Michigan House, hold the state Senate and retain the governor’s office. 
“Our candidates have worked hard this cycle to build strong campaigns that highlight the issues Michiganders care about,” state Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) said in a statement. “We are looking forward to returning to the Senate in January with an expanded majority to continue our work in building a Michigan where everyone can live and thrive.”
But the state’s Republicans, despite warning signs the GOP might have a bad year, are aiming to retain their current House majority and retake the Senate. That hope is at least partly based on the potential to exploit the controversies connected to U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
“With El-Sayed at the top of the ticket, the Senate Republicans are on offense, and the Senate Democrats know it,” Sen. Roger Hauck, R-Mount Pleasant (R-Mount Pleasant) said in a statement. “They’re so desperate that they’re spending $1.3 million they don’t have. Every target district’s early and absentee voting is more Republican than it was in 2022, when Republicans lost shared control of the chamber by 400 votes. The Democratic majority ends Nov. 3.”
The Senate Republican Campaign Committee has made a final round of ad purchases to try and make that goal a reality.
State Sens. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) and Chedrick Greene (D-Saginaw) take questions from reporters. June 10, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Democrats like their chances to expand Senate majority
For the Senate’s Democrats, who currently control the chamber, the most favorable scenario on Nov. 3 would be to hold what seats they have while also expanding their majority by flipping three long-sought after Republican districts.
“The momentum is clearly behind Democrats this election, and across the board, Senate Democrats have strong, passionate candidates who are ready to fight for working families,” Olivia Bradish, spokesperson for the Michigan Senate Democrats said. Bradish added that they have “heavily invested to ensure Democrats defend and expand” their Senate Majority.
At the top of that list is the 9th District held by Republican Sen. Michael Webber of Rochester Hills. He faces Democratic nominee Dr. Theresa Brooks of Troy. Democrats are hoping to defeat Webber, a longtime legislator and a leader in the Senate Republican caucus, and said that Brooks has been knocking on doors almost every day since she won a tough three-way primary. 
Brooks has also outraised Webber, picking up a little more than $320,000 in the latest reporting period, while  Webber raised just under $220,000.
While protecting Webber’s seat is a major priority for the GOP, Democrats are confident that Brooks has the resources, community support and motivation to win.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines, Michigan Senate candidate Theresa Brooks and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/ Michigan Advance)
Next on the list of hoped-for Democratic pickups is the 30th District, held by GOP Sen. Mark Huizenga of Walker. He faces Democratic challenger state Rep. Carol Glanville, also of Walker. Democrats believe Glanville is in a comfortable position and that West Michigan is showing signs of shifting toward greater support for their party and candidates — a trend the party has noticed over the last few years. 
While her roots in the community were helping Glanville, the party noted she’s also outraised Huizenga in the latest period. Huizenga raised just north of $100,000 during the latest reporting period, whereas Glanville raised a little more than $300,000.
Regardless, Republicans also feel good about Huizenga’s chances, touting his bipartisan voting record — which the party said was among the most bipartisan records of any sitting state senator — and the fact that he’s worked hard for the district as its senator over the past four years.
The third pickup opportunity being eyed by Democrats is West Michigan’s 32nd District. Republican state Sen. Jon Bumstead of North Muskegon cannot seek reelection due to term limits, setting up a fight between Democrat Rebecca Amidon and Republican Mason County Sheriff Kim Cole. Although Cole is well established in the district, having served as sheriff since 2013, Democrats believe Amidon is a strong enough candidate to be spending heavily on TV advertising in the district deep into the election cycle.
While winning the district will be a challenge for Amidon given its history as a safe seat for Republicans, Democrats said her message aimed at working families was resonating amid Trump’s economic woes.
That said, the GOP is confident Cole will put the race away early on election night, noting that the seat is still trending toward the Republican Party despite changes in West Michigan demographics that have trended toward Democrats.
State Sens. Sylvia Santana (D-Detroit) and Mark Huizenga (R-Walker) discuss legislation creating a framework for behavioral health transport in the state. May 13, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Hertel legislative legacy included in must hold seats for Senate Dems
Tops on the list of must-hold Senate seats are Sen. Kevin Hertel’s 12th District and the open 13th District race to replace retiring Sen. Rosemary Bayer. 
Republicans have made defeating Hertel a priority, with a barrage of recent ads highlighting his family’s political dynasty as reason to reject him in favor of Republican John Goldwater. Democrats said this will be a tough seat to hold onto, as Hertel won in 2022 by just more than 400 votes, but the positive environment for the party has them optimistic about Hertel’s chances. 
Republicans, meanwhile, are all in on Goldwater’s prospects to flip in Hertel’s seat. They’ve highlighted not only Hertel’s family political dynasty, but also his voting record aligning with Democrats in what was a +7.5 Trump district in 2024.
In the 13th District, Democrat Sean Carlson has similarly been working hard, with more than 5,000 doors knocked in his race against Republican former state Rep. Ryan Berman of Commerce Township. Berman previously sought and lost the GOP nomination for attorney general in 2022. Democrats were optimistic after Carlson outraised Berman nearly 10-to-1 in the last reporting period, gaining more than $364,000 to Berman’s approximately $38,000.
Senate Republicans, however, believe the newly drawn district allows a better chance for Berman to pick up the seat. They’re also banking on Berman’s district having a high population of Jewish voters, who might end up breaking for Republicans due to issues with El-Sayed.
Sen. Kevin Hertel (D-St. Clair Shores) discusses a slate of proposed regulations on data centers at a press conference. June 18, 2025 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
56 seats is the goal for House Democrats this year
The Michigan House Democratic caucus currently holds 52 seats and just needs four more to hold a majority in the lower chamber of the Legislature, which they lost control of in 2024. The party is eyeing nine potential winnable seats out of the 12 that it has targeted, and campaign operatives said that the other three offer some cautious optimism.
“We feel very good about our chances of taking back the House on Nov. 3,” Sam Lundry, executive director of the Michigan House Democratic Fund, said. “We have excellent candidates who know their communities and hear every day from people who need some relief from rising costs. Matt Hall and House Republicans are stuck defending the GOP record of corruption and higher costs, and that’s a tough sell to families watching their bills go up. We have multiple paths to a majority, and we’re taking nothing for granted.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Among the top targets for a flip is the 27th House District, where state Rep. Rylee Linting (R-Wyandotte) is seeking reelection to the seat she won in 2024 against its former incumbent, Jamie Churches, also of Wyandotte. Democrats feel good about the race for Churches, due to her reputation as one of the House campaign arm’s hardest working candidates, along with hopes that the Trump effect puts the seat back into play. They’ve backed that optimism with cash, as Gongwer reported Thursday on a $200,000 television ad buy to support Churches.
Another key rematch for the House this cycle is state Rep. Steve Frisbie (R-Battle Creek) versus Democratic former state Rep. Jim Haadsma in the 44th District. Haadsma lost the district to Frisbie in 2024 by just 79 votes and Democrats like their chances of surmounting that small gap this cycle..
Another chance for Democrats to gain a House seat is in Oakland County, where state Rep. Donni Steele (R-Orion Township) is not seeking reelection to the 54th District, instead seeking election to the state Senate in the 23rd district. 
Sarah Pounds is the Democratic nominee, while Roman Gaskey was nominated by the GOP. The signs are positive for Pounds, who has been supported by national Democrats, with both California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigning for her. Additionally, Pounds polled more than 12,000 votes in the August primary, where she ran unopposed, which was almost 3,000 more votes than Gaskey and his primary opponent received.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (at left) campaigns Sunday in Oakland County with Michigan House candidates Sarah Pounds and Alex Hawkins. Aug. 9, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance
State Rep. Mark Tisdel (R-Rochester Hills), the incumbent in the adjacent 55th District, is seeking reelection and faces Democrat Alexander Hawkins, a military veteran whose job with the Michigan National Guard was defusing bombs. Party operatives believe his military ties can buck the narrative that Democrats running in this cycle are El-Sayed or William Lawrence-style progressives with some baggage.
Other targets for potential Democratic seat expansion include the 68th, 86th and 109th House Districts. Although these seats, on paper, appear harder to flip, the Democrats are cautiously optimistic.
State Rep. David Martin (R-Davison) is the incumbent in the 68th District, Rep. Nancy DeBoer (R-Holland) currently holds the 86th District, and Rep. Karl Bohnak (R-Deerton) represents the 109th District. Each is seeking reelection in what are typically safe Republican seats.
The anti-incumbent environment has Democrats feeling good about their chances, especially in the West Michigan seat held by DeBoer, who is facing Democratic challenger Joseph McClusky, and the Upper Peninsula seat held by Bohnak, who is fending off a strong challenge by Democrat Anna Aho Rink. 
The trend line showing West Michigan becoming bluer over the past few cycles and the fact that El-Sayed drew big crowds up north during his campaign swings puts those two seats, in particular, in the potential pickup category for Democrats.
As both parties target a handful of competitive races to try and tip the scales, control of the Legislature will  ultimately depend on whether Democrats can translate a favorable political environment into gains in districts that have long eluded them, while Republicans are betting that incumbency and the divisions surrounding El-Sayed can blunt Democratic momentum.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: It’s time to end Boston’s unique status of being exempt from the state zoning code
text:
IN AUGUST 1960, amid catastrophic population loss and the prospect of vast amounts of federal aid, State House leaders and then-Mayor John Collins struck a deal exempting Boston from most Massachusetts zoning laws. Sixty-six years later, the post-war urban crisis and the era of federally funded urban renewal are long over, but that deal is still the foundation of Boston’s development process. So why does Boston still operate under real estate development processes built for that bygone era?   
The case for maintaining the archaic status quo grows weaker with every statewide housing reform. Because of that 1960 deal, Boston is exempt from the MBTA Communities Act, statewide legalization of accessory dwelling units (ADU), and the proposed Legalize Starter Homes ballot question. These laws are some of the highest profile legislation Beacon Hill has passed in the last decade, but do not apply to the state’s own capital and largest city.   
The idea that housing reform is needed in Boston has been endorsed by Boston’s most powerful leaders. Both Michelle Wu and Marty Walsh won their first races for mayor on platforms to reform the city’s development process, but both failed to make more than cosmetic changes.  
If Boston’s mayor, the most powerful local elected official in Massachusetts, can’t change the system, what can? The answer is simple: End Boston’s 66-year experiment in DIY development policy and make Boston subject to Chapter 40A. That would legalize ADUs citywide, more than two years after Mayor Wu promised to do so in the 2024 “State of the City” address and help solve Massachusetts’s statewide housing crisis.   
Bringing Boston under Chapter 40A would also ensure the city’s elected and appointed officials and larger real estate ecosystem face the same housing rules, incentives, and consequences as the rest of Massachusetts.   
There is no better time than now: Speaker-in-waiting Aaron Michlewitz and House Majority Leader Mike Moran are both Boston residents. Both face the prospect of forcing their House colleagues to take difficult votes on important housing legislation that their districts are not subject to. Bringing Boston under Chapter 40A would end that contradiction.  
The greatest impact of this change would be in Boston, where the switch to Chapter 40A would require reconciling decades of DIY planning with state standards. The chief site of those changes would be the city’s notoriously long and complex zoning code. This switch would be an opportunity for politicians and activists who routinely criticize the city’s zoning to burnish their pro-housing bona fides to turn that rhetoric into action.   
Benefits would extend well beyond Boston. Massachusetts ranks near the bottom nationally in housing construction per capita. An often overlooked reason is that the state’s largest city not only has a different zoning code, but operates under an entirely different development process. Today, Brookline and Great Barrington, towns on opposite ends of the state, have more similar development processes than neighboring Brookline and Boston.  
Housing is the top issue in Boston and across Massachusetts. Bringing Boston under Chapter 40A would empower elected officials at City Hall and on Beacon Hill with the same tools and incentives as the rest of the state.  
If solving the crisis requires “all hands on deck,” everyone needs to be in the same boat.  
Gregory Maynard is senior fellow at Pioneer City Initiative, a newly launched program at Pioneer Institute.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC’s abortion ban has ‘serious problems,’ federal judge says
text:
South Carolina's abortion ban could be vague enough to be unconstitutional, a federal judge said Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, during a trial in Charleston, S.C. (File/Photo by Getty Images)CHARLESTON — South Carolina’s abortion ban has clear issues, potentially making it unconstitutional, a federal judge said Friday.
U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel, speaking at the end of a three-day trial in Charleston, didn’t give any official verdict on a case challenging the state’s ban on most abortions past six weeks of pregnancy. But he did have major concerns with the law as written, which he said makes its exceptions too vague to follow or enforce.
“I think the statute has serious problems, but frankly, I think the General Assembly can fix it,” Gergel said.
The lawsuit, filed last year, argued the state’s abortion ban was vague enough to violate the U.S. Constitution’s guarantee of due process. Over three days, doctors testified they’re afraid to provide abortions even when the law might allow them.
The law, passed in 2023, prohibits most abortions after a fetal heartbeat is detectable, which the state Supreme Court has set as six weeks. It threatens violating doctors with up to two years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000 and the possibility of losing a medical license.
The trial focused on when, exactly, medical exceptions to the ban apply: abortions needed to save the mother’s life or prevent lifelong impairment or diagnosis of an anomaly so severe the fetus isn’t expected to survive after birth.
The plaintiffs argued that its wording can lead different doctors to reach different conclusions.
The law allows doctors to use “reasonable medical judgment,” but doctors challenging it questioned how a prosecutor would decide that.
Doctors should understand what’s reasonable and what isn’t, attorneys for the governor and attorney general’s office said. Four doctors who testified for the defense said they found the law easy to understand and implement.
“If you are being reasonable, you are not violating the law,” said Grayson Lambert, attorney for the governor.
“That’s a subjective standard,” Gergel replied.
None of the defense’s doctors performed abortions before the law passed because of religious objections, they testified. That means they have no reason to fear the law, unlike the doctors challenging the law, who previously performed abortions as a routine part of their care, their attorneys said.
Gergel repeatedly called the law vague and said he had serious problems with it.
He also questioned how wide his ruling should be, including whether it should apply only to the doctors who sued. He’s unlikely to issue an order halting the law entirely, he said.
If Gergel finds the law unconstitutional, an appeal is certain, Lambert told him.
‘Good faith’ clause
Gergel said there’s a relatively easy fix to the problems he saw: If legislators added a clause protecting doctors acting in good faith, Gergel would consider the law constitutional, he said.
That wording would fall in line with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1992 decision in Planned Parenthood v. Casey, which redefined the guaranteed right to an abortion nationally and allowed more state regulation.
Pennsylvania’s law, which the case challenged, included similar phrases to those contested in South Carolina. But the blanket “good faith” clause made it clear doctors wouldn’t face prosecution if they misunderstood, Gergel said.
The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 decision that returned the legality of abortions back to the states overturned both Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood v. Casey.
As written, the state’s 2023 law has no mention of a doctor’s intention. Other criminal laws require proof that a person intended to harm someone. The abortion law requires only proof that doctors intended to provide an abortion, even if they thought they were following the law, Gergel said.
Doctors don’t have the power of hindsight, he said.
Sometimes, a doctor has to make a call in the moment that another doctor might not agree with, or even that the doctor might not have done in retrospect, Gergel said.
Whether legislators would make that change is another question. Trying to tweak the law would reopen debates on even stricter abortion restrictions.
Gergel can’t change the law. And he probably couldn’t strike only the exceptions, he said, though Lambert tried to argue Gergel could legally get rid of the exception for fatal fetal anomalies.
Legislators clearly intended for abortions to remain legal in certain cases, Gergel said.
Otherwise, he noted, they would have passed a law with no exceptions. Proposals of that sort have failed repeatedly.
Unconstitutionally vague
Doctors who testified during the trial disagreed about when the exceptions applied.
Even the state’s witnesses, chosen to speak about how they found the law clear, disagreed about when an abortion would be legal under the exceptions.
“I think the only thing we can agree on here is none of them agree with each other,” Gergel said.
For instance, one doctor interpreted a requirement that an abortion could be performed only if the fetus had an abnormality “incompatible with sustaining life after birth” to mean the baby would live no more than six months. Another drew the cutoff at a year. And both said they thought chromosomal abnormalities that kill most babies at birth would qualify, even though other doctors pointed out some rare cases when those children lived for years.
“Can we figure out what is ‘reasonable medical judgment’ when there’s such a diversity of opinion?” Gergel said.
Being ambiguous doesn’t necessarily make a law unconstitutional, Gergel said. But when the punishment might mean prison time or the end of a person’s professional career, people need clarity, he said.
That’s especially true in a complicated medical case, Gergel said.
Doctors need to feel certain about which procedures they can perform without wondering whether they’ll go to prison. And police need to understand what’s allowed so they don’t make arbitrary arrests, he said.
“The statute is sort of written like (legislators) are playing checkers and doctors are playing three-level chess,” Gergel said.
None of the doctors who testified during the trial were investigated or charged with a crime for performing an abortion. But those who did offer abortions erred on the side of caution, often sending patients with ambiguous cases out of state, they said.
“Had they kept them in (state), who knows what would’ve happened?” Gergel said.
Some cases are clearly defined, Gergel said. If a woman is in active kidney failure, “a Boy Scout can figure” out she qualifies for the exception, he said.
“I’m trying to figure out, for the not-easy cases, is there some fixed meaning so physicians are not put in jeopardy?” Gergel said.
Without it, the state will continue losing OB-GYNs afraid to practice in the state, Gergel said.
“There won’t be any OB-GYNs left,” he said.
