In his indictment, he is charged with voting in the 2022 primary election In Idaho, when statewide officials and congressional seats were up, as well as the 2024 general election, when President Donald Trump was up for election, along with congressional seats in Idaho and other races. Prosecutors allege he used a fraudulent California birth certificate to get an Idaho identification card and a federal passport, and that he fraudulently received Medicaid from 2020 to 2026. 
The Justice Department announced his prosecution along with other election crime cases on Sept. 18. The Justice Department’s news release of the cases included a photo of Avila Gomez being detained, with his face blurred, by agents of the federal Homeland Security Investigations and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
His attorney, Christopher Sanchez with the nonprofit Federal Defender Services of Idaho, declined to comment.
 State referred batch of noncitizen voting cases to Justice Department about a year ago, public record shows

Around August or September 2025, Idaho State Police referred about a dozen noncitizen voting cases to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho for possible prosecution, according to an internal email from an Idaho state election official that the Idaho Capital Sun obtained in a public records request. 
The referrals trace back to a 2024 audit of all registered voters in Idaho, conducted by the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office.
In the lead up to the 2026 midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake, the Trump administration has ramped up efforts to intervene in state election processes, such as to restrict mail-in voting and obtain state voter rolls. 
The Justice Department has lost 23 lawsuits that sought to force states to provide voter data. The Justice Department’s lawsuit against McGrane in Idaho remains on hold.
Under the second Trump administration, prosecutions for noncitizen voting have been sparse. In July, University of Idaho professor Benjamin Cover, who tracks such cases, said he had only found about two dozen prosecutions since Trump re-gained office, and none were in Idaho.
In a stern letter this summer after the Justice Department threatened to prosecute election officials if they let noncitizens vote in the midterms, a high-ranking attorney in the Idaho Attorney General’s Office asked the federal government for updates on about 15 noncitizen voting cases that the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office had referred to the Justice Department for possible prosecution.
But shortly after McGrane’s attorney sent the federal government that letter, he said that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security issued a report — at Trump’s request — that showed “Idaho has the cleanest voter rolls in the country of those states that had been checked.”
The report showed Idaho had 49 non-citizens on its voter rolls, compared to hundreds or thousands in other states surveyed that had accessed the federal agency’s citizenship database called SAVE. Idaho also had, according to the report, more than 4,300 dead people on its voter rolls. State officials say they routinely clean the registered voter list.
The federal government’s report’s total is higher than the roughly 15 noncitizens who were on voter rolls that Idaho officials referred to the federal government for possible prosecution last year.
Many experts also disagreed with the report’s topline claim: That more than a quarter million noncitizens were registered voters in just four states under review.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Nearly $10M spent by outside groups attacking independent TN gubernatorial candidate
text:
David Hatley, center, is an independent candidate running for governor. Political action committees supporting his Republican opponent, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn have spent $10 million on attack ads. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Two independent expenditure groups have now spent just under $10 million attacking Tennessee independent gubernatorial candidate David Hatley, with the 2026 election less than five days away.
Hatley is running as a “conservative” independent, drawing ire from U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican gubernatorial nominee. Hatley is a Washington County hot tub mogul who has loaned nearly $12 million to his campaign, according to an Oct. 27 pre-election filing.
Blackburn is the frontrunner in the race, but almost immediately after her August primary win, instead of attacking her Democratic Party opponent — Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green — her campaign created a website going after Hatley called “deadbeatDave.com”
The attack advertisements against Hatley are funded by the Tennessee Freedom Fund ($3 million) and the Choose Freedom Fund ($6.5 million).
The Tennessee Freedom Fund has been funded through Blackburn’s Senate campaign account, finance billionaire Jeff Yass and another pro-Blackburn PAC called Team Tennessee, whose top donors include payday lender Advance Financial and tobacco giant Reynolds America.
The Tennessee Freedom Fund is run by staffers for Club For Growth, a conservative group at the forefront of pushing private school vouchers in the state.
But the money backing Choose Freedom is harder to track.



Quotation







This looks less like a donor trying to hide their spending and more about creating distance from partisan activity. Choose Freedom wants people to see its attacks as a legitimate issue, as opposed to the motive being politics and partisan meddling.


– Brendan Glavin, OpenSecrets


The Choose Freedom PAC registered in Tennessee on Sept. 18, and on the same day, it took a donation of exactly $4.2 million, spending the same amount on ads attacking Hatley over legal issues surrounding his finances in the 1990s. Hatley has openly discussed his previous financial crimes on the trail and in a biography he released ahead of his campaign.
The group then took in another $2.3 million on Oct. 13 and spent the exact amount again that same day on more ads attacking Hatley.
Campaign finance records show the donation to the Choose Freedom PAC is virtually untraceable to a person. The donation to the Choose Freedom PAC came from Choose Freedom Inc., a political nonprofit set up to spend tens of millions of dollars in 2026 races across the country, according to The New York Times. 
Almost immediately after the August primary election, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign set up a website to attack David Hatley, a conservative iindependent candidate for governor. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, an organization that tracks money in politics, said Choose Freedom Inc.’s address was registered to Red Curve Solutions in Massachusetts, an accounting and compliance services firm whose major client is MAGA Inc., the primary PAC affiliated with President Donald Trump.
“This looks less like a donor trying to hide their spending and more about creating distance from partisan activity,” said Glavin. “Choose Freedom wants people to see its attacks as a legitimate issue, as opposed to the motive being politics and partisan meddling.”
Choose Freedom PAC’s in Tennessee lists an Alabama office address. The same address is listed for several other PACs run by national conservative groups, like the Alliance For a Better Future and Civic Renewal Fund.
The Lookout emailed a representative listed for the Choose Freedom PAC with questions and received no response. A reporter also called the number listed for the PAC and received a message saying the number couldn’t receive calls.
The Lookout reached out to the Blackburn campaign for this story and received no response
Marsha Blackburn, the $100M woman

Why the attack ads on Hatley help Blackburn
After winning the Republican primary, Blackburn became the favorite to become Tennessee’s next governor, as the GOP hasn’t lost a statewide elected office in two decades.
During the primary, rival U.S. Rep. John Rose spent nearly $14 million of his own money. Blackburn relied on support from the Tennessee Freedom Fund and Team Tennessee.
The cost of the primary sapped Blackburn’s campaign finances: Her campaign had $1 million in cash in the bank with one week left in the campaign, compared with Hatley’s $3.9 million, according to state campaign finance filings.
After the primary, it quickly became clear that Hatley, a self-described conservative businessman, planned to spend millions and court traditional Republican voters.
“I’ve always been pro-life and pro-guns,” Hatley said to the Lookout. “I want to be independent because I don’t want to have party pressure.”
Trump came to Tennessee on Oct. 10 for a rally in Clarksville, which featured Blackburn, among other state GOP lawmakers.
Blackburn was one of the first U.S. House members to endorse Trump in 2016, an early bet that paid off when he endorsed her in her successful U.S. Senate bid two years later. Trump did not endorse Blackburn in the primary, but her campaign materials and independent advertisements emphasized her close ties to the president.
Blackburn said at the rally she was the “only conservative” race.
Trump told attendees, “you have to vote Republican.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama House Speaker calls for pause on Escambia prison construction project
text:
Alabama House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter, R-Rainsville, speaks at a press conference on Feb. 12, 2025 in Montgomery, Alabama as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey listens in the background. Ledbetter sent a letter to Ivey Thursday criticizing cost overruns on the state prisons and calling for a halt to construction on an Escambia County facility, which Ivey later rejected. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The speaker of the Alabama House of Representatives Thursday called for construction on a men’s prison in Escambia County to stop amid rising costs and delays in the completion of another prison in Elmore County.
In a Thursday letter to Gov. Kay Ivey, House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter, R-Rainsville, expressed frustration that her administration had ignored “every request from the Legislature to press pause” on building the Escambia facility and said the Alabama Department of Corrections had “lost all control” over construction of the Elmore facility, named for Ivey.
“Committing taxpayers to another major financial obligation under these circumstances, without first addressing the cost overruns, delays, and apparent failures in project management, is an unacceptable risk to public funds and a failure of fiscal responsibility,” Ledbetter said in his letter. “To make matters worse, you will be exiting office in less than three months, leaving the next administration to clean up the mess.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The letter represented the first major break between Ivey and legislative leaders over the two 4,000-bed facilities. The Legislature in 2021 approved $1.3 billion for the construction of the two prisons, but the costs of the Elmore facility alone have reached $1.25 billion.
Ledbetter and other lawmakers in 2023 appeared resigned to the cost increases. He said at the time that inflation had affected the cost of all goods and services, like construction. But lawmakers in both parties have grown increasingly critical as expenses mount.
Thursday’s letter came a few weeks after the state sold $190 million in bonds to a division of Regions Bank for the construction of the Escambia facility; a few hours before a meeting of the Alabama Corrections Institution Finance Authority, which oversees funding for prison construction; five days before state elections and three months before Ivey leaves office.
The governor’s office said Thursday ACIFA approved a construction contract for the Escambia prison.
Ivey in a statement rejected Ledbetter’s call to stop construction, saying problems plaguing Alabama’s prison system had been neglected for “far too long” and that her administration had worked to address them.
“My administration has been committed and dually-focused on protecting taxpayer dollars while moving forward with these critical and necessary public safety projects,” Ivey said in the news release. “Throughout the appropriations process over the last five years, I am extremely proud that we have been able to save the money necessary to make these facilities a reality in a fiscally responsible way.”
The Alabama Department of Corrections announced earlier in October that the completion of the Gov. Kay Ivey Correctional Complex in Elmore County would be delayed.
Ledbetter wrote that he met with the governor’s staff and ADOC Commissioner Greg Lovelace in July and was told the Elmore facility would not be completed until “sometime between March and May 2027.”
The letter said he told staff and the ADOC of his concerns with moving forward with financing a second prison using taxpayer-backed debt with the Elmore site one year behind schedule and cost overruns that total about $635 million.
The total cost of the project has increased to about $2.2 billion, according to Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, who is a member of the ACIFA.
ACIFA Thursday approved the Escambia construction on a 6-1 vote. Rep. Rex Reynolds, R-Huntsville, the chair of the House Ways and Means General Fund Committee, which oversees Corrections financing, said Thursday he voted against the agreement.
“We have never said we did not want to move forward on Escambia, we just felt like we are in such an administrative posture with trying to get the first prison complete that we maybe should delay that prison until we can be sure,” Reynolds said in an interview Thursday.
He said there could be a contractual problem with the prison in Elmore County that could cost the state even more money.
“Those are the kinds of decisions we need to know before we work on the Escambia prison,” Reynolds said.
Albritton voted to move forward with the construction project.
“If you would take a look at any other capital project of this size, or even half this size, through the nation, through the same timeframe, you will see the same issues,” Albritton said. “Between costs of labor, between materials and COVID costs that have skyrocketed … so do you want to wait to let it go up some more?”
Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, has consistently criticized the cost and delays associated with the project.
“I am not sure what from recent history we saw that gave us any confidence that ADOC and this administration could complete this project,” he said. “We are still nowhere near finished with what is now a well over a billion-dollar Elmore County facility, to now borrow more money to push this facility over a billion dollars. It is a bad idea, it was a bad idea then, it is a worse idea now.”
Speaking at a campaign event in Auburn Thursday evening, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones said he didn’t “get involved in Republican Party squabbles.”
“I’m going to get elected in five days, and then come January we’re going to have a new prison commissioner,” he said. “We’re going to get to the bottom of a lot of things. It was the Legislature that approved all this. There’s a lot of blame to go around for all the problems that we’ve got in our prison system right now. I’ll let them fight it out.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Palace intrigue takes over Tennessee Senate
text:
Palace intrigue: Sen. Ken Yager, left, a Kingston Republican, says GOP Senate leaders are considering allowing Sen. Brent Taylor to vote by proxy in the GOP caucus election to be Senate Speaker. Sen. Jack Johnson, right, of Franklin, is a candidate. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Intrigue is ramping up in advance of a Senate Republican Caucus vote that will choose the next lieutenant governor, the person first in line to succeed an incapacitated governor.
Caucus Chairman Ken Yager confirmed Thursday leaders are considering allowing Sen. Brent Taylor, if he wins the 9th District congressional race next week, to vote by proxy in the caucus officers decision, an atypical move. Taylor’s vote is needed by Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson of Franklin, who’s trying to ward off Sen. Paul Bailey of Sparta for the state’s second most important political job. 
The conflict comes up because the state Senate Republican vote is set for Nov. 10, the same day a congressional caucus election is scheduled in Washington, D.C. Presumably, Taylor would have to be in the nation’s capital if he defeats Democratic Rep. Justin Pearson next week.
The caucus vote in Nashville will decide the outcome because Senate Republicans hold a 27-6 supermajority over Democrats.
“The subject has been discussed, but no decision has been made,” Yager said Thursday. He couldn’t tell how much support exists within the caucus for a move to let Taylor’s attorney cast a vote in his place.
Yager, who said he wants more discussion before deciding whether he would support the move, couldn’t recall anyone being allowed to vote by proxy previously.  
Taylor, who is also running in the District 31 state Senate race against Democratic candidate David Weatherspoon, is believed to be backing Johnson of Franklin over Bailey. Taylor declined to say whom he’s supporting and pointed out contested caucus races are done by secret ballot.
Should Sen. Brent Taylor win his congressional race, he would not be able to be present for the hotly-contested Senate caucus leadership vote. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The race is extremely tight as the candidates battle for 14 votes, the majority needed to replace outgoing Lt. Gov. Randy McNally, who is stepping down from the legislature after nearly 50 years.
Two to three caucus members are uncommitted, and the competitors are trying to maintain their support, sort of like keeping squirrels in a cage.
The discussion about letting Taylor vote absentee marks another effort to give Johnson an advantage in the caucus vote. 
Leaders kicked around the possibility of removing Sen. Janice Bowling from the caucus after she endorsed independent gubernatorial candidate David Hatley instead of the Republican nominee, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the odds-on favorite to win Tuesday.
Bowling recently told the Lookout she doesn’t believe the caucus has any “basis” to remove her, and it doesn’t appear leadership will try to kick her out before the vote. There is a chance, though, they could remove her afterward, even if it makes them look a little heavy-handed.
A billion here, a billion there
With an eye toward the future, Tennessee’s Department of Transportation did exactly as predicted: awarded a bid to a toll-road builder and then started finagling with the money.
The state’s Transportation Modernization Board selected a group called DriveTN for a $9.2 billion toll project from downtown Nashville to Murfreesboro, based mainly on the consortium’s guarantee to pay the state nearly $25 billion.
Initially, the group said it would pay $1.5 billion up front and the rest during an eight-year construction phase. 
But a new “concession agreement” with the partnership led by Spain-based Ferrovial sets up a financial structure allowing the group to pay $7.7 billion during construction and $140 billion over the rest of the 50-year contract.
Tennessee toll lane contractor promises to pay state nearly $148 billion

Ouch, did you say $140 mill? It wasn’t a typo.
“When all payments are converted into today’s dollars, the overall value to TDOT remains the same” as the original concession, the department said in a clarification statement. 
Gee whizzakers, Toto, that explains everything.
The department came out with the explanation more than a day after the Lookout asked whether the $140 billion included in a Tuesday press release was correct. After all, it seems a little steep.
It probably won’t suit the other bidding group, 24 Choice Lanes Partners, that challenged the state’s bid decision, though it sort of falls in line with that consortium’s legal argument.
“As litigation is still pending, we’re unable to comment or answer additional questions at this time,” TDOT said in its clarification.
Democratic state Sen. Heidi Campbell isn’t too happy either.
“This is a time-worn trick,” Campbell said, arguing the bidder didn’t add tens of billions to the deal. “They moved the payments to our grandchildren’s lifetimes and hoped we’d be impressed by the bigger number.”
The money is the same, it’s just added up over half a century and “inflated by time,” Campbell said. “Nothing got bigger, it just got later.”
The Nashville lawmaker added that the state’s announcement describes a payment schedule very similar to what the plaintiffs  alleged in the lawsuit in Davidson County Chancery Court. Campbell noted that the state still hasn’t made the contract public and raised questions about where the $1.5 billion up-front payment went.



Quotation







This is a time-worn trick. They moved the payments to our grandchildren’s lifetimes and hoped we’d be impressed by the bigger number.


– Sen. Heidi Campbell, D-Nashville


Another question could involve maintenance costs on the toll lanes and potential penalties for the state if it improves the free lanes on I-24 or adds mass transit.
Campbell said she welcomes a Comptroller’s Office review of the contract and asked the transportation department to release the full concession agreement immediately, not after the state closes the deal. 
“If this is as good a deal as the governor says, there’s no reason to keep it in the dark,” Campbell said.
Gov. Bill Lee, who endorsed the deal in August by saying it would help pay for road projects statewide, downplayed the restructuring this week.
Asked whether the financial change dilutes the value of the deal for the state and increases Tennessee’s risk, Lee said it does the opposite.
“We actually think it increases the value because it generates a long-term funding stream for our state,” Lee said.
The governor acknowledged there are advantages to taking the money in a lump sum, but he said long-term payments will help the state avoid raising the gas tax. That’s plenty of justification for resolving congested interstates with toll roads.
Tennessee’s newest resident? Gov. Bill Lee announced Tennessee will vie to be picked for new Trump-backed U.S. Space Academy. Rumor is Buzz Lightyear, of Disney and Pixar’s “Toy Story,” could be selected as the commander. (Photo: Getty Images)
“To infinity and beyond”
The governor announced this week Tennessee is in the hunt for a U.S. Space Academy to be run by NASA to train astronauts, scientists and engineers.
Lee said Tennessee is “well-positioned to potentially be a front-runner” for the academy, which would go on a Coffee County megasite and fit with Arnold Engineering Development Center, University of Tennessee Space Institute and Arnold Air Force Base in Tullahoma, as well as the Huntsville Space Center. “That corridor is uniquely positioned, and our state is uniquely positioned. We are innovatively leading in quantum, in nuclear, and it makes a lot of sense for NASA to consider a location like Coffee County for a space center.”
Texas is putting $100 million toward a bid for the academy, and Colorado, home to the NASA Aerospace Workforce Hub, is going for the project announced in August by President Donald Trump. It’s supposed to be similar to one of the nation’s military service academies, which cost upwards of $1 billion a year to run, and everyone knows we have plenty of money, even with a national debt of $40.56 trillion and rising by the second, which could have us all living in the ghetto soon enough.
“Too many lives they’ve spent across the ocean / Too much been spent upon the moon”*
*“Things Going On,” Lynyrd Skynyrd

name: West Virginia Watch
title: PAC in West Virginia rural race has ties to school at center of grant controversy
text:
In recent weeks, residents in Mason and Jackson counties have received mailers attacking Kat Weiland, a Democrat challenging Republican incumbent Del. Jonathan Pinson, R-Mason. (Photo courtesy of Kat Weiland)A super PAC distributing attack mailers against a candidate in the rural 17th House District appears to have had financial ties to a Catholic college in Ohio in the recent past. 
In recent weeks, residents in Mason and Jackson counties have received mailers attacking Kat Weiland, a Democrat challenging Republican incumbent Del. Jonathan Pinson, R-Mason. But who is behind takes a little bit of digging — and reveals a surprising financial relationship with a Catholic college that was embroiled in a court battle last year. 
Weiland said when she ran for office, she didn’t anticipate seeing the type of attacks typically reserved for a high-profile race. 
“Never in my life did I dream that I would go to the post office, open my mailbox and pull out not one, not two, not three, but four fliers and see my face on a political attack mailer,” she said. 
The fliers, depicting Weiland in black and white photos, warn voters that her platform would cost them taxpayer money. 
“More government. A bigger bill for tax payers,” reads one ad. “West Virginia can’t afford Kat Weiland’s agenda.” 
The proposals at issue are universal pre-kindergarten for three-year-olds, childcare subsidies and raising the minimum wage. 
In the corner of the mailer, next to the pre-sorted stamp and above the recipient address, reads “Paid for by Conservative Policy Action.” 
That committee also ran mailers during the Republican primary, mainly in support of state lawmakers who had drawn the ire of the governor, such as Del. Scot Heckert, R-Wood, Sen. Vince Deeds, R-Greenbrier and Del. Jeff Stephens, R-Marshall. 
But in the general election, the PAC has only spent money in the Weiland-Pinson race, which so far has amounted to around $14,000. 
Conservative Action Policy is registered as a super PAC, also known as an independent expenditure committee. They can raise unlimited amounts of money and can spend donations  in support or against candidates in a race. However, they cannot directly contribute to a campaign, nor can they coordinate with a candidate running for office. 
Most of the funding for the PAC has come from a political non-profit called Conservative Policy Solutions Inc., which is led by Matthew Parker, a political consultant from West Virginia who now lives in Oklahoma, according to Federal Election Commission records. 
As a 501(c)4, Conservative Policy Solutions Inc. can donate to political causes. Typically, this type of arrangement is what’s known as “dark money” in politics, money that is used to influence elections but can’t be traced. 
That’s because a non-profit, unlike a political committee, isn’t required to publicly disclose its donors. 
But in this case, IRS records shed a bit of light as to where some funding for Conservative Policy Solutions Inc as to its funding sources in the recent past. 
Tax records in 2024 show Conservative Policy Solutions Inc. raised around $500,000 in revenue, just a year after it was incorporated in Delaware. 
That same year, The Center for the Common Good Foundation gave Conservative Policy Solutions Inc $477,000. 
For the readers with a long memory, that’s the conservative think-tank the College of St. Joseph the Worker tried to set up with a portion of the $5 million it received from the West Virginia Water Development Authority in December 2024. 
The College of St. Joseph the Worker is located in Steubenville, Ohio, just across the river from Weirton in the Northern Panhandle. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia filed suit against the use of taxpayer money for a religious school outside the state and a Kanawha County judge ruled that the school had to change aspects of its plans to avoid violating the separation between church and state. 
The College of St. Joseph the Worker, Conservative Policy Solutions Inc., and Conservative Policy Action PAC did not respond to a request for comment. 
Del. Jonathan Pinson, R-Mason, offered the following statement regarding the mailers: 
“Each year, outside organizations become involved in races statewide. State law allows these organizations to express their views. However, they do not represent me or my campaign, nor do they influence my decisions. I can only speak for my own campaign, my record and my positions on the issues that matter to our community.” 
Weiland said the mailers could possibly backfire. 
“Some of those things seem kind of good,” she said. “We’re talking about childcare. It’s just an idea of having universal 3K. We already have universal pre-K for four-year-olds in West Virginia, which is wonderful. Why not possibly allow universal 3K in West Virginia? If we can send kids to school a year earlier, that’s another year earlier the parents can get back into the workforce.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: “Work a little bit harder.” Tennessee’s women running for governor face challenges men don’t
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, left, Democratic Memphis City Council member Jerri Green and independent Lauren Pinkston are three of the woman vying to be Tennessee's first female governor. (Photos by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Three major candidates for Tennessee governor agree on at least one thing — it’s harder campaigning as a woman. 
No woman has served as governor of Tennessee in the 230 years since the inception of the Volunteer State. The first year women running for the office were considered serious competitors was in 2018 when U.S. Rep. Daine Black and former state House Speaker Beth Harwell lost to now-Gov. Bill Lee in the Republican primary. Prior to that, the last woman to undertake a serious gubernatorial campaign was in 1986 when former Public Service Commissioner Jane Eskind ran in the Democratic primary.
Today, with three women competing in the general election — Republican nominee and current U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Democratic nominee and Memphis City Council member Jerri Green, and former Lipscomb University Professor Lauren Pinkston, an independent candidate — it’s nearly certain that this November Tennessee will elect its first. 
Tennessee’s likely position to make history comes at a time when the number of women serving as governor across the country is at a record high. Although still not representative of the country’s demographics, 14 states have women in the governor’s seat, according to Rutgers University Center for American Women and Politics. Across the country, women make up 35.1% of nominees for governor, the highest since 2018, according to Rutgers. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
What’s less common is that Tennessee has women nominees for both major parties. Only three other states, Minnesota, New Hampshire and Oregon, have races for governor where the major-party nominees are women, reported the Center for American Women and Politics. 
Green is hopeful that with gender equal in the race, misogyny is not going to be on the ballot. 
“It’s going to be woman versus woman, and people are going to have to make a decision based on our policies and our platforms and our plans for Tennesseans and for Tennessee women in particular,” she said.
Pinkston said women across the top of the ballot create a unique opportunity for Tennesseans to vote based on ideas rather than the biases they might have surrounding someone’s race or gender. 
Despite this, Pinkston said as a woman running for office, the level of scrutiny is higher than for a man. Blackburn said she had to prove herself as a woman in politics, and Green said it’s more difficult to raise money as a woman and to deal with constant nasty comments and threats.
Marsha Blackburn: Used to being a ‘first’
On the first day of early voting in Tennessee, a meet-and-greet hosted by the Hamilton County Republican Women’s Club at Morning Pointe Senior Center in Chattanooga is sandwiched between Blackburn voting in the election that could propel her to the governor’s office and an evening fundraising event with her closest supporters in the city. 
Despite an absence of reliable polling data, Blackburn, with nearly 30 years of electoral experience, is considered by many politicos to be the favorite in the race. 
After decades spent serving in public office, Blackburn is accustomed to being the first. She became the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from Tennessee in 2018. She still holds the seat and has said if she becomes governor, she will wait to vacate the seat and choose an interim appointee rather than step down earlier for Gov. Bill Lee to choose.
In 1989, Blackburn became the first woman to hold the position of chair of the Williamson County GOP, one of the few female chairs in the state at the time. Ten years later, in Blackburn’s first year as a Tennessee State Senator, a total of 18 women served in the 132-person Tennessee legislature, among the lowest levels of female representation in statehouses across the country. 
Blackburn said she was the only Republican woman in the state Senate when she was elected.
“Female leaders have to work a little bit harder to secure their place,” Blackburn said in an interview. “But we have been so fortunate to break ceilings and open doors of opportunity for women, and I’ve done that all of my career.”



Q&A: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
What is some of the best advice you’ve gotten from a woman?
“Best advice is ‘don’t back down.’ And that is something that really has been a point made to me by some of my mentors to just, you know, develop that titanium backbone, and do not back down. And I really can hold my own and push back a lot on the negatives because I know who I am, and what I stand for, and I know what I believe, and so that is vitally important.”
What three women, dead or alive, would you invite to dinner?
“Margaret Thatcher, Jean Kirkpatrick, and then if I could talk to Deborah and Esther from Biblical Times, and because I fully believe that God charts your course, and you have to be willing to listen to that and the way they carried that forward, I think that’d be fascinating to hear their version.”  


Blackburn pointed to the few women in the state senate in the late 90s compared to the current U.S. Senate, which has more women serving than ever before, when asked if she thinks her experience as a woman in office has changed over the years.
“There is a conservative majority, and conservative women have stepped up, and they have served well. That’s good. That opens doors of opportunity for other women,” Blackburn said when asked about the environment for women in Congress today compared to the state senate.  
In Blackburn’s 2020 book, “The Mind of a Conservative Woman: Seeking the Best for Family,” and Country, she writes about experiencing bias as a woman. She details being underestimated as a competitive candidate because of her petite stature and blond hair and that she has received threats of rape, violence against her family and herself.
An investigation published by the New York Times earlier this month directly quotes a death threat that names Blackburn. She declined to comment on it.
If elected, she wants to continue opening doors for women. She said she hears from women all across the state about what they want. 
“What they want is more opportunities, not only for themselves, but for others in the community. They want higher wages, so that they can be more productive in their work; they want to make certain that opportunity is there,” Blackburn said. “That’s why I say regularly, one of my goals is to be sure we are the state of opportunity, and I want us to be known as that, so that people know when they come here they can go live their version of the American dream.” 
Blackburn said creating opportunity from the governor’s seat means fostering the environment for job growth and then government getting out of the way and letting the private sector do its part. 
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn speaking at the Faith and Freedom "Road to Majority" on June 17, 2022 in Nashville. (Photo: John Partipilo)


U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn at Gov. Bill Lee's second inauguration on Jan. 21, 2023. (Photo: John Partipilo)U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, pictured in a December 2025  photo from a rally supporting U.S. Rep. Matt Van Epps. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“It also means opening doors and making certain that women know they can apply for different positions and that it’s going to be a level playing field.”
Blackburn said there are plenty of laws on the books when asked if, as governor, there was policy or legislation she would push for to ensure women applying to jobs in Tennessee know there is a level playing field. 
“I think women just want to know if they’re going to get a fair shake,” Blackburn said. “And I want them to know they are going to get that fair shake.”
Her apprehension to push for laws or implement practices as governor that regulate women in the workplace is consistent with her previous votes in Congress.
Historically, Blackburn has voted against laws that require equal pay for women. Most notably in 2009, as a member of the U.S. House, she voted against the Lily Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, which aimed to make it easier for women to file employment discrimination cases based on pay differences between their male counterparts, and the Paycheck Fairness Act intended to prevent sex discrimination in the workplace.
Blackburn has previously said that she voted no because the laws are unnecessary government overreach and increase litigation rather than empower women.
In 2013, Blackburn voted against the bipartisan version of the Violence Against Women Act reauthorization that passed Congress. Blackburn said expanded protections under the act to LGBTQ+, without full legal status and certain Native Americans diluted the aim.  
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, with family and state Sen. Jack Johnson, far right, and his wife, Williamson County Judge Deanna Johnson, celebrate her reelection on November 5. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
She pointed to the Childcare for American Families Act as an example of a bill that helps women.  She championed the bipartisan bill that updates the federal tax code to aid businesses in offsetting the cost of providing childcare for their workers. The bill was first introduced in 2024 and passed with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025
“That’s one of the biggest issues women have: having the ability to have somebody that they can rely on to provide that childcare for their precious little ones,” Blackburn said. “And securing that has opened some doors for people for consistent employment and for moms to be able to return to the workforce.”
When campaigning, Blackburn has often said she is a mother and grandmother first and she doesn’t miss cooking Sunday lunch for all of her family. She said someone in the family will text her to inquire about the menu if they haven’t heard from her by noon on Saturday.
Jerri Green: “You govern differently”
Green, the Democratic nominee for governor, said she realized women face a ton of glass ceilings at an early age. 
More precisely, it was at eight or nine, Green said, when she dressed up as Sandra Day O’Connor for Halloween.
“I thought she was the coolest,” Green recalls thinking about the first woman to serve as a U.S. Supreme Court Justice. “I guess I was just excited to see other women come before me do great things. There were definitely women role models in my life that were taking big risks, that were going into male-dominated fields, and you know, probably somewhere along the line, young Jerri picked up on that, and it’s now, I guess, manifesting here 48 years later.”
Green is running to represent working families, motivated to throw her hat in the ring by her three children, whom she refers to as her special interests. Green wants to expand paid family and medical leave, deliver affordable child care, and provide a real living wage. Her tagline is “One Tough Mother.”
“The truth of the matter is, a lot of the skills of motherhood really do translate well into being a part of either an executive administration or the legislative branch,” Green said. “It’s a really diverse set of skill sets that you get, whether it’s multitasking or dealing with a lot of different personalities, all of those things that you end up doing as a mother translate well into government.”



Q&A: Councilmember Jerri Green
What is some of the best advice you’ve gotten from a woman?
“Pat Head Summitt is one of my heroes and has been for a while, and she didn’t give me this piece of advice directly, but she has this saying . . . It’s left foot, right foot, breath, and so I say that to myself a lot when it gets hard.”
What three women, dead or alive, would you invite to dinner?
“Dolly Parton, Pat Head Summitt, and gosh, It’s a toss-up between Ruth Bader Ginsburg or Betty White. I hear Betty White had good dirty jokes, so maybe Betty White.” 


Women across the state are fired up, Green said. 
“They’re the ones that go to the grocery stores and fill up the gas tanks, and they see that the prices are too high. They’re the ones that, you know, balance the utility bills and the medical bills. They’re the ones that are in the sandwich generation of trying to feed their 16-year-old and take care of their 70-year-old parent, you know, without any good paid parental leave or good wages, and I know that women in particular are really ready for change,” she said.
Green said women running for office face challenges men are less likely to.
There is a barrage of nasty and sexual insults, sometimes in the comments, sometimes in the DMs,” Green said.  “I mean, I know I’ve gotten violent rape threats, but not even to that degree. I mean, I’ve experienced it. I know Marsha has. People are always commenting on our looks in a way that they don’t do that to Bernie (Sanders) or to Mitch McConnell. You know what I mean? But it seems to be fair game if you’re a woman.”
Jerri Green at the Tennessee Press Association and Middle Tennessee State University 2026 Gubernatorial forum, Oct. 27, 2025 at MTSU in Murfreesboro, Tennessee. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Memphis Councilmember Jerri Green, photographed in Nashville, January 20, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)

When Green was elected to Memphis City Council in 2023, six other women won their races,  ushering in the first female majority in 200 years.
Since then, the council has increased pre-k funding, passed paid parental leave for the first time in the city’s history, invested in youth mental health services, created a nursing suite in the council chambers, and moved the council’s meeting time so it was not during carpool line time so more mothers could participate, Green said.
Green said, “I just think when you are a parent, you are a mother, you govern differently. When you’re a woman, you govern differently, and it’s past time that we have that perspective in Nashville as well.”
One day, Green said, she hopes that there are so many women in places and seats of power that it doesn’t need an article or remember a time there weren’t. 
Democratic nominee for governor,Jerri Green at a Memphis forum at Teamsters Local 667 October 09, 2026 in Memphis, Tennessee. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)
Lauren Pinkston: “No greater threat to unchecked power than a free woman with a conscience”
Pinkston grew up in a very conservative rural Tennessee culture, a part of a conservative church culture.
 “In my worldview and in the worldview that I was raised in, women were second class. We were trained to be subordinate,” Pinkston said.
As an independent candidate for governor, Pinkston pushes back against the two-party system and ran on the promise of offering a third option for those dissatisfied with both major parties. 
The same sentiment of pushing back exists when Pinkston talks about challenging her own faith tradition and what it taught her about women. 
“We were trained to believe that women couldn’t be trusted in leadership, and I had to do a lot of my own work to try to understand that my role and my duty to my community is to be my full self, regardless of my gender,” Pinkston said.
However, Pinkston’s belief that she can be her full self regardless of gender is not one held by everyone. While discussing the campaign, she describes defending the version of herself today, a candidate for Tennessee governor, against critics. 
Like Greene, Pinkston said her dedication as a mother has been questioned. Pinkston said she has been accused of not loving her children because she chooses to work outside the home or has been told that her role is in the kitchen.
“I am very, very clear that I can do both things at the same time. I’m a pretty incredible cook, actually, and I also am pretty intelligent when it comes to policy work,” she said. “Right, like those two things can coexist at the same time.”



Q&A: Lauren Pinkston
What is some of the best advice you’ve gotten from a woman?
“I would say for any woman running, never forget who your real people are, right? Know who you’re going to for truth, and stay anchored there. Some of the best advice that I got when I started this campaign was: if you’re walking out the door to go to a political event and it looks like your husband’s not going to vote for you, you stay home. And they would say that to a husband too: if you’re walking out and it looks like your wife’s not going to vote for you, you know, stay home. 
“Involve your family in the entire process and create space for the family to push back into grief. I left for a weekend recently, and the kids just all kind of huddled around me and had a good cry because they are tired and they’re feeling this. But after November 3, I am still a wife. I am still a mother. I am still a resident of Columbia, Tennessee, and that’s not going to change.” 
What three women, dead or alive, would you invite to dinner?
“Sacagawea, Eleanor Roosevelt and Condoleezza Rice”



“My husband is a rock and has been a steady force of support over the past year of campaigning,” Pinkston said, her voice breaking as she described threats she has received during the campaign. 
“I am so incredibly proud of the fact that after running so hard for an entire year, my marriage is stronger even than it was a year ago, and that my family is stronger even than it was a year ago,” she said.
David Hatley, the other major independent gubernatorial candidate, has self-funded more than 30 times the amount Pinkston has raised.
Lauren Pinkston, independent candidate for governor, listens to supporters at a September event in Brentwood. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) Lauren Pinkston turns to David Hatley during the Tennessee Press Association-Middle Tennessee State University 2026 Gubernatorial Forum on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Despite the long shot, Pinkston has said she would not back down and refused a request by Green last month to drop out of the race.
Pinkston highlighted her policy plan to add 50,000 childcare slots in her first four years as governor to enable women to contribute to the workplace. 
“We have a 90,000 childcare slot deficit in the state of Tennessee, and so we have a community and we have a society that is saying, ‘Go to college, women, go to college,’ and now women outnumber men in their college registration and their college attendance,” Pinkston said. “But once women get out of college and they start their careers, we don’t have any supports that are there for them.”
Pinkston quotes a phrase she coined and printed onto campaign t-shirts: ‘There is no greater threat to unchecked power than a free woman with a conscience.’
She said when she sees women wearing a shirt emblazoned with the phrase, it’s clear it resonates with them too. 
“Women have been sitting in the middle of this political divide, bridging gaps at dinner tables for so long, and we stand on the shoulders of women who have done this for centuries.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming ‘supremacy’ over our water is a gut punch to all Idahoans
text:
The Snake River flows alongside the Idaho Falls greenbelt. (Photo courtesy of Hyo Lee/U.S. Department of Energy)Throughout history there has been one thing all Idahoans agreed on — water is the lifeblood of Idaho. Water has made our southern Idaho sagebrush country bloom with farms and ranches, and water has been crucial for the protection of our wildlife and our outdoor way of life.
Protecting Idaho’s water rights from outside threats has been an article of faith — almost a religion — and any attempt by outsiders to get their hands on our water has been fighting words for all Idaho politicians regardless of political party or persuasion.
Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights

That’s why the Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming “supremacy” over Idaho’s water serving the Idaho National Laboratory is a gut punch to the people of Idaho.
But our current political leaders, unlike those throughout history, have played a role in giving the Trump administration the notion that Idaho is a lap dog for whatever the president wants by their silence and eagerness to partner with the federal government regardless of the consequences for Idahoans, their economy and their way of life.
Last summer, without informing the people of Idaho, Gov. Brad Little signed a memorandum of understanding with the Trump administration hoping that the Idaho National Laboratory could become a Nuclear Lifestyle Innovation Campus and accept 33 percent of all radioactive waste generated in the country.
Little has not explained how this campus and taking the waste will affect our precious water supply nor how it will impact the Snake River Aquifer, which supplies a significant amount of water to our southern Idaho farms, ranches, trout farms and cities. Other than a few comments for a story published by the Idaho Capital Sun, the governor has said little about how this major initiative will affect Idaho.
Our congressional delegation has also remained silent on this issue except to say the campus will bring economic prosperity and jobs to eastern Idaho.
Now, through the lawsuit the Trump administration has filed in U.S. District Court, we know that the federal government views the water it receives from Idaho as its water and that Idaho has no legal right to curtail water to INL even during one of the worse drought seasons in the state’s history.
The Trump administration argues that federal installations like INL are “shielded by the supremacy clause” from state regulations unless “Congress has provided clear and unambiguous authorization for such regulation.”
The Trump administration also argues, as it has while promoting the Nuclear Lifestyle Innovation Campus and the radioactive waste repository, that Idaho’s decision to curtail INL’s water has “safety, economic and energy consequences.”
Moreover, the Trump administration says that “curtailment of INL’s water right would disrupt this national nuclear energy momentum,” another way of saying it would disrupt President Trump’s quest to build nuclear reactors across the country.
But the Nuclear Lifestyle Innovation Campus is but only one issue where our water could be in jeopardy and where our governor and congressional delegation have remained silent when the future of Idaho is at stake and should be debated.
In September, the Washington Sun revealed that a Nevada company was eyeing plans to build a 4-million-square foot data center complex on 3,700 acres of public land in southern Ada County. This complex would be 5.5 times bigger than a data center Meta built near Kuna.
Rhea Data, a subsidiary of Las Vegas-based Arevia Power, said the preliminary design for the complex would include a natural-gas power plant, electrical infrastructure and rights of way expanding into Elmore County.
In addition to the Ada County data center, the Idaho Statesman reported this week that Copia Power, a California-based company, wants to build a data center on 3,700 acres of public land north of Twin Falls. The so-called Falcon Data Center would be built on land where the Lava Ridge wind project would have been built before getting killed by the Idaho congressional delegation and the Trump administration, both of which oppose clean energy projects.
These two Idaho-based data centers on public land are two of the dozens of data centers the Trump administration wants to build on 17,600 acres across the West on public lands.
Data centers proposed on federal land in eastern Oregon, Idaho and other Western states

In states from Pennsylvania to Ohio to Washington, the construction of data centers has been one of the hottest issues during this election cycle. But in Idaho, there has been no debate on whether using thousands of acres of public lands to build data center complexes is a good idea.
Again, neither Gov. Little nor our congressional delegation has said a peep about whether we should use public land — historically, designated for multiple use — and convert it into one use for private companies.
Again, the governor and the congressional delegation have not explained how the 4-million square foot Ada County data center will get its water or how much water it will consume even though we all know that data centers require significant supplies of water. And now yet another data center, this one in the heart of Idaho’s agricultural area, will also likely consume massive amounts of water. Where will that water come from?
This fall, Idaho’s U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, who is seeking a fourth term in office, has declared his opposition to selling off our public lands in both his television ads and his mailbox pamphlets. But he has not said a word about giving 3,700 acres of public land in the state’s most populous county to a for-profit company to build a data center complex.
He has said nothing about how the Nuclear Lifestyle Innovation Campus could affect Idaho’s water supply. Silence from such a prominent member of the United States Senate is like writing a blank check to the Trump administration to do whatever it wants in our state.
Had Gov. Little and the congressional delegation shared more information with Idahoans and allowed Idahoans to voice their opinions regarding these issues in open forums and debates, the Trump administration might not have felt so bold as to file a federal lawsuit to grab our state’s water just weeks before the November election.
One hopes that Idaho can win this water grab by the Trump administration. Water is the most precious gift mother nature has given Idaho, and it is only going to become more valuable because of how our climate is changing.
Idaho must control its own water because every drop is precious and every drop is crucial for the future of our great state.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Ballot measure proposes expanding Arkansas constitution’s right to bear arms
text:
An unloaded Glock 19X handgun sits next to a magazine and 9 mm ammunition at a gun range. Several states have enacted laws that allow judges to temporarily remove guns from people in crisis, but a growing number of states are banning the measures. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)A proposed constitutional amendment aimed at solidifying Arkansans’ right to keep and bear arms is needed to better protect that right, supporters say, but opponents argue it will make it more difficult to implement gun safety regulations. 
Issue 2 would amend the state constitution to clarify that the right to keep and bear arms includes “without limitation” the possession and use of ammunition, firearm accessories and firearm components. 
Arkansas’ constitution currently says the state’s citizens “shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for their common defense.”
The proposal is one of four ballot measures being considered by Arkansas voters in this year’s midterm election. [Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The proposal comes as the U.S. Supreme Court prepares to consider whether bans on assault weapons violate the Second Amendment. Gun Owners of Arkansas President Gary Epperson said in an email that once that issue is settled, he expects the battle to shift to efforts to restrict access to ammunition and accessories. Issue 2 incorporates language into the Arkansas constitution in anticipation of that, Epperson said. 
The proposed constitutional amendment is supported by GO-AR for Issue 2, a ballot question committee comprised of Gun Owners of Arkansas board members. The nonprofit advocacy group has donated more than $20,000 to the committee, which has used the funds for advertising, signs and printed materials, according to an October finance report. 
Epperson, who’s also the committee’s president, said they proposed the wording of Issue 2 and lobbied legislators to get it on the ballot via their referred amendment process. 
The Arkansas constitution allows state lawmakers to refer up to three proposed amendments to voters on the general election ballot. Republicans Sen. John Payton and Rep. Matt Duffield sponsored the resolution that created Issue 2.
Opponents of the measure have argued that declaring the right to keep and bear arms includes “without limitation” the possession and use of ammunition and firearm accessories could open the door to legal challenges that undermine responsible gun ownership and public safety, according to the Public Policy Center at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture.
Issue 2 also proposes deeming the right to keep and bear arms as “a natural, fundamental, and individual right that shall not be infringed.” 
Casey Cromer, Northwest Arkansas Moms Demand Action group lead, questioned how this language would affect the ability to prohibit certain people, like felons or someone convicted of domestic violence, from possessing firearms. Moms Demand Action is a national organization that advocates for expanded background checks and other measures to address gun violence.
“If their right to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed as a natural and fundamental right, how are our courts going to enforce that,” Cromer said. “It seems like this extreme and absolute language…will create unintended consequences.”
U.S. Supreme Court upholds law that prevents domestic abusers from owning guns

As a gun owner, Cromer said the right to bear arms is an important one, but she also believes there should be “commonsense laws around that.”
“We’re not against guns, we’re against gun violence and people dying by gun violence,” she said. 
Critics of the proposal have also argued it’s not needed because the state’s constitution already protects an individual’s right to bear arms, and the amendment does nothing to help protect children, according to the Public Policy Center.
The current wording in the state constitution “is weak and could be exploited,” said Epperson, who noted the amended language raises judicial standards so a court would have to apply strict scrutiny. This is the highest standard of review courts use to evaluate the constitutionality of government action, according to Cornell Law School’s Legal Information Institute.
The amendment proposes adding language to the state constitution that would allow Arkansans to keep and bear arms for “lawful hunting and recreational use” and for “any other lawful purpose.” Adding the term “lawful” covers self-defense and future technologies, Epperson said. 
The League of Women Voters of Arkansas, a nonpartisan organization focused on protecting and expanding voting rights, opposes Issue 2. 
Kristin Foster, executive director of the Arkansas chapter, said that while the organization supports lawful hunting and recreational use, the expansion in Issue 2 “was more broad than we feel comfortable with and is inconsistent with our national position.”
“For us it kind of came down to support for regulating firearms for consumer safety and supporting licensing procedures for gun ownership that include background checks or identity verification, and gun safety education,” Foster said.  
Epperson said Issue 2 is needed because the state’s current constitution only gives Arkansans the right to keep and bear arms for the “common defense.”
“With this wording anti-gun legislators could create havoc with the individual right to keep and bear arms,” he said. “Relying on the U.S. Supreme Court could take multiple generations before they would select a court challenge even if they did.”
Issue 2 would be effective Jan. 1 if voters approve it.
You can read the proposed constitutional amendment in its entirety here.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: In contested majority-Black legislative districts, candidates focus on affordability
text:
A person reviewing a grocery receipt. Legislative candidates in potentially close races around the Black Belt and central Alabama all said that they favor repealing the state portion of the grocery tax to help address the high price of food. (Photo by Ming Tang Tung/Getty Images)Four majority-Black legislative districts where Republicans did notably well in 2022 will be contested again this fall.
The contests include three districts in the Black Belt region as well as an open seat in Anniston left by Rep. Barbara Boyd, D-Anniston, who is retiring from the Legislature.
“These are districts where there is a little bit more competitiveness between the two parties, whereas most districts in Alabama politics are more heavily favored by one party or the other,” said David Hughes, an associate professor at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who analyzed the races. “These at least have voters who have a demonstrated record of a bit more bipartisanship compared to elsewhere.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
One is House District 69 that includes Autauga, Lowndes, Montgomery and Wilcox counties. In that race, Rep. Kelvin Lawrence, D-Hayneville, is facing Republican nominee Josh Pendergrass, who ran in 2022 for District 88 but dropped his campaign after he realized he lived outside of the district.
Rep. Thomas Jackson, D-Thomasville, is also seeking another term for House District 68 in Clarke, Conecuh, Marengo, Monroe, Perry and Wilcox counties, against second-time challenger Fred Kelley. Sen. Robert Stewart, D-Selma, is trying to keep his seat against Thayer Spencer in Senate District 23, which includes Butler, Clarke, Conecuh, Dallas, Lowndes, Monroe, Perry, and Wilcox counties.
Multiple messages were left with Spencer seeking comment.
In House District 32, located in Calhoun and Talladega counties, Democratic nominee Debra Foster is going against Republican Joey Callahan.
The races were relatively close in 2022 thanks in part to a weak Democratic statewide ticket, a generally favorable environment for Republicans and low turnout in blue areas. Jackson defeated Kelley that year by just under 600 votes, a margin of 3%. Lawrence beat Republican Karla Knight Maddox by about 10%, 55% to 45%.
Another factor is ongoing population loss in the Black Belt, a Democratic stronghold, and more equal distribution of white and Black voters. In Alabama’s racially polarized electorate, white voters tend to support Republicans, and Black voters tend to support Democrats.
House District 32, Hughes said “is competitive in the sense that there are a pretty good number of Black voters in Talladega County, around the city of Talladega, but not the same concentrated population that we see in parts of western Birmingham or Montgomery.”
House District 69, represented by Lawrence, includes parts of Autauga County with a significant number of Republican voters. Stewart’s district incorporates significant parts of southern Alabama with fewer Black residents, according to Hughes.
However, the national environment this year is much more favorable to Democrats, with Donald Trump facing sagging popularity and voter concerns about the cost of living.
Affordability concerns
Both Democrats and Republicans said they wanted to prioritize affordability and prioritized grocery tax elimination and reduction of the gas tax.
“People are having to determine whether to pay for rent or they buy groceries, or their rent or their medicine,” Lawrence said. “That should not happen in 2026 here in Alabama or in the United States.”
Pendergrass said he wants to review the grocery tax imposed by local municipalities.
“We need to work on the state level with local counties and municipalities and figure out a way on how we can get them to also remove the tax on groceries so that it is zero percent,” he said.
Kelley said he wants to go further and ease the gas tax.
“Did you know there is a 30-cent per gallon state gas tax?” Kelley said. “If we repeal 10-cents per gallon on every gallon sold in Alabama just today, how much money would that be?”
The tax was part of a law in 2019 that was passed by the Legislature for road and bridge maintenance. Kelley later said in an interview Thursday that “is not a good idea” after he researched the issue after the interview.
Democrats for their part have also proposed legislation to eliminate the state tax on groceries. It was a focal point of a news conference the party hosted on Monday concerning affordability. Former Rep. John Knight, D-Montgomery, said he introduced legislation more than 30 years ago to repeal the sales tax on food, but it did not pass.
Some Democrats said they want to increase people’s earnings. Stewart in January filed a bill that would have established a $10 minimum wage in the state for businesses with 51 employees or more.
“Our state does not have a minimum wage, so I sponsored legislation to create a minimum wage,” Stewart said.
Several candidates also said rural healthcare is a priority.
“People are without health insurance,” said Foster, running in House District 32. “People are sick and can’t go to the doctor. Hospitals are closing. They don’t have hospitals that are close to them. When you are sick, it is a matter of life and death if you don’t get care expeditiously.”
Foster said she wants to expand Medicaid, which Alabama has not done.
“Medicaid will not only give people access to healthcare, but it is also going to allow us to draw doctors and nurses to the community,” she said. “Not only that, it is also an economic engine because it is going to bring jobs to the state.”
Callahan said he wants to provide funding through community block grants.
“You bring that money back and you find out the communities that need it,” he said.
Other candidates said that economic and workforce development is a priority. Several said they want to develop programs through the community college system.
“That takes state money, but I think it could be done with private partnerships along with tax money,” Callahan said. “The more people make, and the more opportunities people have to create wealth for themselves, then the more they can afford.”
Pendergrass said he wants to invest in two-year colleges and provide students with a path to obtain a credential while in high school.
“What can we do spending priority wise to make sure as many of our students as possible finish high school with at least part of their associates degree done if not the whole thing,” he said.
One possibility would be to allow school districts to partner with local two-year colleges to educate students.
Jackson said he wants to help farmers in his district. He filed HB 523 in the 2026 session that would have allowed the Commissioner of Agriculture and Industries to create the Agricultural Enhancement Program funded by the Legislature to provide money to farmers to help pay for investments in their farms.
He also wants to continue his efforts to fight voter disenfranchisement.
“Voting rights was passed in 1965,” Jackson said. “Now they are trying to make it hard for people to register to vote.”
Jackson filed HB 59 in 2025 that would have required each county to provide at least one precinct to allow people to vote the week before the election. The bill never made it out of the House Constitution, Campaigns and Elections committee.



				Meet the Candidates
 Kelvin Lawrence 
Age: 52
Residence: Hayneville

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Former Tuberville player joins Doug Jones on campaign trail in Auburn
text:
Former Auburn University football player Victor Horn speaking at a rally for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones on Oct. 29, 2026, at the Moors Mill Club in Auburn, Alabama. Horn endorsed Jones because he said Tuberville's demeanor has not changed since he was a coach, and Jones' outperforms his former coach. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)AUBURN —  Former Auburn University football player Victor Horn joined Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones at a campaign stop in Lee County, his opponent’s home county. 
More than 300 people attended the rally as Jones drew comparisons between himself and U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the Republican nominee. Jones played clips of Tuberville’s speeches on the floor of the Senate and on the campaign trail, a hallmark of Jones’ rallies and town halls. 
“I’m going to show you some things. Bear with us, but I want you to hear Tommy talk about what he thinks about your friends, your neighbors, what is going on in the state of Alabama,” Jones said. “Don’t take my word for it. Listen to his own words.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Horn said he has supported Jones for years, and asked to come on the campaign trail. He said that Tuberville’s apparent leadership style in the U.S. Senate mirrors that when he coached at Auburn University from 1999 to 2008. Horn played for the team in the early 2000s, according to the Auburn Football website, before he transferred to The University of Alabama.  
“Those videos that you guys see (of Tuberville) of the flip-flop back and forth and creating a vision, that’s what he did on the football team. Those opportunities are not really because of that. Those guys got together and learned to work together to make Auburn successful for you fans, and it wasn’t because of Tubby,” Horn said. 
A message seeking comment from the Tuberville campaign was left Thursday evening.
“Those are the same, similar tactics: manipulation, lies, deceit, having players turn on each other,” Horn said. “It’s all for him. It’s not for Auburn.”
Tuberville has said he will be a governor for all, but Jones challenged that. 
“You cannot do that when that is what you believe. When that is what is near in your heart, but you cannot expect much different from someone who has spent his entire career trash-talking as a football coach,” Jones said. “That’s what football coaches often do. Some do it better than others. He was damn good at it. Just trash-talking and us versus them. This is not a game, folks. We’re not hiring a coach. We’re hiring a governor.”
Jones also sharply criticized campaign mailers sent across the state this week by ProgressPAC, the fundraising arm of the Business Council of Alabama. The flyers displayed AI-generated images and text of Jones in front of the state of Alabama with the flag of the Soviet Union.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones speaking at a rally on Oct. 29, 2026, at the Moors Mill Club in Auburn, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Alabama law prohibits AI-generated campaign advertisements within 90 days of an election without a disclaimer, but BCA’s mailer included in fine print that read, “This media has been manipulated by technical means and depicts speech or conduct that did not occur.”
“I’ve seen a lot of things in my days in politics. I have never, ever seen someone who will send a mailer and literally say it’s all a lie,” Jones said. “I want y’all to think about that when we talk about the power structure in Alabama and who’s calling the shots. That’s who’s calling the shots right here.”
Jones also reiterated his support of public schools and universities. Tuberville on Monday said fewer students should go to universities like Auburn and Alabama and get jobs instead. 
“Our universities are more than sports; they’re what’s driving the engine of the Business Council of Alabama. For God’s sake, they’re what’s driving our economy,” Jones said. “We know that, and that is a responsibility that we all have. It starts in education from an early age.”
Horn told attendees that when talking to their friends and neighbors about Tuesday’s election, to take their emotions about Auburn football out of it. 
“Look at him and his profile compared to Doug. (Tuberville) has not changed. He will not change. He’s not just Auburn’s coach, but Cincinnati’s coach, Ole Miss coach, everybody’s coach. He’s not committed to the city of Auburn, Auburn University, Auburn football, or the state of Alabama,” Horn said. “Doug Jones is an Alabama son. He’s a native. He’s a people person. He doesn’t mind a conversation with you, talking about what’s going on in Alabama. That’s what we need.”
The election is in four days. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: Wasted opioid settlements are a new low in the West Virginia exploitation story
text:
Majority of the money cities and counties received from the state's opioid settlement has gone to law enforcement, according to a spending report from the West Virginia First Foundation.
(Photo by Douglas Sacha/Getty Images)West Virginia is a special place, known to outsiders as “Almost Heaven,” as John Denver sings in his song “Take Me Home, Country Roads.” However, West Virginians know there is an eerie emphasis on the word “almost” in our mountain mama’s hymn. The word “almost” speaks to the promise and potential found in West Virginia. Or, as a neighbor back home in Union once put it: “It’s called Almost Heaven, because we’re close to dying every day.”
One of the reasons our health outcomes remain poor in West Virginians is a long history of exploitation in our state. Our coal miners’ bodies were exploited and discarded. Then decades-long opioid crisis further exploited that pain. As a result, West Virginia has secured more than a billion dollars in the opioid settlements which is the highest per capita of any state.
And yet, the cycle of hope and exploitation continues, except this time, in perhaps its most sinister form: government officials using the pain from the opioid crisis to pay off government debt instead of investing in the public health solutions we need to stay healthy and thrive.
This is not the first time West Virginia’s state and local government response to the opioid crisis made it far worse than it should have been. After being too slow to adopt evidence-based syringe service programs, they rolled them back in the middle of the crisis and contributed to a predictable, preventable, and tragic spike in HIV. West Virginia remains the only state with a moratorium on new methadone clinics, despite methadone being a highly effective medication to treat opioid addiction. Combined, these hostile policies have effectively denied thousands of people access to life-saving approaches. 
Yes, outside companies started the fire, but it is difficult to look at the West Virginia government response and see anything other than throwing more gas on it. And now those same governments that led our inadequate response to the opioid crisis over the past three decades, are fumbling the response again. This time with the money won on behalf of people impacted by the opioid crisis: the opioid settlement money.
In the years one and two of local government opioid settlement spending, more $7.5 million went to law enforcement. Basically no money is going to harm reduction approaches like syringe service programs and relatively little, approximately $900,000 going increasing access for opioid addiction treatment medications. In contrast, more than $4.3 million was spent on jail bills.
Since this money started flowing in 2022, approximately 4,244 people died from an overdose death in West Virginia. Deaths that could have been prevented if we invested in public health approaches like evidence-based prevention, harm reduction, treatment and recovery supports like this money was supposed to be. Yet just like for the past 30 years, we’ve not seen those investments. Does anyone seriously think that buying a shooting range, drones, K9s and a Batman impersonator is going to turn around West Virginia’s failed approach to the crisis? Instead, it looks more like the government equivalent of buying a jet ski with lottery winnings. And it’s a deep betrayal of all the lives lost and impacted by this crisis.
Now you might be wondering why this is happening and what can be done to stop it?
One of the clearest reasons for this spending is that the West Virginia Attorney General, now governor, allowed for spending on jail bills and police equipment in the West Virginia settlement agreement. Those two unique insertions into the standard agreement language accepted by the other 49 states gave decisionmakers in West Virginia the opportunity to ignore the other almost 100 public health examples for how to spend the money on harm reduction, treatment and recovery support. It gave decision makers the opening to invest in the same things that haven’t worked for our state, further diverting these finite resources away from what does work.
And yes, West Virginia’s approach is an outlier. In fact, just across the border, Virginia explicitly says opioid settlement money is not allowed to be spent on jail bills and law enforcement equipment. Yet in West Virginia, it was added to the agreement as explicitly allowable. Turns out, the plan in West Virginia was always to exploit our pain and turn it into a government handout.
As a West Virginian and a public health expert, this is outrageous. Decision makers have a responsibility to act as stewards of this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to make amends with a community that has been so damaged. This means investing in evidence-based addiction treatment, harm reduction and recovery support. Money spent on off-target things like jail bills must be clawed back and spent on actual solutions. The state must revisit their agreement that allows for this wasteful spending and develop an unallowable spending list like Virginia and six other states have created. 
Our government pursued these lawsuits to hold the companies accountable for what they did to our communities. But that accountability flows both ways. If you use the deaths of our neighbors and the pain of children who lost parents to get this money, you can’t just turn around and use it to buy a drone and act like that is helping. Decision makers must fix the broken addiction ecosystem by investing in public health approaches, or they too must be held accountable.
