name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: If you care about affordability, vote with climate in mind
text:
(Photo by Kevin Mohatt for Colorado Newsline)Like many Americans, the issue that is top of mind for me as we approach the midterms is affordability, or rather, a lack thereof. That’s why I’m disappointed to see how few voters, and even candidates, are focused on climate change this election.
Wait — really? Yes.
Whether we talk about it or not, climate change is fueling America’s affordability crisis, and Colorado is no exception. However, with the right climate policies, we can lower energy costs, pay less for groceries, and save money on healthcare. But we need state and local leaders who understand these critical connections and prioritize climate action as a result.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As a renter without central air conditioning, I am all too aware of how often I turned on my window unit this summer to try and keep up with Colorado’s record-breaking temperatures. Across the U.S., higher temperatures are driving up energy bills as the need for air conditioning grows. Since 1970, Denver has seen a 56% increase in demand for home cooling that is exacerbated by shifting seasons and lingering summer heat, which has been on full display this October.
Climate-fueled extreme weather is also driving up utility prices. In the western U.S., regulators have raised customers’ electricity rates to cover costs related to wildfire mitigation and damages, something that will presumably continue as climate change feeds into increasingly exceptional drought conditions and greater fire danger across our state.
Coloradans need forward-thinking candidates who prioritize reliable, sustainable and cost-effective energy. Forcing outdated technology like coal plants to keep running is expensive, and these rising costs hit us, consumers, the hardest. Alternatively, the vast majority of newly commissioned renewable energy is cheaper than fossil fuels (and less affected by volatile oil prices), a key reality for our policymakers to understand as energy demand only continues to grow. In regards to domestic oil and gas production, Colorado is the first state to implement methane policies that are in line with the EPA’s 2024 methane standards, which is projected to prevent enough natural gas waste to meet the heating and cooking needs of over 20,000 homes. This election is a key moment for maintaining this positive momentum.
In addition to utility statements, I have dreaded seeing my grocery receipts lately. There are, of course, many factors that contribute to rising food costs, but we should not dismiss the role that climate change plays in raising our food bills.
More erratic weather, from severe droughts to unprecedented floods, impacts soil health, affects crop yield, and makes for an overall vulnerable supply chain. Warming temperatures can also increase the abundance and virality of plant pathogens on crops. What is more, unseasonable temperatures and changing planting zones have the potential to cost farmers an entire harvest, as we saw for Colorado growers earlier this year. On a global level, climate change is expected to raise the price of staples like potatoes, olive oil and chocolate.
The good news is that — as with energy — we have climate-smart solutions that save farmers money, lower carbon emissions and increase yield while making crops more resilient to extreme weather events. As more farmers adopt these practices, we need policies that prioritize supporting beneficial, practical solutions that are good for our wallets and the environment.
No discussion of affordability in the U.S. would be complete without addressing the cost of healthcare. According to the American Medical Association, healthcare spending saw an increase of 7.2% in 2024, the highest growth rate since 2003. How does this relate to climate change? Simply put, climate change is making us sicker. Extreme heat leads to more ER visits. Wildfire smoke exacerbates asthma. Ground ozone — one of the most common pollutants in Denver that increases alongside temperatures — raises the risk of respiratory infections and pulmonary inflammation. It’s no wonder The Lancet medical journal called climate change “the greatest global health threat facing the world in the 21st century.”
You don’t have to care about melting glaciers or species extinction to care about climate change. You simply need to care about your health and what it’s costing you. But there are solutions. New research from Columbia University links policies that promote cleaner air to improved early childhood development. Pollution safeguards — like the ones I mentioned addressing methane waste and leaks — have the power to save Americans billions in avoided health costs and even prevent pollution-related illness and death.
I’m voting with climate in mind this election, because I care about affordability. If you, too, are feeling the high costs of living, join me in speaking out about the impacts of climate change and supporting candidates who understand the need for pragmatic and commonsense climate solutions here in Colorado.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Musk replaces Kentucky’s McConnell as GOP’s influential money man
text:
CEO of Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk speaks last year at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Maryland. Last week’s SpaceX IPO, which made Musk the world’s first trillionaire, is a vivid illustration of wealth concentration in the United States, which has been accelerating since 2022. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)Kentucky elected Mitch McConnell to the U.S. Senate 42 years ago, and through all those years, McConnell worked relentlessly to radically change American law and politics to allow billionaires and corporations to pour massive amounts of money into election campaigns.
While demolishing campaign finance laws, McConnell and associates raised billions of dollars for Republican candidates around the country, making him the leader of his party in the Senate and opening the floodgates to a deluge of dollars into U.S. elections. That’s what bankrolls the constant stream of yammering political ads on television.
As McConnell moves off the national stage, it’s ironic that Elon Musk is replacing Kentucky’s senior Senator as a leading source of Republican campaign funds.  He’s a businessman and government contractor who’s never been elected to anything.  
Musk is using the opportunity provided by McConnell’s work to funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns and gain more influence than elected members of Congress have over U.S. policy.
McConnell’s Congress has abandoned its constitutional responsibility to act on behalf of Americans, and the weakness of this “do-nothing” Congress has left a vacuum that Musk is eagerly filling. 
Musk bought his way into this position when he gave about $300 million in 2024 to support the campaigns of Donald Trump and the GOP.  He’s enhancing his position by giving nearly $450 million to Republicans so far in this election cycle, and his total will be much higher when reports are filed after the election.  
This year, Musk has given $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the Super PAC formed years ago by McConnell associates to funnel money to Republican candidates.  McConnell used massive fundraising to build Republican influence in the Senate, and enact policies favoring campaign funders: banks, hedge funds, insurance and pharmaceutical companies, along with coal, gas, and oil interests.  
  In contrast, Musk is using his vast contributions to build his own influence, enhance his own businesses, and implement his own policies.  
Musk and his companies, particularly SpaceX, have acquired enormous power inside the federal government – power unprecedented  in American history. That’s helped make Musk the richest person in the world, with much of his wealth coming from American taxpayers through huge contracts and favorable treatment by the U.S. Government.
Last year, The New York Times reported that across government, “SpaceX is positioning itself to see billions of dollars in new federal contracts or other support . . . The boost in federal spending for SpaceX will come in part because of actions by President Trump and Mr. Musk’s allies and employees who now hold government positions.  The company will also benefit from Trump policies that prioritize hiring commercial space vendors for everything from communications systems to satellite fabrication, areas in which SpaceX now dominates.”
Although the U.S. pays for SpaceX’s satellite systems that Ukraine uses to defend itself against Russian missile and drone attacks and to operate drones to strike Russia, Musk and SpaceX can control the systems.  It’s not clear if he had U.S. approval, but Musk recently slowed or stopped the systems from operating – Ukraine lost control of its drones and couldn’t get life-saving early warnings about Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
Musk’s actions come while Trump is boosting Russia’s war on Ukraine by waiving U.S. sanctions and buying Russian diesel fuel, so Musk and Trump are teaming up to drive American foreign policy away from an ally and into the arms of an adversary.
For years, Mitch McConnell and the Senate supported Ukraine and opposed Russian aggression.  Now, because of McConnell’s work to allow unlimited campaign spending by billionaires, Elon Musk plays a more influential role in American policy than a meek and submissive Senate.  Americans will wonder if that’s what McConnell intended as his legacy.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: State of the Race: Dembo, Alvarado make final pitches in central Kentucky with party support
text:
On Thursday, the first day of early voting in Kentucky, people formed a line outside the Tates Creek Library in Lexington to make their choices. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)NICHOLASVILLE — With just days left before to sway voters in Kentucky’s central congressional 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado are making their final pitches with entourages of fellow party members. 
As Republicans nationally batten down the hatches as Democrats are predicted to take control of the U.S. House during midterms next week, GOP House Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota joined Alvarado and U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, the current 6th district congressman and U.S. Senate candidate, in Jessamine County Wednesday to drum up volunteers before they knocked doors. 
Emmer was dismissive of polls showing a Democratic advantage, saying it’s “not necessarily fake, but it’s not right.” Within the 6th District, Democratic-sponsored polls publicly released have shown Dembo with a slight lead. Independent race raters like The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball have moved the seat from safe GOP hands to a toss-up. Emmer said polling has changed as people have shifted from using landlines to cell phones. 
“The other thing that has changed — we’re on the Republican side, and even if you’re just right of center, you don’t trust people that are sending you text messages because we don’t want to be in your database,” he said to the room in the local county GOP headquarters, which murmured agreement. 
Barr noted that if Democrats win, that means a change of leadership in the U.S. House. Alvarado would support current House Speaker Mike Johnson, of Louisiana, Barr said, while questioning who Dembo would back. 
“Are you, Mr. Dembo, going to support Hakeem Jeffries? Are you going to support Alexandria Ocasio Cortez? Are you going to enable the extreme far left — the socialists taking over the United States Congress?” Barr said. GOP candidates around the country have claimed Democrats have become engulfed by socialism this election cycle. Jeffries, of New York, is the current Democratic floor leader. 
Asked about who he’d back Wednesday afternoon as he waited to vote early at the Tates Creek library, Dembo told the Kentucky Lantern that was like “putting the cart before the horse” and he’s focusing on the election, which was five days away. 
“No one’s talked to me about that. No one’s requested my support or vote,” Dembo said. “What I’ll say is, anyone who asks for my support, I’m going to need to sit down with and make sure they understand the importance of Central Kentucky and they have the best interests at heart. I’m not going to vote for someone who’s not going to be able to help me in standing up for Central Kentuckians.” 
On the other hand, if the district swings in Alvarado’s favor and Democrats still control the House, Alvarado told reporters he’d draw on his experience as a Republican state senator when Democrats still held the House. The GOP flipped the Kentucky House in 2016. Alvarado began serving in the Senate in 2015. 
“When I was in the General Assembly, lots of bills that I got done that people on both sides liked was often nonpartisan stuff, and I managed to get those bills to both chambers and got a lot of things accomplished for the state moving forward,” Alvarado said. “So, I think I can use that same experience, have relationships with people on both sides of the aisle.” 
The final push
On Thursday evening, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear joined Dembo at a rally at Wise Bird Cider in Lexington. The governor later traveled to a Louisville rally featuring Charles Booker, the Democratic candidate for U.S. senate. 
As polls in the 6th District will close early at 6 p.m. EST election night, Beshear said the outcome of the race could be a signal for the rest of the country that evening. 
“Zach Dembo is going to be one of the first flips from Republican to Democrat,” Beshear told reporters. “He has all the momentum because he’s worked hard for it, and this president and a Republican-controlled Congress is just making life hard for every Kentucky family — Democrat, Republican or Independent.” 
Democrat Zach Dembo, left, and Gov. Andy Beshear, right, speak to reporters. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Earlier Thursday, Dembo’s campaign released an ad featuring the candidate and Beshear sharing a beer while highlighting that Alvarado was former Gov. Matt Bevin’s running mate in 2019. Beshear won that election. Alvarado’s campaign issued a flurry of endorsements from Kentucky Republicans, including Auditor Allison Ball and Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell. 
Back in Jessamine County, Alvarado said he felt like his campaign had momentum as early voting began in Kentucky. He claimed victory over Dembo in recent debates at Estill County High School and on Fox56. Alvarado said he also feels his ads are moving voters. 
“I think we’re surging. He’s peaked already. He’s on the decline,” Alvarado added. “We feel very optimistic about the election.” 
Republican congressional candidate Ralph Alvarado speaks to reporters in Jessamine County. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
According to federal finance reports as of Thursday afternoon, the No Going Back PAC, which is tied to President Donald Trump’s political operation, spent more than $650,000 on ads against Dembo this week. Meanwhile, PACs backing Dembo spent more than $320,000 on ads in that same time frame. 
PACs against Alvarado spent more than $1 million this week on advertising. They include End Citizens United and Kentuckians Not Corruption. PACs supporting Alvarado have spent more than $150,000. 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Early voting in Kentucky continues through Saturday.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: With student IDs barred from the New Hampshire polls, campus organizers increase voter outreach
text:
Dartmouth College students attend a Dartmouth Civics voter registration information event, complete with an ice cream truck, Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Dartmouth Civics)Will Nelson knows his way around a student voter registration drive. 
As a Dartmouth senior and co-president of Dartmouth Civics, a nonpartisan election information organization, Nelson has helped staff countless tables along innumerable campus walkways, from national spectacles like the 2024 presidential election to local town meetings in Hanover. 
Armed with stickers, pens, information sheets, and the occasional box of donuts, Nelson and others help students navigate voter registration and make a voting plan, whether in New Hampshire or via an absentee ballot in their home state. 
“We’ll bring an ice cream truck and we’ll say, ‘OK, town meeting is next week. Here’s how you can register to vote. Here’s what town meeting means in the tradition of New England local governance,’” Nelson said in an interview. 
But this year, that voter outreach got a little more complicated.
A state law passed in April prevents New Hampshire high school and college students from using their school identification cards to vote. Now, in the Nov. 3 midterm election, all New Hampshire residents — including students — must produce government-issued photo identification at the polls.
For students at Dartmouth and other college and university campuses in the state, the law will end the convenience of voting with the cards they carry to get into most buildings on campus. 
But it will not bar most students from voting at all, Nelson has stressed. And most students likely have access to the kind of identification now required, he said. 
“You can still vote here, especially if you’re already registered,” he said. “You just need a different form of identification to check in at the polls.”
The Nov. 3 midterm elections, in which Democrats are vying to retake the U.S. House and Senate, and Republicans are defending their hold, have infused campuses in New Hampshire with unusual energy. 
Yet after the passage of the new state voter ID law, and amid a series of recent legal twists and turns over its fate, some college students assume it will bar them from voting.
Dartmouth Civics has made every effort to get through to students that it does not. 
“There are so many students saying, ‘Oh, I didn’t think I could vote in New Hampshire anymore,’” Nelson said. “I think there’s just been a lot of confusion about this law change.”
Acceptable IDs for students
The new law gives students options to prove their identity. The list of acceptable forms of ID includes a driver’s license from any U.S. state, a non-driver’s state or municipal ID card, a passport or passport card, or any federally issued identification, such as a U.S. armed services identification card.
Ayotte signs bill barring use of student IDs to vote

The identification must have either an expiration date or a date of issuance, according to Oct. 23 guidance from the Secretary of State’s Office. For voters under 65 years old, an ID card may be used up to five years after its expiration; voters older than 65 are not bound to an expiration date, the guidance states.
New Hampshire residents who don’t have physical access to their government ID can use a photograph of their ID. That option allows college students whose passports or other identification cards are at their parents’ home to present to poll workers a photo of that identification card taken by their parents. 
However, students and other residents who don’t have a government-issued identification card will not be able to vote unless they obtain one first. That can be done at a Division of Motor Vehicles with an appointment.
Hanover Town Clerk Terry Walsh said Dartmouth students have been generally well equipped.
“The vast majority of students who’ve been coming in to register to vote, either now or in the past, are already coming armed with a passport or an out-of-state driver’s license,” Walsh said in an interview. “There were not many who were coming with only a student ID, even in the past. Even in the before times.”
Walsh said the ability for a student to show a photo of their identification on their phone — as well as to use a driver’s license from any state — will help students.
“I don’t think it’s going to be a huge change,” she said, speaking on the impact of the new law. 
And while the Secretary of State’s Office has promoted the option for students to obtain a non-driver’s identification card from the Division for Motor Vehicles, and get a waiver from the usual $20 fee, Walsh said she had not heard from any student interested in doing so.
Nelson said he has also not heard of any fellow students attempting to obtain a New Hampshire non-driver’s ID card.
What you need to register
Students who are voting for the first time in New Hampshire may need to register to vote at the polls on Election Day. To do that, they will need proof of identity, age, domicile, and citizenship, but they may sign an affidavit attesting to their citizenship if they don’t have documentation. 
When it comes to proving domicile, Dartmouth College and Hanover have a residency verification arrangement to help students: Ahead of Election Day, the college provides the town with a list of its enrolled students and their dormitory arrangement. That allows poll workers to verify a student’s domicile for the purposes of same-day voter registration, even if that student did not bring that documentation, Walsh said.
That arrangement isn’t available to non-student residents of Hanover seeking to register on Election Day, Walsh noted; they will need to bring proof of residency.
“For students, it’s actually easier because we have ways to prove where they live on campus,” she said. “If it’s a voter who’s coming in same day and didn’t happen to bring their copy of their lease or who doesn’t have it on their phone, it can be more difficult for them to get it.” 
In the wake of the April law barring student identification cards, campus groups across the state have sought to update students on what they need to vote. Most of that energy has come from partisan groups, like campus Democrat or Republican organizations, or Turning Point U.S.A., the conservative advocacy group founded by Charlie Kirk, Nelson noted.
Stickers and pamphlets at a Dartmouth Civics voter registration information table, Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Dartmouth Civics)
For its part, Dartmouth Civics does not endorse political parties or candidates, though the organization has spoken out against Republican state laws seeking to add voting restrictions, including House Bill 323, Nelson said. 
The organization also does not seek to influence where a student votes; volunteers are equally happy to help students register to vote and request and return an absentee ballot in their home state, Nelson added. And with polling indicating a number of neck-and-neck races that could determine control of the U.S. Senate, like Alaska, Maine, Michigan and Texas, many Dartmouth students from those states are opting to vote absentee, Nelson said.
“Folks who are from Nebraska or Kansas or Texas or places like that who in the past may have voted here, are more keen to do mail-in balloting (back home),” he said. 
To reach students, Dartmouth Civics has tried a number of attention-grabbing techniques, from the ice cream trucks to outdoor concerts. On Election Day, the group will run “walking trains” from the student union building to the polling station at Hanover High School to help guide and encourage students to vote, Nelson said. 
“We just say, ‘Hey, do you have a plan?” he said. “Like, if you want the info, we have the info.’”
Back and forth in court
As campus groups have held similar registration drives, the student ID ban itself has suffered wild swings in the courts. 
In August, a voting advocacy group, the Coalition for Open Democracy, sued the state in federal court to strike down the state’s law, arguing it creates a burden on voting that violates the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, which lowered the voting age to 18, as well as the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The state argues the law does not pose a meaningful burden on voting and advances legitimate state interests of election security and voter confidence. 
US Supreme Court ruling restores NH ban on use of student IDs at polls

Although an Oct. 2 lower court ruling effectively paused enforcement of the law, briefly allowing student ID cards to be considered at the polls, the U.S. Supreme Court moved quickly and reversed that ruling Oct. 22, allowing the ban to fully take effect while the lawsuit continues in the U.S. District Court of New Hampshire. 
In Durham, home to the University of New Hampshire, Town Clerk Rachel Deane said the town has done everything it can to be a resource to voters, including by participating in information sessions on campus throughout October.
“The Town of Durham is ready to help anyone who may be impacted by New Hampshire’s new voter laws,” she wrote in an email. “Our number one priority is ensuring that every person who is legally eligible to vote has the opportunity to do so and we are committed to working with any voter who may need help understanding the requirements to register or cast a ballot.”
Nelson is happy to tout the work he and others have done to educate students. But he said he still opposes the student ID ban, and noted that other colleges and universities might not have such robust efforts. 
“We’re worried about the students who don’t have all of that engagement or (are) trying to figure it out on Election Day,” he said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: With thousands newly able to vote, a Va. ballot measure could unlock voting rights for more
text:
Seychell Williams stands on the steps of Virginia's State Capitol on Oct. 28. 2026, days ahead of voting for the first time and the three-year anniversary of her release from prison. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virignia Mercury)Nov. 3 will be Seychell Williams’ first time voting, a civic duty she said she’s excited to experience. 
Despite advocating for criminal justice reform laws at the state Capitol over the years, she’s been unable to vote herself due to a past felony conviction for which she served five years in prison. 
She chose to skip the early voting or mail-in options to savor the experience in person. 
“It’s my first time so of course I want to be out on Election Day,” she said.
Williams is among more than 200,000 Virginians who regained their voting rights after a court ruled earlier this year they never should have lost them based on a Reconstruction Era law. 
In addition to that case, Gov. Abigail Spanberger restored about 60,000 others’ rights over the summer.  
But the third in a slate of constitutional amendments on Election Day ballots will determine if voting restoration will become automatic after incarceration, or remain a petition-based system. 


Proposed Constitutional Amendment Question 3
Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the existing prohibition on voting by persons found to be mentally incompetent to instead apply to persons who have been found to lack the capacity to understand the act of voting?


Proposed Constitutional Amendment Question 3
Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the existing prohibition on voting by persons found to be mentally incompetent to instead apply to persons who have been found to lack the capacity to understand the act of voting?
 
Virginia’s constitution permanently disenfranchises people with felonies unless a governor pardons them or they successfully petition a governor to restore their voting rights. That process is subjective and not always transparent.
Williams plans to vote for the amendment, along with two other referendums to enshrine reproductive rights and same-sex marriage protections into the constitution.
Since learning of her voting eligibility last month, she said she’s been alerting as many people as possible to check their status and register.
The Virginia Department of Elections mailed notices to eligible people following the Readmission Act case. 
But “one touch often isn’t enough,” Free Our Vote technology officer Tyler Richardett said, “especially for a group who may have believed they were permanently disenfranchised.” 
His organization has partnered with Campaign Legal Center — who’d been involved in the Readmission Act case — as well as Virginia Civic Engagement Table and Vote Riders to help spread the word through text messages and more mailed notices. 
“To get a few more touches” and expand outreach, Richardett said his organization sourced court and corrections data to piece together eligible people that meet the criteria. 
As of late October, over 1.3 million Virginians have voted early, roughly 350,000 more than the early voting total from the 2022 congressional midterm elections. 
While midterm elections represent voters’ support or rebuke of political parties in power in Congress, Virginia’s constitutional amendments like Ballot Question 3 may also be driving turnout. 
Virginia-based criminal justice reform organizations have also been conducting outreach and holding events to boost turnout and inform new voters. 
Williams has contributed through her nonprofit called the Ruby Grant Project, which supports people reentering society from incarceration and was named for her grandmother who’d conducted prison ministry. 
She’d also been a speaker at the Virginia Justice Conference in Richmond last month. The conference’s organizer Sheba Williams (no relation to Seychell Williams), said that the Secretary of the Commonwealth’s office had set up a table at the event to help people look up their status.  
Richardett called it “extra special” and “serendipitous” that many of the likely new voters may choose to vote for Ballot Question 3 so that “others can follow behind them.” 
Constitutional: The amendment that could restore formerly incarcerated Virginians’ voting rights

Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, and Democratic lawmakers had unsuccessfully carried legislation in past years to move the referendum forward. 
It finally passed the legislature two years in a row — as required by law to amend the constitution — before appearing on ballots this year. 
It’s “taken us a long time to get this on the ballot,” Sheba Williams, who’d worked with lawmakers on the legislation, said. “It’s very difficult to change the constitution.” 
But that also means it will be harder to undo it.
As a new voter, Seychell Williams said she wants to make sure others can enjoy the ability to weigh in on who represents them and shoring up their rights as citizens. 
“I’m going to be at every Election Day going forward,” she said.
Read more about Virginia’s three pending constitutional amendments here.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Secretary of education says Virginia will ‘move the achievement needle forward’
text:
Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith and Del. Jessica Anderson tour the Peake Childhood Center in Newport News on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration is focused on early education and college and career readiness, two of several academic priorities ahead of the state’s next legislative session.
Starting in January, the executive branch and lawmakers are expected to discuss a slate of K-12 topics, including school technology, expanding career and technical education and preparing children under five for kindergarten by closing the childcare affordability gap. 
At Wednesday’s Board of Education work session, Secretary of Education Jeffrey Smith shared the foundation of the administration’s K-12 education plans, urging the board to continue partnering with the secretariat to strengthen instruction and improve K-12 processes and systems.
“Nothing is more important than the core business of teaching and learning, and how we set young people up for success, and the fact of the matter that there are no shortcuts to excellence,” said Smith.
Board members spoke with Smith about how to apply the priorities in practice. 
President Mashea Ashton, appointed by former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, asked which initiatives the department should stop to avoid “initiative fatigue.” Smith said the focus must remain on teaching and learning, using evidence-based strategies to determine value. 
Board member Jamelle Wilson and Vice President Kimberly Bridges, both appointed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger, highlighted the need for wraparound services, or a network of support for students, to address rising anxiety rates and support student well-being. 
Questions also surfaced about how success will be measured. Smith said the agency will use student achievement indicators, including reading and math scores, attendance and overall student success outcomes.
Secretary of Education Jeffrey Smith addressing the Board of Education during an Oct. 28, 2026, work session at Reynolds Community College. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury).Board member William Robinson listens to a presentation from Secretary of Education Jeffrey Smith during the Board of Education's  Oct. 28, 2026, work session at Reynolds Community College. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)State lawmakers recognize Secretary of Education Jeffrey Smith during a press conference at the 2026 General Assembly session in Richmond. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury).
The agency’s final strategic plan, which mirrors the secretariat’s priorities, will be released next month. The board reviewed a draft at its work session on Wednesday.
Smith said the secretariat is working with the Department of Education on a draft budget proposal and legislative items. He also said the administration is prioritizing Early Childhood Care and Education, including preparing young children for kindergarten and making affordable options available to all.
Virginia currently lacks at least 140,000 child care slots needed to support working families. State leaders are considering three funding options to expand access, raise educator pay and help providers cover costs.
The most expensive option, costing $4.5 billion annually over the next 10 years, would cap families’ child care costs at 0% to 10% of income. The plan would serve an additional 240,000 children and reach 66% of working families.
Smith said his K-12 education policy priorities also focus on improving instructional quality, strengthening the educator workforce and ensuring that schools have the resources and support necessary to improve student outcomes. 
Key initiatives include expanding access to high-quality instructional materials, implementing evidence-based literacy instruction through tools called the Science of Reading, and advancing the Science of Math. 
Strategies to recruit and retain effective educators, strengthen wraparound services that support student well-being and readiness to learn and address barriers to academic achievement are also on the to-do list.
Additional priorities include expanding dual enrollment, career pathways and postsecondary opportunities to strengthen college and career readiness. 
On technology, education leaders support the safe, responsible integration of artificial intelligence and other technologies to enhance instruction and student learning. Smith’s approach to assessment and accountability emphasizes high academic expectations, school-level support and implementation of the latest School Performance and Support Framework. 
Reforming the education funding formula, which helps the state determine how much it needs to fund schools, rounded out the list of priorities. 
Lawmakers could partially replace the Standards of Quality formula by using student-based calculations for special education and English learner funding. Another option would be to fully replace the staffing-based formula with a new student-based formula.
Smith thanked the board for its contributions to K-12 education, emphasizing the importance of building on existing schools’ and school systems’ strengths rather than treating them as damaged. 
“Our schools and school systems, they’re not broken,” Smith said. “It’s how we build from those places of strength and ensure they have the resources, processes, and systems needed to focus on continuous improvement.”
He highlighted the need for continuous improvement, adequate resources, and effective processes and systems that support students and families.
Smith also stressed the importance of establishing durable systems that will outlast current leadership and sustain progress for future generations. These priorities align with the governor’s mission to “build a durable future with opportunity for all Virginians.”
“We’re going to move that achievement needle forward and make certain that, at the end of the day, young people can decide where they want to go and what they want to do,” Smith said.
Smith said the agency and secretariat reviewed more than 200 bills during the last legislative session and provided technical support on more than 100 education bills that passed into law. 
Lawmakers will convene in Richmond starting on Jan. 13 to discuss education legislation and other issues.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Chesterfield County school board race raises questions over candidates’ experience, social stances
text:
Political signage lined the driveway of North Courthouse Road Library, an early voting site in Chesterfield County, Va., on Saturday, Oct. 24. (Photo by Eliza Martin/MNS)CHESTERFIELD COUNTY, Va. – On a recent Saturday, volunteers from Chesterfield County’s Republican and Democratic parties spent the crisp autumn morning handing out yard signs, sample ballots and campaign flyers outside the North Courthouse Road Library, a space temporarily transformed into a political battleground. 
Two women, Christina Brady and Elizabeth Schultz, are facing off in a special election to represent the Clover Hill District seat on the county school board, which the former representative vacated last year after posting a controversial social media message following the shooting death of right-wing activist and media personality Charlie Kirk.
The board is composed of five members, each representing one district. The Clover Hill district includes 13 schools. The winner will serve the remainder of the term, which ends Dec. 31, 2027. 
Schultz warmly greeted the Republican volunteers outside the library who supported her race against Brady for the school board seat, one of more than 300 up for grabs across Virginia this November. 
“(School board members) are directly impacting the lives of students, teachers, school leaders, community stakeholders, everybody that’s invested in what’s going on in their local schools,” said Kimberly Bridges, a Virginia Board of Education member and education professor at Virginia Commonwealth University. “It’s an important role, but it’s often an overlooked role in elections.”  
Five miles from the library, the Brady campaign handed out canvassing assignments to volunteer groups at its headquarters. Settling into a couch, Brady recounted her family’s move to Chesterfield to provide her 3-year-old daughter a strong education. She said she’s been eyeing the school board seat since it was vacated. 
“I am committed to ensuring that Chesterfield County Public Schools continue to get better because I am going to be in that public school system for the next 15 years,” Brady said. “I’m directly impacted by every positive and every negative thing that happens.” 
Brady said the district needs to fully fund its school infrastructure, pointing to crumbling structures, mold and portable trailers serving as classrooms. Her other top issues include balancing classroom technology use and ensuring accessible resources for students, including 504 plans, individualized education programs and mental health support. 
This is Brady’s first time running for elected office. Her uncontested campaign took a turn in August, when her opponent joined the race just days before the filing deadline. 
Schultz — who previously served for eight years on the Fairfax County school board and worked as a U.S. Department of Education official and a Virginia Department of Education assistant state superintendent — said she was called back into politics, literally.  
Local Republicans phoned her on a Sunday morning, asking her to join the race. Glancing down at the gold crucifix around her neck, Schultz recalled her response: “I’ve got to go to Mass and I’ve got to pray about it.”
Ultimately, she saw the election as an opportunity to give back to the district from which her son recently graduated. If elected, Schultz said she will focus on parental rights, building maintenance and students’ privacy in locker rooms and bathrooms.
“I have the ability with the background and experience that I have to maybe lend something to the Chesterfield School Board that gave so much to us,” Schultz said. “I felt like I had a duty and so I responded.” 
Mahdi Dublin, a middle school administrator with children enrolled in the Clover Hill district, said he respected Schultz’s credentials. 
“As a lifelong educator, I’m not a big fan of people who are not familiar with public education coming in and making a whole lot of decisions that affect public education when they haven’t lived that life and haven’t walked that walk,” Dublin said. 
Schultz’s experience didn’t relieve other concerns for Cynthia Losen, a retired teacher and Brady campaign volunteer. 
“The other lady’s a nut,” Losen said, citing a now-deleted tweet featuring a 2017 photo of Schultz with Gavin McInnes, founder of far-right neo-fascist group the Proud Boys. 
The photo was taken at the “DeploraBall,” an event celebrating President Donald Trump’s first inauguration. Another of Schultz’s posts in 2017 mentioned McInnes and included “#proudboys.” Schultz has since deleted her account.
Elizabeth Schultz, who is running to represent the Clover Hill district on Chesterfield County Public Schools Board, posted this tweet Feb. 3, 2017, one of several now-deleted public posts referencing far-right neo-fascist group the Proud Boys. (Photo courtesy Twitter/@ThinkSchultz)
When asked about the posts, Schultz said looking back, she wonders whether she “should have posted things or not posted things.” 
Referring to the photo with McInnes, she said, “This was before he was involved in — or there was any other — things that surfaced.” 
Proud Boys members attended the 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville that left one woman dead, and “clashed with Black Lives Matter protestors across the country” after the death of George Floyd at the hands of police in 2020, George Washington University’s Program on Extremism reported. 
The group also participated in breaching the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 following former President Joe Biden’s election and Republican candidate Donald Trump’s loss, with several members convicted of seditious conspiracy for their actions that day. 
Outside the Clover Hill High School homecoming football game on Oct. 23, Jason Spoon handed out flyers for Shultz’s campaign. Spoon is the director of Speak Up! Chesterfield, a faith-based group advocating for parental rights in school systems, among other issues. 
While Spoon said he homeschools his own children, he praised Schultz’s state-level work regarding gender identity in schools. 
“She helped write some of the transgender policies keeping students who feel that they are a different gender out — if they’re biologically a male — keeping them out of a female space,” Spoon said. 
Inside the stadium, many parents said they weren’t familiar with either candidate. 
Suzy Juhase, a small-business owner and Clover Hill parent, hadn’t been following the race but said an ideal school board member would be open-minded, regardless of political affiliation. Her top concern is technology use, and she said she teaches her children to respect all gender identities. 
“Anything that has to do with the kids is important to me, because they’re the future,” Juhase said.
Virginia localities weigh 1% sales tax for school construction as voters decide on expansion

Bridges said even taxpayers without ties to schools will “feel the impact” of the school board’s work. She pointed out a 1% sales tax referendum on the ballot that would provide additional funding for school maintenance and construction, if voters approve. Whomever is elected will be “at the forefront” of allocating those dollars, she said. 
Races that receive less attention, including school board elections like the one in Chesterfield, often result in small victory margins, Bridges added. 
“Even in these lower turnout races, because they are lower turnout, every individual vote can really make a difference,” Bridges said. “A lot’s on the line for Chesterfield.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Super PAC makes late entry into CD2 race; incumbent deletes a social media video
text:
The homepage of Common Sense America PAC, a newly registered Maryland-based political action committee supporting Republican Victor Mellor against incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner. (Screenshot)U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner had a question for a newly formed Maryland super PAC that committed nearly $41,000 to support his Republican opponent in Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District race: Why are you trying to influence an election in a place you’ve never even visited?
The two-term Democratic incumbent put the question to the group’s treasurer himself, then posted a video of their conversation on social media Tuesday.
“This is a super PAC run by a guy who’s never been to Rhode Island, who doesn’t seem to know much about Rhode Island, but wants to try to tell us who we should elect to Congress,” Magaziner said in the video.
But the videos about Common Sense America PAC had been taken down from Magaziner’s social media pages as of Thursday. 
Campaign spokesperson Jess Vaughn told Rhode Island Current the posts were deleted “out of an abundance of caution” after reviewing the laws governing recorded calls. The super PAC’s treasurer, Hong Chuan Liang, said he didn’t know he was going to be part of campaign material.
Violating Maryland’s recording law can be charged as a felony, punishable by up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
“When he called me, he didn’t tell me whether he was recording,” Liang told Rhode Island Current in an interview Wednesday afternoon. “In Maryland, this is an all-party consent state.”
Magaziner made the call from Rhode Island, where state law generally allows someone to record a conversation with the consent of just one party — including the person recording it.
But interstate calls can raise questions about which state’s laws apply. Federal law generally permits recording a call with one party’s consent, but state courts have allowed the stricter state law to govern. 
Vaughn said the campaign reviewed the law and thinks the recording is legal. And, Magaziner is not letting the video’s deletion take away from his overall message about the outside group.
“Rhode Islanders should have no patience for an out-of-state super PAC supporting out-of-state candidate Vic Mellor’s campaign to be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s agenda in Congress,” he said in a statement to Rhode Island Current.
Mellor’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment on the Common Sense for America PAC. In posts on X Tuesday and Wednesday, Mellor defended the group’s donors and accused Magaziner of hypocrisy over his own campaign financing, pointing to outside spending in support of the Democrat and an $800,000 loan he made to his first congressional campaign in 2022.
Liang said he was grateful Magaziner took the video down, but criticized the congressman for disclosing the donors’ names, saying it was not something a politician should do.
“If you have big donors, millionaires, (it’s) a different story,” he said. “This is all working-class people.”
Who’s behind this super PAC?
Common Sense America PAC registered with the Federal Election Commission on Oct. 5. The group’s statement of organization lists a Rockville, Maryland, address in a business park that includes a mortgage brokerage and title company, just behind a community college.
The group reported $40,600 in independent expenditures exclusively to support Mellor on Oct. 21 and 22, including advertising expenditures involving Google, Roku, Paramount and Disney.
Liang, 63, described himself to a Current reporter as a nearly retired “old guy” whose role in the PAC is limited to ensuring compliance with federal regulations.
“I don’t own the PAC — I’m not the decision maker,” he said.
Liang previously served as treasurer of Common Sense Maryland, a super PAC registered at the same Rockville address in 2024. That group reported independent expenditures supporting Donald Trump’s reelection and opposing Democratic congressional candidate April McClain Delaney in Maryland.
Liang declined to identify who created Common Sense America PAC, saying only that some of its supporters came from communist countries who “enjoy the freedom of this country.”
Campaign finance filings show Common Sense America PAC raised $8,950 through Oct. 14, including $8,750 in itemized contributions from six people living in Maryland, Virginia and New York. 
One donor, Peiliang Cui, is a Virginia-based financial adviser who previously served as treasurer and director of Act 4 Greater America Corp. A 2021 IRS filing described that organization’s primary purpose as promoting “Christian foundation,” socially conservative and traditional values.
In December 2021, the Federal Election Commission upheld a $5,455 civil penalty against Cui  for filing the group’s 2020 year-end report late. The commission also sought clarification about large contributions and missing expenditure descriptions. 
Act 4 Greater America Corp. filed a termination report in July 2022.
Cui did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, left, and Republican challenger Vic Mellor exchange remarks during their first general election debate at WPRI 12’s East Providence studios on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Aaron Aguilar/WPRI 12)
Against socialism
Common Sense America PAC’s website offers broad statements about its political values, noting its dedication to “informed civic participation, strengthening public engagement in the democratic process, and promoting responsible government.” But the site offers little detail about its leadership or why they support Mellor’s candidacy.
Liang described Common Sense America as a small grassroots conservative group focused on Christianity and traditional values, law and order, and security. He said the super PAC also wants to remove LGBTQ-related content from books available to schoolchildren and strongly opposes socialism.
“We don’t want our country here to turn into that type of country,” Liang said. “We believe (Mellor) has the right voice, we believe he has the right background.”
The rise of the Democratic party’s leftmost wing formed a major concern this election cycle among Rhode Island’s conservatives, with socialism a topic repeatedly invoked by Mellor in televised debates for both the primary and the general election.
But Mellor’s own record includes a recent episode that complicates his presentation as a staunch anti-leftist: a trip to Cuba in which he met with the country’s leadership.
Mellor registered with the U.S. Justice Department as a foreign agent for work involving Cuba’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, according to a June filing. He said in a July 25 statement that he traveled to the communist-controlled island for humanitarian purposes and that a meeting with Cuban leadership developed during the trip.
Does this move the needle?
Polls show Magaziner will likely secure a third term as the 2nd Congressional District’s representative.
A survey published Oct. 20 by the Pell Center at Salve Regina University showed Magaziner with 52% support among likely voters, while 39% supported Mellor. Undecided voters comprised 7% of respondents.
The poll produced similar results to the WPRI/Emerson College poll released Oct. 13. In that poll, Magaziner led Mellor 55% to 39%.
“It’s not a winnable seat for Republicans,” Matt Ulricksen, an associate professor of political science at the Community College of Rhode Island, said.
The GOP last held the seat in 1991 when Claudine Schneider was succeeded by now-U.S. Sen. Jack Reed and the district has been represented by a Democrat ever since. Republicans saw their best chance in years to flip the seat in 2022, when longtime Democratic Rep. Jim Langevin’s retirement opened the race during a midterm election year that favored the party nationally. 
Former Cranston Mayor Allan Fung, who had twice run for governor, lost to Magaziner by about four percentage points even after outside groups poured millions of dollars in the race.
“Fung’s race is the high watermark for Republican candidates in this district,” Ulricksen said. “I would be shocked if Mellor gets anything close to that especially in a non-presidential year with Trump’s approval ratings underwater, like significantly underwater.”
Reporter Alexander Castro contributed to this story.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana health officials warn against amoeba infections from tap water
text:
Louisiana health officials are warning the public not to use tap water for nasal rinses or contact lenses after two serious amoebic infections have been reported this year. Although the patients reported using tap water for sinus irrigation, the state health department said it has not established tap water as the source of their infections. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Department of Health is urging the public not to use tap water for their sinuses or contact lenses following a fatal Acanthamoeba infection this year, one of 10 infections in the state reported since 2024. 
Health officials did not say when or where the infected person died. It’s one of two “serious” infections identified this year, both in patients with weakened immune systems. 
The other eight infections were cases of Acanthamoeba keratitis, an eye infection that can cause permanent vision loss. Seven infections involved people who wore contact lenses, and five people lost their sight permanently, according to the health department.
Both persons with serious infections reported using tap water in nasal irrigation systems, but the health department said tap water has not been established as the source of the Acanthamoeba. The microbe can also been found in garden and agricultural soil, freshwater bodies, swimming pools and indoor systems such as heating and air conditioning units, and humidifiers, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.    
A 2023 study cited in a CDC report found that non-keratitis Acanthamoeba cases are extremely rare, totaling fewer than 12 a year in the United States. But 82% of those cases were fatal.  
Acanthamoeba is distinct from Naegleria fowleri, more commonly known as the brain-eating amoeba. Naegleria is found most often in warm freshwater lakes, ponds, rivers and canals. 
Lillian Smart, an 8-year-old from Ruston, died in August after being infected with Naegleria, which health officials said she contracted from swimming in a North Louisiana lake. At least five deaths in Louisiana have been attributed to Naegleria infections since 2011. 
The health department’s advisory Thursday on Acanthamoeba inflections stressed the need for the public to use distilled, sanitary or previously boiled water in neti pots and other sinus rinsing devices as well as in continuous positive airway pressure machines for sleep apnea. 
Tap water is also not suitable to clean or store contact lenses, which should be removed before swimming, showering or using a hot tub, health officials said.  

“Although these infections are rare, they can have devastating consequences,” state epidemiologist Theresa Sokol said in a news release. 
Officials also stressed that drinking tap water does not put a person at risk for contracting Acanthamoeba infections.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Lierman seeks another term, Dunn just wants an ear in subdued comptroller’s race
text:
Comptroller Brooke Lierman invited women's advocates and laid-off federal workers to an Oct. 19, 2026, event to discuss a new report on how women fare in Maryland's economy. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Republican comptroller nominee Sonya Dunn acknowledges she’s got her work cut out for her in her bid to unseat Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D), the first woman to hold the office when she was elected in 2022.
Dunn, a first-time candidate with little name recognition, has just a fraction of the campaign funds raised by Lierman, a two-term member of the House of Delegates and the daughter of a prominent Maryland Democrat. And besides that, Dunn has to cope with what she calls “the scarlet R” — being a Republican candidate in a deep-blue state.
“It is hard running with the scarlet R behind my name — I call it the scarlet R on my chest,” Dunn said in a recent interview. “But I’m trying to let people know that when you meet one Republican, you don’t meet every Republican.”
For her part, Lierman — who beat former Harford County Executive Barry Glassman, a Republican, by about 23 percentage points in 2022 — is looking ahead to expanding on the changes she’s made to the office in her first four years, including updates to the decades-old computer systems that Maryland uses to collect taxes and handle its payroll.
With a second term, she’s hoping to think bigger, she said.
“Now, we have a platform to jump off of and build from in my next term, so that we can really do big things, be imaginative, creative about how we can really make government work better for people and small businesses,” Lierman said.
Sonya Dunn, the Republican nominee for Maryland comptroller, speaks at the Maryland Association of Counties conference in August. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)
Dunn, who describes herself as a moderate, fiscal conservative, hopes Maryland voters can see past the GOP. She also hopes that her background in IT services will make her a compelling alternative to Lierman, given the technological challenges faced by the comptroller’s office.
Dunn runs a technology and communications consulting company named JEMH Enterprises — for the first initial of each of her four children’s names.
“We can do better, Maryland,” Dunn said. “And I feel that I can bring what Maryland needs, especially from a technology standpoint in operations management, to get that on the right track.”
Lierman acknowledges that updating the technology that powers the comptroller’s office has been an arduous four-year battle. She brought on a chief information officer and other staff members, who she says have completed more than 100 information technology modernization projects in the past three years.
“That includes everything from rebuilding the fiber under our building that was so old it was breaking and we were losing connectivity, to moving 4 billion records from our old tax system to our new tax system,” Lierman said.
In early September, the state launched an upgraded Maryland Tax Connect website, which for the first time allowed individual taxpayers — not just businesses — to go online to file tax returns, make payments and check the status of their refunds. It replaced several internal systems that had been used for the better part of three decades.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Dunn points to complaints she’s heard from individuals and tax professionals with Tax Connect gripes, including about desired features that the system doesn’t offer. But Lierman argues she’s the perfect person to guide any continued work on the system.
“Now that we’re in that new system, we’ll be able to constantly improve that system and make it easier to use and simpler to use,” Lierman said.
Another focus for her presumptive second term will be reaching more low-income Marylanders with word that they are eligible to file for the “Earned Income Tax Credit,” which returns up to $4,000 per year to eligible filers.
Under Lierman, the percentage of eligible Marylanders to actually apply for the credit has been slowly climbing, from 84.2% in 2023 to 86% in 2026.
“The Earned Income Tax Credit is one of the most effective anti-poverty tools that the government has. It’s one of the few tools that actually helps with upward economic mobility in America today,” Lierman said. “We’ve got to make sure, though, that it is actually reaching the people who need it.”
Lierman said she’ll also be working to improve the state’s collection and auditing systems, to ensure that unpaid taxes are collected — especially as the state faces budget shortfall after budget shortfall.
In September, an audit performed for the legislature pointed to problems with collecting unpaid taxes, arguing that the comptroller’s office could be using tactics such as wage garnishments more frequently to obtain owed funds.
Campaign signs during early voting for Republican comptroller nominee Sonya Dunn and Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D). (Photo by William J. Ford/Marylander Matters)
The audit identified 1,900 individuals with balances totaling $25.5 million who collectively earned $280.7 million during 2024 and 2025, but were not subject to wage garnishments.
Between fiscal year 2022 and 2025, the outstanding individual taxes owed to Maryland increased from just over $1 billion to $1.58 billion, according to the audit.
Lierman contends that, early in her tenure, she determined that her office needed more personnel, and better technology, to perform audits to uncover unpaid taxes. She argues that the office has come a long way.
These days, the comptroller’s office can scrape publicly available data to locate Airbnb owners, NFT sellers and others who aren’t reporting all of their income to the state government.
“We have done some of our first cryptocurrency capital gains audits in the agency’s history,” Lierman said. “We have really modernized our ability to audit.”
On the other hand, Lierman says she “fundamentally disagree[s]” with the audit’s contention that the office should be garnishing wages more frequently. The state has a duty to collect what is owed, Lierman says, but also to make sure that consequential enforcement actions against individuals and businesses are warranted.
Her office has prioritized other enforcement tools, like instituting payment plans and referring delinquent taxpayers to the Motor Vehicle Administration so they face administrative penalties, like being unable to renew their driver’s license.
“Our goal is compliance, not punishment,” she said. “We should not be in the business of bankrupting people. We should be in the business of helping make sure that they can stay open so they can pay what they owe.”

title: Trustees take legal action as controversy over changes to MSU Board Code of Ethics continues
text:
Michigan State University Trustees Mike Balow and Rema Vassar. June 3, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvancePolicy changes intended to tamp down infighting within the Michigan State University Board of Trustees are now drawing legal scrutiny as two of its members have filed complaints in federal court seeking to halt the enforcement of the board’s updated Code of Ethics and Conduct. 
MSU Trustee Mike Balow on Wednesday filed a lawsuit against Board Chair Brianna Scott and Stefan Fletcher, the board’s secretary and chief of staff, arguing that revisions to the Board of Trustees code of conduct unlawfully restrict trustee speech. 
In May, the Board of Trustees voted 5-3 to add provisions barring trustees from divulging confidential information to unauthorized individuals before that information is made public and instructing them to “act ethically and not provide inaccurate, misleading, or false information concerning the university.”
The new provisions also bar trustees from representing their personal opinions as that of the university, and state that trustees will not undermine decisions made by the majority of the board.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
After the revisions were approved, trustees were required to sign a statement of acknowledgement, agreeing to follow the code of conduct’s terms. Trustees who did not sign were warned they could face sanctions including public censure, loss of privileges such as complimentary access to university sporting events and removal from any leadership position on the board.
Two trustees refused to sign: Balow and Trustee Rema Vassar. They were later censured as a result.
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a civil liberties group focused on free speech issues, sent a letter to the university in May raising concerns about the revisions while offering itself as a resource to revise the Code of Ethics and ensure its compliance with the First Amendment. 
The group now represents Balow in his lawsuit against Scott and Fletcher.
“The people of Michigan elected Michael to be a watchdog, not a lapdog,” Greg Greubel, a senior attorney at FIRE said in a statement. “The freedom to voice opposition strengthens the university by encouraging ideas to be challenged and solutions to be worked out.”
According to the complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan, Scott and Fletcher have “cut Balow off from the ceremonial gatherings, conferences, sporting events, and other occasions at which trustees ordinarily interact with students, faculty, alumni, donors, and members of the public” due to his refusal to sign the statement agreeing to the revised code of ethics.
Michigan State University Trustees Rema Vassar and Mike Balow. June 3, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Balow’s attorneys argue that “Each day these restrictions remain in place, Balow loses opportunities to interact with the individuals he was elected to represent.”
“Asking hard questions and demanding honest answers is the only path to solid governance,” Balow said in a statement. “Healthy friction leads to accountability and transparency that boards often talk about, but don’t always deliver. It’s not easy, but it’s necessary.”
Last week, Vassar filed her own lawsuit against Scott, Fletcher, the Board of Trustees, MSU President Kevin Guskiewicz, Vice President for Legal Affairs and General Counsel Brian Quinn, and former trustees Dan Kelly and Dianne Byrum.
Vassar, who was previously investigated for misconduct alongside Trustee Dennis Denno, argued university officials had orchestrated a campaign of intentional discrimination and retaliation against her as the first Black woman to chair the board of trustees. 
Michigan State University Board of Trustees Chair Rema Vassar speaks to media after an MSU Board of Trustees meeting on Feb. 2, 2024. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)
As part of the suit, she has requested the board cease enforcing its requirements for trustees to sign a statement of acknowledgment regarding the Code of Ethics.
Amber McCann, a spokesperson for the university, told Michigan Advance the university would address Vassar’s suit through the appropriate legal channels. 
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Scott, who is seeking reelection for another 8-year term, called Balow’s lawsuit “petty and frivolous” and that she looked forward to seeking sanctions.
“The purpose of the Code of Ethics and Conduct is to help ensure the Board can effectively govern in service to students, faculty, staff, parents, research partners, taxpayers and the broader public,” Scott said. “The code does not limit speech or restrict members of governing boards from raising concerns, providing oversight or questioning decisions; instead, it establishes good and commonsense governance practices.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Travel reports provide needed window of transparency but could be improved
text:
Reports covering July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2026, showed how often top state officials are traveling and how much they are spending. (Getty Images)For the second year, statewide elected officials and top agency leaders in Gov. Mike Braun’s administration filed reports detailing their travel in the past year.
We tallied up the days and cost of the trips and overall it was minor — about $132,000. Which is just as important as if it had been $1.3 million. It shows restraint and responsibility on their behalf.
Either way, the point is transparency and I applaud lawmakers for instituting these reports in 2025.
All the officials regularly travel in-state to various constituent events, meetings and conferences. So, we focused more directly on out-of-state travel. Here are some of the findings we reported:
A sample of Comptroller Elise Nieshalla’s travel report. (Screenshot)
– Braun hardly leaves the state. He had only one reported trip outside Indiana and it was paid by campaign dollars because he was attending a Republican Governors Association meeting in Washington, D.C.
– Attorney General Todd Rokita goes to the nation’s capital a lot. He listed seven trips to Washington, D.C. in a year’s time. Two visits listed no state expenses, while the other five totaled nearly $3,400.
– Energy and Natural Resources Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski was high on the list for spending at about $25,000. She accounted for about 62% of the $40,460 in expenses listed by Braun’s cabinet. Her largest expense was $8,283.97 for an April 20-May 1 visit to Seoul and Busan in South Korea.
– Education Secretary Katie Jenner reported substantially less spending — $5,815.78 — but listed more dated travel-related events than any other cabinet secretary. Her report contained 22 out-of-state activities. Those out-of-state entries covered 41 distinct calendar dates, including 39 weekdays.
I do think there is room for improvement in this process, though, starting with a uniform spreadsheet. Each individual approaches the report differently and there in no consistency in format or information.
Some simply list the city they went to with no accompanying information. I went through social media posts to try to create some context to the entries. That’s how we tied Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith’s D.C. trip to a White House Christmas party and several of Rokita’s trips to events involving transgender topics.
A sample of Attorney General Todd Rokita’s travel report. (Screenshot)
I understand some discretion is needed in these, but a basic explanation is necessary. It could say the person spoke at a community’s Rotary meeting, attended a business opening, met with constituents etc.
Some officials also listed trips paid for by sponsoring organizations without disclosing those amounts or sometimes who paid. That information is very important given the quid-pro-quo possibilities in government.
Management and Budget Secretary Lisa Hershman listed 37 travel entries, including a Texas meeting, but supplied no numeric expenses. Business Affairs Secretary Mike Speedy likewise listed no numeric costs for 19 travel entries.
I’d like to give a shout out to Comptroller Elise Nieshalla for the best report. She provided a specific location, dates, purpose, expenses and fund for every single item. That included meeting with specific mayors, a tour of the CANDLES Holocaust museum, recording a podcast, attending an Association of Indiana Counties conference and stopping at the Seymour Tribune.
Everyone should be more like Elise.
